No; the collective rule can violate IIA even when each individual ranking is transitive.
Yes; adding an alternative necessarily changes every pairwise preference.
No; IIA places no restriction on a social ranking rule.

stem: In this setting, every voter ranks A above B but the social rule ranks B above A. Which condition fails?
choices: Independence of irrelevant alternatives only
Transitivity of each voter's preferences
Pareto efficiency or unanimity
The median voter assumption

stem: A policy analyst notes that a student says Arrow proves democracy is useless. What is the best correction?
choices: The theorem proves dictatorship is ethically best
It applies only to market prices
It guarantees majority rankings are transitive
The theorem identifies a tradeoff among axioms; real institutions choose which conditions to relax

stem: A classroom example assumes that a voting rule must convert rankings over at least three alternatives into a social ranking while satisfying unrestricted domain, Pareto efficiency, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and nondictatorship. What does Arrow's theorem imply?
choices: No rank-order rule can satisfy all of those conditions for every possible preference profile
Majority rule always satisfies them
A dictator is required by moral law
Voting is impossible with two alternatives

stem: A designer claims that Arrow’s theorem proves no useful election rule can exist. Which correction best states the limitation of that claim?
choices: The theorem guarantees all voting rules satisfy every fairness condition.
The theorem concerns satisfying a specified set of conditions together; a rule can remain useful while relaxing a condition.
The theorem applies only when there are exactly two alternatives.
The theorem says individual preferences cannot be transitive.

stem: Suppose that one-third ranks A>B>C, one-third B>C>A, and one-third C>A>B. What happens under pairwise majority voting?
choices: A is a Condorcet winner
Every pair ties
A cycle can occur: A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A
The median option always wins

stem: An economist observes that pairwise social preferences are A>B, B>C, and C>A. What is this called?
choices: A dominant strategy equilibrium
Adverse selection
A Lorenz ordering
A Condorcet cycle

stem: Consider a case in which an agenda setter chooses which pairwise vote occurs last when preferences cycle. Why can sequence matter?
choices: Different agendas can produce different final winners
Cycles guarantee the same winner
Every voter becomes indifferent
The agenda removes majority rule

stem: In this setting, all voters have single-peaked preferences along one policy line. What is the likely effect on majority cycles?
choices: It guarantees Arrow's axioms for every domain
The restriction helps prevent cycles and supports a stable median outcome
It creates more multidimensional cycling
It makes preferences intransitive individually

stem: A policy analyst notes that one-third ranks A>B>C, one-third B>C>A, and one-third C>A>B. What happens under pairwise majority voting?
choices: A is a Condorcet winner
Every pair ties
A cycle can occur: A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A
The median option always wins

stem: Three equal-sized groups rank A>B>C, B>C>A and C>A>B. Which option wins a pairwise contest between A and B?
choices: B by two groups to one
A unanimously
They tie
A by two groups to one

stem: Evidence indicates that an agenda setter chooses which pairwise vote occurs last when preferences cycle. Why can sequence matter?
choices: Different agendas can produce different final winners
Cycles guarantee the same winner
Every voter becomes indifferent
The agenda removes majority rule

stem: Suppose that all voters have single-peaked preferences along one policy line. What is the likely effect on majority cycles?
choices: It guarantees Arrow's axioms for every domain
The restriction helps prevent cycles and supports a stable median outcome
It creates more multidimensional cycling
It makes preferences intransitive individually

choices: A is a Condorcet winner
Every pair ties
A cycle can occur: A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A
The median option always wins

stem: Three equal-sized groups rank A>B>C, B>C>A and C>A>B. Under sequential pairwise voting with sincere votes, compare agenda 1 (A versus B, then the winner versus C) with agenda 2 (B versus C, then the winner versus A).
choices: Both agendas select A.
Agenda 1 selects B; agenda 2 selects C.
Both agendas select C.
Agenda 1 selects C; agenda 2 selects A.

stem: In this setting, an agenda setter chooses which pairwise vote occurs last when preferences cycle. Why can sequence matter?
choices: Different agendas can produce different final winners
Cycles guarantee the same winner
Every voter becomes indifferent
The agenda removes majority rule

choices: It guarantees Arrow's axioms for every domain
The restriction helps prevent cycles and supports a stable median outcome
It creates more multidimensional cycling
It makes preferences intransitive individually

stem: Suppose that voters have single-peaked preferences over one tax-rate line and choose by majority rule. Which position is pivotal?
choices: The mean income regardless of voting
The most extreme voter's ideal point
The median voter's ideal point
A randomly chosen policy

stem: An economist observes that two office-seeking candidates care only about winning and voters choose the closer one on a single policy dimension. What tendency follows?
choices: Both move toward opposite extremes
Policy location becomes irrelevant
The candidate at the mean always loses
Both candidates have an incentive to move toward the median voter

stem: Consider a case in which policy is multidimensional and voters' preferences are not single-peaked. Can median-voter convergence be assumed?
choices: No; the theorem's key assumptions may fail
Yes, it holds under every preference domain
Yes, because mean and median are identical
No, because majority voting is impossible

stem: In this setting, the decisive voter lies at the 50th percentile of ordered ideal points. Why is this voter called median?
choices: The voter has average income
Half the ideal points lie on each side
The voter is indifferent among all policies
The voter dictates outcomes without elections

stem: Five voters have single-peaked preferences over one spending level, with ideal points 1, 3, 4, 8 and 10. Which level is the median ideal point and defeats any alternative in pairwise majority voting under these assumptions?

choices: The arithmetic median on the first dimension must still win every multidimensional comparison.
Adding a dimension guarantees unanimous agreement.
The original theorem’s assumptions no longer suffice to guarantee a median policy winner.

stem: The Signal Breaker opens the first gate: 'Every choice leaves something behind.' What is a tradeoff?
choices: Giving up one thing to get something else
A tax placed on buyers
A legal maximum price
A measure of total national output

stem: A student works an extra shift instead of studying for an economics exam. What is part of the opportunity cost of working?
choices: Only the wage earned from working
The value of the lost study time
Only the price of the textbook
The total GDP of the economy

stem: A bookstore considers staying open one more hour. The hour adds $240 in sales margin and $170 in staffing and utility cost. Which comparison matters?
choices: The $240 added benefit versus the $170 added cost
Total yearly sales versus total yearly operating and staffing cost
Average hourly sales versus the original opening expense
Past rent payments versus today’s entire revenue

stem: A business can earn $900 from one more project, but completing it costs $650. What should it do?
choices: Complete it because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost
Reject the project because any cost is bad
Ignore the extra revenue
Complete the project only if GDP rises

stem: The Signal Breaker shows a simplified diagram of households, firms, markets, and money flows. Why do economists use models like this?
choices: To include every detail of the real economy
To eliminate scarcity
To simplify reality and focus on key relationships
To avoid making assumptions

stem: The Signal Breaker says: 'Prices guide resources without a central commander.' What is this describing?
choices: A price ceiling
A GDP deflator
A discouraged worker
Market allocation

stem: The Signal Breaker asks: 'Which statement is positive?'
choices: Investment spending raises GDP, other things equal
The government should spend more
GDP is the fairest possible measure
Every country should maximize GDP at all costs

stem: In the circular-flow model, households usually provide which resource to firms?
choices: Final goods and services
Factors of production
Price ceilings
GDP deflators

stem: The Signal Breaker asks which question is macroeconomic.
choices: How many workers should one coffee shop hire?
How should one consumer spend a gift card?
How fast is the nation's GDP growing?
How should one firm price one sandwich?

stem: The Signal Breaker's final gate asks: which pairing is correct?
choices: GDP growth is micro; one firm's hiring decision is macro
Both are always micro
Both are always normative
GDP growth is macro; one firm's hiring decision is micro

stem: In a city housing market, a binding rent ceiling leaves 80,000 units demanded but only 52,000 supplied. Tenants who secure units save $300 each, while 28,000 households are rationed out. Which conclusion best captures the welfare tradeoff?
choices: The ceiling creates winners and losers
All renters benefit because the legal price is lower
Landlords benefit because quantity supplied rises
The market clears because the legal price is lower

stem: Suppose a city simultaneously subsidizes new apartment construction and caps rent below equilibrium. What combined market effect is most plausible?
choices: The subsidy makes the ceiling irrelevant in all cases
A binding ceiling can still ration supply
The ceiling shifts demand left and eliminates scarcity
The policy must create a surplus because supply increases

stem: A tax on luxury goods sharply reduces sales, and the government collects much less revenue than expected. What most likely explains the disappointing revenue?
choices: The tax must be too small to matter
The burden must fall entirely on buyers
Elastic participants avoid the taxed exchange
A tax always increases total revenue

stem: A binding minimum wage raises pay for workers who keep jobs but reduces hiring for low-skill labor. What is the strongest policy interpretation?
choices: The policy eliminates scarcity in labor markets
The policy guarantees higher employment and higher wages for all workers
The policy only changes CPI and has no employment effects
The policy creates a tradeoff between higher wages for some and job loss for others

stem: A city imposes rent control below equilibrium. Rent is lower for some tenants, but apartments become scarce and quality declines. Which chain is best?
choices: Binding ceiling → shortage → rationing and weaker maintenance
Binding floor → surplus → higher apartment quality
Tax wedge → higher seller revenue → no shortage
CPI bias → labor force exit → real wage growth

stem: A price ceiling is imposed during an inflation spike. Official prices stop rising, but buyers wait longer and pay side fees. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Inflation is fully eliminated because the listed price cannot rise
The posted price is capped, but the full economic cost to buyers may still rise.
The good becomes less scarce because the posted price is lower.
The CPI must perfectly capture waiting time

stem: A tax is placed on a good with very inelastic demand and elastic supply. Which outcome is most likely?
choices: Sellers bear most of the burden and quantity rises
Buyers and sellers split the burden exactly equally by law
Buyers bear most of the burden and quantity falls relatively little
The tax has no effect because supply is elastic

stem: A tax on sellers shifts supply upward, raises the price buyers pay, lowers the price sellers receive, and reduces quantity. What is the best overall description?
choices: The tax creates a price floor and expands the market
The tax only affects sellers because they mail the check
The tax eliminates deadweight loss
The tax creates a wedge and shrinks the market

stem: The Market Marshal asks why a tax on buyers and an equal tax on sellers lead to similar market outcomes. What is the best answer?
choices: Both create the same wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive
Only seller taxes reduce quantity
Only buyer taxes change demand
The legal taxpayer always bears the full burden

stem: Refer to the PPF graph. A proposal values each extra unit of X at 2 units of Y. Comparing the average tradeoff over A to B and D to E, which movement passes that benefit-cost test?
choices: A to B passes; D to E fails
Both pass because each ends on the frontier
D to E passes; A to B fails
Neither passes because every frontier movement sacrifices Y

stem: After a binding rent ceiling is imposed, some landlords move units into unregulated short-term rentals. Which lesson about price controls follows?
choices: A policy can change incentives and reduce quantity supplied in the regulated market
A ceiling increases quantity supplied because landlords must meet the stronger demand at the lower price.
A ceiling eliminates opportunity cost for landlords
A ceiling is nonbinding if landlords find loopholes

stem: Suppose an equal per-unit tax could legally be collected from either buyers or sellers. In the standard supply-demand model, why is the equilibrium incidence similar either way?
choices: Only a buyer tax reduces quantity because it directly affects demand.
Either tax creates the same wedge between buyer price and seller price
Only seller taxes raise prices
The tax disappears if buyers legally pay it

stem: A company pays bonuses for speed. Output rises, but quality complaints increase. What does this show?
choices: Incentives do not affect workers because quality is separate from the bonus.
Marginal analysis requires ignoring quality
Incentives work, but poorly designed incentives can distort behavior
The policy created a price ceiling

stem: A transit policy cuts bus fares and initially boosts ridership, but crowding later pushes some passengers back to cars. What broader lesson about incentives and feedback effects is strongest?
choices: Lower prices always increase welfare for every rider
Crowding proves the law of demand is false
The bus market has no scarcity because fares fell
Policy changes incentives, but secondary effects can offset part of the intended response

stem: A price-ceiling model predicts a shortage. In practice, the city also sees black markets, quality cuts, and favoritism. What does that comparison reveal about economic models?
choices: The model captures the core shortage logic, while real-world institutions shape how the shortage appears
The model is useless because it did not list every consequence
The model proves black markets cannot happen because the legal price is fixed.
The model becomes normative once real examples are added

stem: At a $12 equilibrium wage, firms hire 1,000 workers and 1,000 workers want jobs. A $16 minimum wage leads firms to demand 850 workers while 1,250 workers want jobs. Prices then rise 20%. Which interpretation is strongest?
choices: The nominal wage floor creates a 250-worker shortage, and inflation raises the real wage further
The nominal wage floor creates a 400-worker surplus, but the real value of the $16 wage is partly eroded by inflation
The nominal wage floor creates no unemployment because 1,250 workers want jobs
The nominal wage floor creates a 150-worker surplus because employment falls from 1,000 to 850

stem: A binding minimum wage raises labor costs in restaurants. Restaurants hire fewer low-skill workers and raise menu prices. Which chain best synthesizes the effect?
choices: Price ceiling in labor market → labor shortage → lower production costs → lower CPI
Tax wedge in output market → more labor demanded → lower unemployment
Price floor in labor market → lower labor demanded → higher production costs → higher output prices
Substitution bias → higher labor productivity → no job loss

stem: The Market Marshal says: 'This policy improves pay for some workers, worsens access to jobs for others, and may raise consumer prices.' Which policy is most likely being described?
choices: A nonbinding price ceiling above equilibrium
A decrease in CPI caused by quality improvements
A tax cut on sellers in a competitive market
A binding minimum wage above equilibrium

stem: During a supply shock, equilibrium rent would rise to $1,400, but a city caps rent at $1,000. Quantity demanded is 70,000 units and quantity supplied is 45,000 units. Tenants also spend more time searching. What is the best answer?
choices: There is a 25,000-unit shortage, and the full economic cost includes nonmoney costs like search time
There is a 25,000-unit surplus, and the full economic cost falls to exactly $1,000
There is a 45,000-unit shortage, and search time is counted perfectly in CPI
There is no shortage because the legal rent is lower

stem: A government caps gasoline prices below equilibrium during an oil shock. Official gasoline prices stop rising, but stations run out, drivers wait in long lines, and black-market resale appears. What is the deepest problem with saying inflation was solved?
choices: Inflation is solved because CPI captures all waiting costs perfectly
A binding cap shifts scarcity into nonprice rationing
The market has a surplus because buyers want more gas
The price ceiling shifts supply right by lowering the posted price

stem: A binding price ceiling causes landlords to reduce maintenance. Rent is cheaper for lucky tenants, but housing quality falls. Which pair of concepts best explains these effects?
choices: Tax incidence and real interest rates
Catch-up growth and discouraged workers
Price control incentives and CPI quality-measurement limits
GDP final-goods accounting and nominal wages

stem: A $4 tax is placed on a good. After adjustment, buyers pay $2.75 more and sellers receive $1.25 less. Which conclusion is best?
choices: Sellers bear more of the burden, so supply is likely less elastic than demand
Buyers and sellers split the burden equally because the tax is $4
The legal taxpayer must be the buyer because buyers pay $2.75 more
Buyers bear more of the burden, so demand is likely less elastic than supply

stem: A tax reduces quantity only slightly but raises the buyer price substantially. Which market condition best explains this?
choices: Demand is relatively inelastic, so buyers keep purchasing despite the higher price
Demand is relatively elastic, so buyers leave the market completely
Supply is perfectly elastic, so sellers bear the full burden
The tax must be legally assigned to buyers

stem: The Market Marshal compares two taxes. Tax A is on insulin with very inelastic demand. Tax B is on restaurant meals with more elastic demand. Which tax likely creates less quantity reduction but places more burden on buyers?
choices: Tax B, because restaurant meals are easier to avoid
Tax A, because insulin demand is less elastic
Both taxes have identical effects because all taxes create wedges
Neither tax affects quantity if sellers legally pay it

stem: A supply shock raises food prices. The government caps prices below equilibrium. Official prices rise less, but shortages emerge, quality falls, and households spend more time searching. What is the best synthesis?
choices: The ceiling eliminates inflation and improves allocation because prices are lower
The ceiling suppresses posted prices but worsens allocation and hides part of the full cost of scarcity
The ceiling creates a surplus because the lower price encourages producers to supply more.
The ceiling shifts demand left because consumers want more food

stem: A government raises the minimum wage during high inflation. Nominal wages rise for workers who keep jobs, firms reduce low-skill hiring, and consumer prices rise in labor-intensive sectors. Which answer best captures the whole chain?
choices: The policy guarantees real wage growth and higher employment because legal wages increased
The policy has no price effect because only labor markets change
Some gain higher pay; others lose jobs; real gains depend on prices
The policy lowers unemployment because more workers want jobs at the higher wage

stem: The Market Marshal presents a final scenario: unemployment falls, CPI inflation slows because price ceilings cap posted prices, real wages appear stable, and productivity is flat. Which warning is most important?
choices: The economy is clearly stronger because unemployment and CPI inflation both fell
Stable real wages prove productivity increased because purchasing power did not fall.
Price ceilings improve welfare whenever they slow posted-price inflation.
The indicators may be distorted by labor-force exits, hidden price-control costs, and lack of productivity growth

stem: An economist shows a PPF shifting outward after years of investment in capital and technology. What is the best interpretation?
choices: The economy's productive capacity has increased
The economy moved inside the PPF because resources are idle
The CPI basket became fixed
A tax wedge disappeared

stem: A minimum wage is raised above the equilibrium wage for low-skill labor. What is the expected market result?
choices: A shortage of labor, meaning firms cannot find enough workers
No change because price floors never bind
An automatic increase in productivity
A surplus of labor, meaning more workers want jobs than firms want to hire

stem: At $10 per hour, firms hire 1,000 workers and 1,000 workers want jobs. At a $15 minimum wage, firms want 800 workers and 1,200 workers want jobs. What is the labor surplus?
choices: 400 workers
200 workers
800 workers
1,200 workers

stem: Why can a minimum wage help some workers while hurting others?
choices: All workers are guaranteed jobs at the higher wage
Workers who keep jobs earn more, but some workers may be priced out of employment
Firms hire more workers because labor is now more expensive
The CPI stops measuring prices

stem: A tax is imposed on sellers. Buyers pay a higher price, sellers receive a lower price, and fewer units are sold. What concept ties these effects together?
choices: A price floor that creates a labor surplus
A tax wedge that shrinks the market
Substitution bias in the CPI
Discouraged-worker measurement

stem: A tax is legally imposed on buyers instead of sellers. What does tax-incidence analysis imply?
choices: Buyers always bear 100% of the burden
Legal assignment alone does not determine the burden
Sellers always bear 100% of the burden
The tax disappears from the market

stem: Demand is less elastic than supply. Which side bears more of a per-unit tax?
choices: Sellers bear more because buyers can easily leave
The government bears the burden
No one bears the burden because taxes do not affect prices
Buyers bear more because they respond less to the price change

stem: An economist observes that gasoline prices rise after a supply disruption. A city responds with a binding price ceiling. What is the most likely result?
choices: A surplus because suppliers produce more at the lower price
No effect because ceilings above equilibrium are always binding
A shortage because the legal price is held below the market-clearing price
Higher productivity because gasoline is cheaper

stem: A storm reduces supply while demand stays the same. Before any price control, what happens in the market?
choices: Equilibrium price falls and equilibrium quantity rises
Both price and quantity rise
Equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity falls
Both price and quantity fall

stem: A binding price ceiling holds the posted price below equilibrium. What happens to the underlying scarcity?
choices: Scarcity disappears when prices are legally capped
All consumers get more of the good
Shortages cause waiting, side markets, favoritism, or lower quality
The CPI cannot measure any price change

stem: An economist says a country spends more on education and infrastructure today to raise future productivity. What core economic idea is present?
choices: A guarantee that inflation becomes zero
A binding price ceiling in labor markets
A discouraged-worker effect
Current resources versus future capacity

stem: A maximum legal price is binding only when it is set:
choices: Below equilibrium price
Above equilibrium price
Exactly at zero
Above quantity supplied

stem: A binding price ceiling usually creates:
choices: A shortage
A surplus
A tax wedge
An outward PPF shift

stem: A rent ceiling is set at $900 when equilibrium rent is $1,300. What happens?
choices: The ceiling is binding and creates a shortage
The ceiling is nonbinding and has no effect
The ceiling creates a surplus
The ceiling shifts supply right

stem: A legal maximum price is above equilibrium. Why is it nonbinding?
choices: The market price remains below the legal maximum
All ceilings create shortages
Sellers must charge the maximum
Demand must fall to zero

stem: A legal maximum below equilibrium and a legal minimum above equilibrium have what in common?
choices: Both are binding price controls
Both create market equilibrium
Both create tax wedges
Both increase quantity traded

stem: Which policy-price pairing is nonbinding?
choices: A price ceiling above equilibrium
A price ceiling below equilibrium
A price floor above equilibrium
A rent ceiling below market rent

stem: A minimum legal price is binding only when it is set:
choices: Above equilibrium price
Below equilibrium price
Exactly at zero
Below quantity demanded

stem: A binding price floor usually creates:
choices: A surplus
A shortage
A tax wedge
A demand increase

stem: A minimum wage is set at $15 when equilibrium wage is $11. What happens?
choices: The floor is binding and creates a labor surplus
The floor is nonbinding and has no effect
The floor creates a labor shortage
The floor shifts labor demand right

stem: A legal minimum price is below equilibrium. Why is it nonbinding?
choices: The market price remains above the legal minimum
All floors create surpluses
Buyers must pay the lowest possible price
Supply must fall to zero

stem: At a binding price ceiling, Qd = 90 and Qs = 60. What is the shortage?
choices: 30 units
60 units
90 units
150 units

stem: At a binding ceiling, buyers want 120 units and sellers offer 75 units. What happens?
choices: A shortage of 45 units
A surplus of 45 units
A shortage of 195 units
No shortage

stem: A rental schedule lists monthly rent, apartments wanted and apartments offered: $800: 120, 60; $1,000: 100, 80; $1,200: 90, 90. An enforced rent ceiling is $1,000. What shortage follows?
choices: 20 apartments
80 apartments
180 apartments
0 apartments

stem: At a binding cap on storage-unit rents, 150 customers each want one unit and owners offer 110 units. All offered units are rented. A manager reports, "The shortage is 110 units because that is how many were rented." Which correction is accurate?
choices: 40 units are unfilled demand; 110 units are rented.
110 units are unfilled demand; 40 units are rented.
40 units are excess supply; 110 units are rented.
260 units are unfilled demand; 110 units are rented.

stem: A price-taking firm is one that:
choices: Cannot individually influence the market price
Sets any price it wants
Faces no competitors
Always earns zero profit

stem: Which definition best captures an economic incentive?
choices: Something that changes the costs or benefits of an action
A rule that removes meaningful choice from an action
The behavior observed after a policy is introduced
A market price recorded before a decision is made

stem: A decision should continue when:
choices: Marginal benefit is at least marginal cost
Total cost is zero
Average cost is falling
Demand is perfectly elastic

stem: A market failure occurs when:
choices: Market outcomes do not efficiently allocate resources
Every buyer and seller agrees on price
Demand slopes downward
A firm earns profit

stem: In a market system, prices help allocate resources by:
choices: Eliminating all tradeoffs
Coordinating buyers' and sellers' decisions
Fixing output at one level
Replacing incentives

stem: The economist's role in policy analysis is primarily to:
choices: Clarify likely tradeoffs and consequences
Choose everyone's values
Guarantee a policy works
Eliminate scarcity

stem: A higher market price normally signals producers to:
choices: Increase quantity supplied
Decrease quantity supplied
Demand less automatically
Ignore the market

stem: Whether a tax is legally collected from buyers or sellers, its economic burden depends mainly on:
choices: Relative elasticities
Which side writes the check
The number of firms only
The tax's label

stem: Voluntary trade can benefit both sides when:
choices: Each expects to gain from the exchange
One side is forced to trade
Prices are zero
All goods are identical

stem: Which event shifts demand?
choices: Consumer income changes
The good's own price changes
Quantity supplied changes
There is movement along the demand curve.

stem: If consumer income rises and tablets are a normal good, what happens?
choices: Demand for tablets increases
Quantity demanded falls
Supply of tablets increases
Demand for tablets decreases

stem: Consumers expect the price of laptops to rise next month, so they buy more laptops today. What happens today?
choices: Current demand increases
Current quantity demanded falls
Supply decreases
Demand stays fixed because only current price matters

stem: A recession lowers consumer income. If restaurant meals are a normal good, what happens to demand for restaurant meals?
choices: Demand decreases
Demand increases
Quantity demanded increases because price changed
Supply increases

stem: Two neighbors specialize in the chores for which each gives up less valuable alternative work, then exchange help. Why can both benefit?
choices: Specialization can raise combined output available to share
Exchange makes both neighbors completely self-sufficient.
Scarcity disappears once the chores are divided
The faster neighbor must perform every chore

stem: A voluntary coffee purchase makes both participants better off. Does this show market failure?
choices: No; mutually accepted trade alone identifies no efficiency wedge
Yes; buyers and sellers always have unequal power
Yes; every price excludes some consumers
No; market failure requires government ownership

stem: Pollution from a factory that harms nearby residents is an example of:
choices: A price floor
A negative externality
A perfectly efficient market
A positive externality.

stem: A public good is usually:
choices: Always sold by one monopoly firm
A legal maximum price
Hard to exclude people from and shared by many users
A substitute for every other good

stem: A seller with substantial influence over the market price has:
choices: A price ceiling
A PPF
A circular flow
Market power

stem: Which situation is most likely a market failure?
choices: A factory pollutes a river used by nearby households
A buyer voluntarily purchases coffee
A seller lowers price during a sale
A student chooses to study

stem: The circular-flow model shows how dollars, goods and services, and resources move between:
choices: Households and firms
Banks and foreign governments
Workers and tax agencies
Retailers and central banks

stem: In the simple circular-flow model, households usually supply:
choices: Finished goods and services
Factors of production
Price ceilings
Tax wedges

stem: In the simple circular-flow model, firms usually supply:
choices: Labor services to households
Household income to product markets
Goods and services
Tax revenue to resource markets

stem: A production possibilities frontier shows:
choices: The exact market price of each good
Government’s preferred production mix
The economy’s current unemployment rate
Currently feasible combinations of two goods

stem: A point inside the PPF usually means:
choices: Resources are not being used efficiently
