stem: Refer to the PPF. Moving from point C to point D increases production of X but reduces production of Y. Suppose each additional unit of X generates a benefit equivalent to 3 units of Y. What is the net benefit, measured in units of Y, from moving from C to D?
choices: 3 Y

stem: Production moves from F to C and then from C to D with resources and technology unchanged. Which explanation, supported by the graph’s output changes, explains why only the second move sacrifices Y for more X?
choices: F to C uses idle resources to add 7 X and 15 Y; C to D reallocates fully employed resources, adding 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
F to C uses idle resources to add 7 X and 10 Y; C to D reallocates fully employed resources, adding 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
F to C expands productive capacity to add 7 X and 15 Y; C to D uses idle resources to add 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
F to C expands productive capacity to add 7 X and 10 Y; C to D uses idle resources to add 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.

stem: Use the graph. Compare the average opportunity cost of Good X over B to C and C to D. Which costs and explanation best fit the PPF?
choices: About 0.63 then 1.43 Y per X; expanding X production uses resources increasingly less suited to producing X.
About 1.43 then 2.5 Y per X; expanding X production uses resources increasingly less suited to producing X.
About 1.43 then 2.5 Y per X; the change shows that resources are equally well suited to producing X and Y.
About 0.63 then 1.43 Y per X; the change shows that resources are equally well suited to producing X and Y.

stem: The first ten generators cost two forgone repairs; the next ten cost six more. A buyer offers four repairs in exchange for each ten-generator block. Blocks must be produced in order. Which production choice yields the most net repairs?
choices: Produce only the second block because its opportunity cost is higher
Produce neither because any generator production sacrifices repairs
Produce one block, gaining two net repairs
Produce both blocks because their average cost equals the offer

stem: From an efficient starting point, reallocating crews to the first four school reopenings forgoes 12 bridge repairs; the next four forgo 20 more. A planner uses the first block's cost to estimate all eight. What is the error?
choices: The estimate is correct because equal numbers of schools must cost equal repairs
The estimate is 12 repairs too high because the first block is already planned
The estimate is 20 repairs too low because the first block has no opportunity cost
The estimate is 8 repairs too low because the later marginal tradeoff is steeper

stem: A factory raises both outputs after reorganizing idle workers. Later, training expands the maximum output possible even when all workers are occupied. Which evidence separates the two improvements?
choices: The first can occur within existing capacity; the second changes the efficient production boundary
Any simultaneous output increase proves the frontier shifted
Any training program moves production along an unchanged frontier
Both improvements establish that the original output was outside the frontier

stem: Worker training improves human capital and shifts the PPF outward for both goods. Which economic relationship does this illustrate?
choices: A price ceiling creates a shortage
Human capital raises productive capacity
A tax wedge reduces market size
A positive statement becomes normative

stem: A student says, “A point outside the PPF is inefficient because the economy is not producing there.” What is wrong with that statement?
choices: A point outside the PPF is always efficient
A point outside the PPF shows idle resources
It is unattainable with current resources, not merely inefficient.
A point outside the PPF means opportunity cost is zero

stem: A cyber-security team can run one more audit. It costs 90 staff-hours and is expected to prevent 120 hours of incident response, but the audit also displaces training worth 20 hours. What is the net marginal effect?
choices: A gain of 10 staff-hours
A gain of 30 staff-hours
A loss of 70 staff-hours
A gain of 210 staff-hours

stem: A straight-line PPF trades one turbine for three pumps. An observed move gains two turbines while pumps stay unchanged, with technology and resources fixed. Which explanation is consistent with both facts?
choices: The straight frontier proves every observed move must lose six pumps
The turbine gain by itself proves the PPF shifted outward
The observation establishes zero opportunity cost everywhere on the frontier
The starting point was inside the frontier, so the move could use idle capacity

stem: Refer to the graph. Tastes shift demand from D1 to D2 while supply remains S1. Which explanation uses both intersections to distinguish the demand shift from the market's movement along supply?
choices: Demand shifts right, and equilibrium moves along S1 from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2
Supply shifts right, and equilibrium moves along D1 from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2
Demand shifts left, and equilibrium moves along S1 from P3, Q2 to P2, Q1
Supply shifts left, and equilibrium moves along D2 from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2

stem: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Starting at D2 and S1, supply increases to S2 while demand stays at D2. What happens?
choices: Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2.
Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q3.
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P1, Q2.

stem: Compare two changes: first, D1/S1 to D2/S1; second, D1/S1 to D1/S2. Which statement correctly classifies both changes and gives their ending equilibria?
choices: First, demand increases and ends at (P3, Q2); second, quantity demanded increases along D1 and ends at (P1, Q2).
First, demand increases and ends at (P3, Q3); second, quantity demanded increases along D1 and ends at (P1, Q3).
First, quantity demanded changes along an unchanged demand curve and ends at (P3, Q2); second, demand shifts and ends at (P1, Q2).
First, quantity demanded changes along an unchanged demand curve and ends at (P3, Q3); second, demand shifts and ends at (P1, Q3).

stem: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Starting at D1 and S2, supply decreases to S1 while demand stays at D1. What happens?
choices: Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q1.
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2.
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2.
Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.

stem: Refer to the graph. The market moves from D1/S1 to D2/S2. An analyst claims that simultaneous demand and supply increases must leave price unchanged. Then part of the supply increase is reversed: supply lies strictly between S1 and S2 at every shown price, while demand stays D2. Which assessment is correct?
choices: The original offset is specific to the graph; afterward price is between P2 and P3 and quantity between Q2 and Q3.
The original offset is a general rule; afterward price stays P2 and quantity stays Q3.
The original offset is specific to the graph; afterward price is between P1 and P2 and quantity exceeds Q3.
The original offset is a general rule; afterward price reaches P3 and quantity falls below Q1.

stem: A disease reduces berry supply while a nutrition trend raises berry demand. The final quantity is above its original level. Which conclusion follows with ordinary downward demand and upward supply?
choices: Price is higher; the demand increase more than offsets the supply reduction’s effect on quantity.
Price is lower; greater final quantity proves that supply increased.
Price is unchanged; the higher quantity shows that the two shifts offset completely.
Price is higher; the observed quantity proves that the supply reduction dominated demand.

stem: Two initially identical device markets face the same increase in demand. Only Market Y also loses a component supplier. Compared with Market X’s final equilibrium, what must be true in Market Y?
choices: Y has a higher price and lower quantity, although its quantity relative to the original equilibrium is uncertain.
Y has a lower price and higher quantity, although its quantity relative to the original equilibrium is uncertain.
Y has a higher price and quantity, because both changes increase demand.
Y has the same price and quantity, because both markets face the same demand change.

stem: Lunch-delivery demand falls while improved routing lowers delivery costs. Final price is lower and the number of deliveries is unchanged. Which explanation is consistent?
choices: Demand fell and supply rose; their quantity effects offset at the final equilibrium.
Demand and supply both fell; their quantity effects offset at the final equilibrium.
Demand and supply both rose; unchanged deliveries reflect offsetting quantity effects.
Only demand fell; a fixed upward-sloping supply curve kept deliveries unchanged.

stem: The price of tablets falls, and consumers buy more tablets. No non-price determinant changed. What happened?
choices: Quantity demanded increased along the existing demand curve.
Demand increased and the curve shifted right
Supply increased and the curve shifted right
Demand decreased because price fell

stem: The price of a substitute for coffee rises. What happens in the coffee market, holding other factors constant?
choices: Demand for coffee increases, raising equilibrium price and quantity
Quantity demanded of coffee decreases along the same curve
Supply of coffee increases because coffee is now profitable
Demand for coffee decreases because substitutes are now expensive

stem: The price of peanut butter falls. What happens to the demand for jelly, assuming they are complements?
choices: Demand for jelly increases
Quantity demanded of jelly falls along the same curve
Supply of jelly decreases
Demand for jelly decreases because peanut butter is cheaper

stem: Bicycles are a normal good. Income and production-input costs rise, yet equilibrium bicycle sales fall. A manager concludes that bicycle demand must have fallen. Evaluate the conclusion.
choices: Incorrect: demand rose, but the supply reduction more than offset its effect on quantity; price rose.
Correct: lower equilibrium sales establish a demand decrease even when income rises.
Incorrect: supply rose, but demand fell enough to reduce both price and quantity.
Correct: higher input costs reduce bicycle demand directly while supply stays fixed.

stem: A production improvement increases supply while tastes shift away from the product. An analyst predicts that price and quantity must both fall. What is the precise correction?
choices: Price must fall, but quantity falls only if the demand reduction outweighs the supply increase’s quantity effect.
Quantity must fall, but price falls only if the production improvement outweighs the taste change.
Price must rise, but quantity can rise or fall depending on the relative shifts.
Neither direction can be inferred because simultaneous shifts make both variables indeterminate.

stem: A market price is above equilibrium. What pressure does the market create and why?
choices: Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
Upward pressure on price because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
No pressure because high prices clear every market
Downward pressure on quantity demanded because demand shifts left

stem: A market price is below equilibrium. What pressure does the market create and why?
choices: Upward pressure on price because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
No pressure because buyers prefer low prices
A supply increase because the legal price is low

stem: A coffee shop sees more customers after a celebrity endorsement. At the same time, wages for baristas rise. If the relative sizes of the two shifts are unknown, which equilibrium outcome can be predicted with certainty?
choices: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity fall
Price falls; quantity rises

stem: A new production method makes shoes cheaper to produce. At the same time, a fashion shift makes shoes less popular. What is certain?
choices: Price falls; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity falls; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity rise
Price rises; quantity falls

stem: A hurricane disrupts production and reduces supply while households expect prices to rise tomorrow and rush to buy today. What is the strongest prediction for today’s market?
choices: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity fall
Price falls; quantity rises

stem: A student says, 'Demand increased because the price rose.' What is the correct response?
choices: A demand increase can raise price; a price rise alone moves along demand.
That is correct because demand always means the current price
That describes a supply increase
That proves the good is inferior

stem: Fewer buyers want a product and several producers exit. Final price is above the starting price. Which interpretation is consistent with both shifts and that observation?
choices: Quantity falls; the supply reduction’s upward price effect outweighs the demand reduction’s downward effect.
Quantity rises; the demand reduction’s downward price effect outweighs the supply reduction’s upward effect.
Quantity stays fixed; an increase in price prevents either curve from shifting.
Quantity falls; the higher price proves that demand increased rather than decreased.

stem: Refer to the graph. Compare a $20 ceiling with a $40 ceiling, assuming efficient matching and no other restrictions. Which policy comparison is correct?
choices: $20 permits 150 trades and creates a 100-unit shortage; $40 allows the 200-unit equilibrium
$20 permits 250 trades and creates a 100-unit shortage; $40 allows the 200-unit equilibrium
$20 permits 150 trades; $40 forces 250 trades and a 100-unit surplus
Both ceilings leave the market at 200 trades because both are legal maximum prices

stem: Refer to the graph. A $40 floor is enforced. Private buyers purchase their quantity demanded, and government buys 50 additional units at the floor. If sellers produce the quantity on supply, what remains unsold and what does government spend?
choices: 50 units remain unsold; government spends $2,000
100 units remain unsold; government spends $2,000
50 units remain unsold; government spends $4,000
No units remain unsold; government spends $2,000

stem: A $50 price ceiling is imposed with demand and supply unchanged. Which statement correctly classifies the policy using the equilibrium shown?
choices: Nonbinding: the legal price is above the $30 equilibrium price, so the market stays at equilibrium.
Nonbinding: the legal price is above the $40 equilibrium price, so the market stays at equilibrium.
Binding: the legal price is above the $30 equilibrium price, so transactions must occur at $50.
Binding: the legal price is above the $40 equilibrium price, so transactions must occur at $50.

stem: A $10 price floor is imposed with demand and supply unchanged. Which statement correctly classifies the policy using the equilibrium shown?
choices: Nonbinding: the legal price is below the $30 equilibrium price, so the market stays at equilibrium.
Nonbinding: the legal price is below the $40 equilibrium price, so the market stays at equilibrium.
Binding: the legal price is below the $30 equilibrium price, so transactions must occur at $10.
Binding: the legal price is below the $40 equilibrium price, so transactions must occur at $10.

stem: An enforced $20 price ceiling is imposed. What additional consequence, beyond the lower posted price, follows from the quantities shown in the graph?
choices: A shortage of 100 units makes waiting, search, or another form of nonprice rationing necessary.
A shortage of 50 units makes waiting, search, or another form of nonprice rationing necessary.
A surplus of 100 units leaves sellers competing to dispose of unsold goods.
A surplus of 50 units leaves sellers competing to dispose of unsold goods.

stem: A city caps rent below equilibrium. The advertised rent falls, but apartment searches become longer, maintenance falls, and landlords screen tenants harder. What is the best economic diagnosis?
choices: The ceiling lowers the posted price but creates shortage and nonmoney rationing
The ceiling lowers the posted price and therefore eliminates scarcity
The ceiling raises quantity supplied and creates seller competition
The ceiling is nonbinding because landlords still choose tenant quality

stem: A minimum wage is set above the equilibrium wage. Some workers receive higher pay, firms hire fewer workers, and more workers seek jobs. What is the cleanest interpretation?
choices: The floor helps some employed workers but creates a labor surplus
The floor helps all workers because everyone now earns the legal wage
The floor raises labor demand because the wage is higher
The floor is nonbinding because firms still hire some workers

stem: A binding rent ceiling reduces the number of apartments rented, eliminating the gains from some mutually beneficial rentals. Which way of allocating the remaining apartments would cause an additional loss of total surplus?
choices: Some available apartments go to lower-value applicants while higher-value applicants go without
The remaining apartments all go to the highest-value applicants
The lower rent transfers money from landlords to continuing tenants
Landlords supply exactly the number of apartments willing buyers rent

stem: After a higher hourly minimum wage, a firm raises hourly pay but reduces scheduled hours and employer-paid training. A report calls the higher hourly rate proof that every worker gained. Which review addresses the missing incentive responses?
choices: Compare hours, total earnings and training changes for affected workers
Use the hourly rate alone because other employment terms are not wages
Infer that lower hours prove every worker lost despite higher hourly pay
Treat the firm's adjustment as proof it did not respond to the wage rule

stem: A legal maximum price is set above equilibrium. A student predicts a shortage. What is wrong?
choices: A ceiling above equilibrium is nonbinding and does not create a shortage
Any price ceiling always creates a shortage
A ceiling above equilibrium creates a surplus
A ceiling above equilibrium is actually a price floor

stem: A legal minimum price is set below equilibrium. A student predicts a surplus. What is wrong?
choices: A floor below equilibrium is nonbinding and does not create a surplus
Any price floor always creates a surplus
A floor below equilibrium creates a shortage
A floor below equilibrium is actually a price ceiling

stem: At a binding rent ceiling, 4,000 households demand apartments and landlords offer 2,700. A construction program adds 500 apartments at that rent, while new arrivals raise quantity demanded by 200. Assuming all offered apartments are rented, what changes?
choices: Rentals rise by 500 and the shortage falls by 300
Rentals rise by 500 and the shortage falls by 500
Rentals rise by 200 and the shortage falls by 700
Rentals rise by 700 and the shortage stays unchanged

stem: At a price floor of $18, quantity supplied is 900 units and quantity demanded is 550 units. Which answer best states the result?
choices: A surplus of 350 units
A shortage of 350 units
A surplus of 550 units
A shortage of 900 units

stem: A binding price ceiling on gasoline leads stations to sell out early. Some stations favor regular customers. What is the best interpretation?
choices: The shortage creates nonprice rationing
The market clears because the legal price is low
The ceiling creates a surplus
The ceiling increases supply

stem: A binding price floor on milk leaves producers with unsold inventory. Which hidden cost is most likely?
choices: Waste, storage costs, or government purchases to support the price
Long lines among buyers because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Black-market premiums from buyers competing for scarce milk
No cost because producers receive a higher legal price

stem: A rent ceiling causes landlords to convert apartments into short-term rentals outside the regulated market. What does this show?
choices: The ceiling reduced regulated rental supply by changing landlord incentives.
A ceiling always increases quantity supplied
A ceiling eliminates opportunity cost for landlords
A ceiling is nonbinding if landlords find loopholes

stem: An evaluator says, "Option A saves more staff time, so it is the best policy." Which reply separates the testable component from the hidden value premise?
choices: Measure the time savings, then ask why that objective should outrank other consequences
Treat the entire sentence as positive because staff time is measurable
Treat the time-saving estimate as normative because it supports a recommendation
Conclude more accurate timing data will uniquely determine the preferred policy

stem: A minimum wage is set above equilibrium, but employment does not fall much. Which explanation best fits supply and demand logic?
choices: Labor demand may be relatively inelastic over that range
The law of demand has been disproven
The wage floor must be below equilibrium
Higher wages always increase quantity demanded for labor

stem: Use the graph. A clerk uses only the buyer-price increase as the tax rate and multiplies by the original quantity, reporting $300. Which correction addresses both errors?
choices: $6 on 80 units gives $480; use both sides of the wedge and the post-tax quantity.
$8 on 70 units gives $560; use both sides of the wedge and the post-tax quantity.
$6 on 80 units gives $480; the buyer-price increase alone and the untaxed quantity are the correct definitions.
$8 on 70 units gives $560; the buyer-price increase alone and the untaxed quantity are the correct definitions.

stem: Refer to the tax graph. A seller argues that its legal duty to remit the tax means it bears the entire revenue rectangle. What do the price changes and continuing quantity show?
choices: Each side bears $3 per unit and $240 of the $480 rectangle
Sellers bear $6 per unit and all $480 of the rectangle
Each side bears $3 per unit and $300 of the $600 rectangle
Buyers bear $6 per unit and all $480 of the rectangle

stem: Refer to the graph. A report attributes the smaller market after the tax to the buyer–seller price wedge. Which quantity comparison and explanation support that account?
choices: From 100 to 80 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
From 100 to 65 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
From 100 to 80 units; the tax leaves buyer and seller prices identical, so it creates no wedge.
From 100 to 65 units; the tax leaves buyer and seller prices identical, so it creates no wedge.

stem: Refer to the tax graph. An analyst calls the government receipt the entire efficiency loss. With no externalities and using the straight curve segments around the two equilibria, which correction is right?
choices: Revenue is $480; deadweight loss is $60
Revenue is $600; deadweight loss is $60
Revenue is $480; deadweight loss is $480
Revenue is $240; deadweight loss is $120

stem: At Q = 80 in the tax graph, how much higher is Supply + tax than Supply, and what does this vertical distance mean?
choices: $6; sellers need a buyer price $6 above their net supply price to cover the per-unit tax.
$4; sellers need a buyer price $4 above their net supply price to cover the per-unit tax.
$6; the tax makes sellers willing to receive $6 less net of tax at every quantity.
$4; the tax makes sellers willing to receive $4 less net of tax at every quantity.

stem: A $4 tax is placed on concert tickets. Buyers pay $2.50 more than before, sellers receive $1.50 less than before, and fewer tickets are sold. Which statement is strongest?
choices: The burden is shared, quantity falls, and the side less able to adjust bears more
The burden falls only on sellers because the legal tax is charged to sellers
The burden falls only on buyers because the buyer price increased
The burden disappears because tax revenue offsets the lower quantity sold

stem: A market has an $8 tax, a total buyer price of $26 and a net seller receipt of $18. Buyers bear 75% of the per-unit burden. What was the untaxed price, and which side is less price responsive over this change?
choices: $20; buyers
$24; sellers
$20; sellers
$24; buyers

stem: A seller-side tax shifts the supply curve upward. Which statement best explains why buyers still pay part of the tax?
choices: Elasticities determine how the tax is split.
Buyers voluntarily pay taxes for sellers
The demand curve shifts right by the tax amount
The tax creates a price ceiling

stem: A tax is placed on buyers instead of sellers. In a standard supply-demand model, why is the final outcome similar to an equal seller tax?
choices: Both taxes create the same buyer–seller price wedge.
Only buyer taxes reduce quantity
Only seller taxes raise prices
The tax disappears if buyers legally pay it

stem: A $7 tax reduces quantity from 500 to 420 units. What does this show beyond tax revenue?
choices: The tax shrinks the market by discouraging mutually beneficial trades
The tax increases market size because government collects revenue
The tax leaves buyers and sellers unaffected if revenue is spent
The tax creates a surplus because quantity falls

stem: In a competitive cigarette market, demand is less price-elastic than supply. A small per-unit tax is collected from sellers. With other market conditions unchanged, which conclusion about the economic burden follows?
choices: Buyers bear more because demand is less price-responsive than supply.
Sellers bear more because the government collects the tax from sellers.
Each side bears half because both participate in the taxed transactions.
Buyers bear the entire tax because demand is less elastic than supply.

stem: In a competitive luxury-boat rental market, demand is more price-elastic than supply. A small per-unit tax is collected from renters. With other market conditions unchanged, which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Sellers are more likely to bear more of the tax burden.
Buyers are more likely to bear more of the tax burden.
Buyers and sellers are likely to share the tax burden equally.
Sellers are likely to bear the entire tax because they receive payment.

stem: Before tax, price is $20 and quantity is 1,000. After a $6 tax, buyers pay $24, sellers receive $18, and quantity is 850. What is tax revenue?
Before tax, price is $20. After tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. Which statement correctly splits the burden?
choices: Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2
Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $4
Buyers bear $6 and sellers bear $0
Buyers bear $24 and sellers bear $18

stem: A linear market has demand P = 30 − Q and supply P = 6 + Q. Compare an $8 tax with a $14 ceiling. Under the ceiling, available units go to the highest-value buyers and lowest-cost sellers, with no search costs. With no externalities, which comparison is correct?
choices: Both trade 8 units and retain $128 of total surplus; the ceiling gives consumers $64 more surplus
Both trade 8 units, but the tax destroys its $64 revenue and leaves only $64 of total surplus
The tax trades 8 units, but the ceiling trades all 16 units demanded at $14
Both retain $144 of total surplus because revenue and lower prices are transfers

stem: A $6 tax is legally remitted by buyers. Before it, 120 repairs sold for $25 each; afterward, 100 repairs sell, buyers pay $29 in total and firms keep $23. A firm says buyer remittance leaves its sales receipts unaffected. What refutes the claim?
choices: Net sales receipts fall by $700, although the seller burden is only $2 per remaining repair
Net sales receipts fall by $600, equal to the full government receipt
Net sales receipts rise by $400, because buyers pay $4 more per repair
Net sales receipts remain $3,000, because firms do not remit the tax

stem: Supply is perfectly inelastic at 200 units and demand slopes downward. A $6 tax is imposed in a competitive market with no externalities or collection costs. Which combination follows?
choices: Sellers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is zero
Buyers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is zero
Sellers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is $1,200
Buyers and sellers each bear $3, revenue is $600, and quantity falls

stem: A tax is imposed on a market where demand is perfectly inelastic. Who bears the tax burden?
choices: Buyers bear the burden because quantity demanded does not respond
Sellers bear the burden because they collect the money
The government bears the burden
No one bears the burden because quantity does not change

stem: A tax causes buyers to pay more, sellers to receive less, and quantity to fall. Which statement is false?
choices: The side legally assigned the tax must bear the entire burden
The tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices
The market quantity falls after the tax
Buyers and sellers can both be worse off per unit traded

stem: A city taxes ride-share trips. Riders pay higher prices, drivers receive less per trip, and fewer trips occur. What is the best synthesis?
choices: The tax wedge is shared and shrinks the number of exchanges
The tax affects only riders if they see the fee at checkout
The tax affects only drivers if the platform remits it
The tax increases quantity because government revenue rises

stem: A board ranks plans only by the number of people served and selects A. New evidence shows B serves more people but offers less privacy. Which conclusion distinguishes logic from values?
choices: Choosing A would necessarily show the new service count is false
Its stated rule now favors B; preferring A would require changing or qualifying that rule
The privacy difference makes the service-count evidence normative
More people served proves B is morally superior under every criterion

stem: A university raises parking fines. Students respond by arriving earlier, carpooling more, and contesting tickets more often. What principle ties these reactions together?
choices: People respond to incentives, including responses the university did not intend
People ignore incentives when rules are created by institutions
Opportunity cost disappears when penalties are legal
Markets allocate resources only when prices are zero

stem: A forecast says a digitization plan will reduce waiting. A recommendation says it should be adopted only if access for people without internet is protected. Waiting falls but offline access worsens. Which inference is sound?
choices: Observed waiting reductions prove the plan satisfies the value criterion
The forecast becomes normative because implementation affected access
The forecast is supported, while the recommendation's stated condition is unmet
The failed access condition refutes the waiting-time forecast

stem: A subscription service makes cancellation require a phone call but lets upgrades occur with one click. Cancellations fall and complaints rise. What is the strongest inference?
choices: Exit friction can reduce cancellation despite dissatisfaction; easier upgrades do not remove the cost of leaving.
Stronger service preference best explains retention; complaints mainly show that retained users demand more service quality.
One-click upgrades best explain retention; the phone requirement mainly reallocates existing demand across service tiers.
The phone call screens out low-value cancellations; fewer cancellations therefore indicate higher consumer welfare.

stem: A report states that volunteers prefer evening shifts and therefore evening-only service is fair. A representative survey confirms the preference. What remains unresolved?
choices: Whether a confirmed preference statement can count as positive
Whether using a survey converts the fairness conclusion into a measured fact
Whether the fairness judgment proves daytime users have no unmet needs
Whether fairness should be judged by volunteer preferences rather than users' access

stem: A repair subsidy pays for every completed repair. Claims rise sharply, but most claimants would have repaired anyway; some shops relabel routine servicing. What evidence best identifies the intended response?
choices: Additional genuine repairs relative to comparable users without the subsidy
The total number of paid claims, treating each as a newly induced repair
The size of the subsidy budget, treating expenditure as added repair benefit
The stated repair goal, treating relabeling as evidence of no behavioral response

stem: A circular-flow model shows households supplying labor to firms and receiving wages. Which market is being described?
choices: The market for factors of production
The market for final goods and services
The market for price ceilings
The market for tax revenue

stem: A rule gives priority to people facing the greatest hardship. New data show that a different group meets that description. What change is consistent with keeping the same normative principle?
choices: Change the priority group because the evidence changed who satisfies the criterion
Keep the old group because normative principles cannot use evidence
Declare hardship measurement normative solely because it informs policy
Treat the data as proof that greatest-hardship priority is the only fair principle

stem: A software platform ranks creators by daily posting frequency. Posting rises, but creators split one useful guide into many thin updates. What does the response reveal?
choices: The ranking rewards posting frequency, so creators can raise measured output while reducing useful content per post.
The ranking reveals stronger reader demand for short posts, so more posts establish an increase in information value.
The ranking lowers the cost of writing, so thinner posts indicate a productivity gain at unchanged information quality.
The ranking rewards guide quality indirectly, so splitting a guide raises both measured output and the original learning benefit.

stem: A researcher predicts that simplifying an application raises completion when eligibility is unchanged. A trial simplifies the form and broadens eligibility; completion rises. Which statement is justified?
choices: Only recommendations can be evaluated when two policies change together
The prediction is positive, but the joint change does not isolate the form's effect
The rise proves the form alone caused every added completion
The extra eligibility change makes the original claim normative

stem: A city reduces bus fares to increase ridership. Ridership rises, but crowding makes some riders switch back to cars. What is the strongest lesson?
choices: Lower fares attract riders, but congestion raises time costs and feeds back to reduce part of the initial ridership gain.
The initial fare response proves demand shifted right; riders returning to cars show the fare cut later shifted supply left.
Returning riders reveal more elastic money-price demand; their switch implies the initial ridership increase was measured incorrectly.
Crowding raises the service’s money price implicitly; the resulting ridership decline establishes that the fare policy reduced total welfare.

stem: A warehouse has packed 900 orders; that work is irreversible. The last 100 avoid $2,100 of penalties if completed tonight. Overtime costs $1,600 and displaces training worth $700. An outside packer can finish them for $1,900 without using warehouse staff. Which decision maximizes incremental value?
choices: Use the outside packer: its $200 gain exceeds overtime’s $200 loss and leaving the orders unfinished.
Use overtime: its $500 gain exceeds the outside packer’s $200 gain because training is not a cash payment.
Leave them unfinished: both methods cost more than zero, and previous packing costs must be recovered first.
Use overtime: the 900 completed orders make finishing the final 100 worthwhile regardless of displaced training.

stem: A software firm has spent $2 million irreversibly. Updating costs $90,000 and adds $70,000 in revenue. Canceling avoids the update but triggers a $35,000 support-termination payment. Selling the unfinished code yields $15,000 and requires $10,000 of handover work, with no termination payment. Which option is best from today?
choices: Sell: its $5,000 net receipt exceeds updating’s $20,000 loss and cancellation’s $35,000 loss.
Update: its $70,000 revenue exceeds the sale receipt, so the remaining $90,000 cost should be ignored.
Cancel: avoiding the $90,000 update cost is sufficient even though selling has a positive net receipt.
Update: the $2 million already spent makes the smallest additional cash outlay the relevant criterion.

stem: A transit line can add up to three buses in order. Their direct marginal benefits are $140k, $105k and $78k; each costs $100k. Adding any buses requires $30k of dispatch setup. Only a three-bus plan also enables transfers worth $60k. Which plan has the highest net benefit?
choices: Three buses: net benefit is $53k, exceeding $15k for two and $10k for one.
Two buses: stop before the third because its direct $78k benefit is below its $100k cost.
One bus: its $40k direct surplus exceeds the second bus’s $5k direct surplus.
No buses: dispatch setup makes every positive-size plan have negative net benefit.

stem: A town charges for trash bags and collects recycling free. Recycling tonnage rises, but contamination rises too. Which finding would best support successful conservation rather than merely relabeling disposal?
choices: Residents report noticing the fee without any measured disposal change
Clean recovered materials rise and total discarded material falls in a comparable audit
Recycling collections rise even if processors reject the extra material
The town collects more bag-fee revenue regardless of waste volumes

stem: A team earns a $20,000 bonus if quarterly sales exceed $1 million. It has $990,000 and can move $20,000 of January sales into December by offering a $2,000 discount. No extra annual units are sold; annual base commissions are unchanged. Which evaluation distinguishes the team’s incentive from the firm’s result?
choices: The team gains $20,000 in bonus while the firm loses $22,000 from discount and bonus; higher quarterly sales need not mean higher annual value.
The team gains $18,000 in bonus while the firm gains $18,000; accelerated sales are additional annual revenue.
The team gains nothing because annual units are unchanged; the firm loses only the $2,000 discount.
The team gains $20,000 while the firm gains $18,000; the shifted January revenue is a new annual benefit.

stem: An unemployed worker could accept a job paying $500 weekly with $100 of unavoidable weekly commuting cost. Benefits are $400 weekly in month one and $175 later, and stop upon employment. Ignoring other differences, how does the immediate net gain from accepting change, and what can be inferred about search?
choices: The gain falls from $100 to $325 weekly; the later benefit cut weakens the incentive because it reduces income.
The gain rises from $0 to $225 weekly; the schedule strengthens the later financial incentive but does not uniquely determine effort.
The gain rises from $0 to $225 weekly; search effort must therefore rise by the same percentage for every worker.
The gain stays $400 weekly; accepting pays the same wage, so changing benefits cannot affect search incentives.

stem: On an unchanged efficient frontier, moving from 50 drones and 80 scanners to 65 drones and 50 scanners costs 2 scanners per added drone. The next 10 drones would reduce scanners from 50 to 20. A planner claims a constant cost of 2 and wants 10 more drones only if each is worth at least 2.5 scanners. Which evaluation is correct?
choices: The next block costs 3 scanners per drone, so it fails the 2.5 threshold and indicates rising opportunity cost.
The next block costs 2 scanners per drone, so it passes the threshold because the previous average applies to every move.
The next block costs 0.33 scanner per drone, so it passes the threshold after inverting the ratio.
The next block costs 30 scanners per drone, so the frontier must have shifted inward rather than displaying changing tradeoffs.

stem: A country starts inside its PPF with idle workers. Hiring them raises both outputs until the old frontier is reached. Later, technology improves only scanner production and the country can produce more scanners at the same drone output. Which diagnosis distinguishes the two changes?
choices: Both changes shift the frontier outward equally because any rise in both observed outputs proves general capacity growth.
The first improves resource utilization; the second expands productive capacity asymmetrically, rather than merely moving along the old frontier.
The first is growth and the second is improved utilization because scanner output rises without reducing drones.
Neither changes productive capacity because every increase in one output must reduce the other under scarcity.

stem: On one efficient frontier, the first 20 solar units sacrifice 5 food units and the next 20 sacrifice 14. A storage innovation then halves the food sacrifice required for each of those solar blocks, leaving maximum food output unchanged. Which conclusion separates the original tradeoff from the innovation?
choices: Original marginal cost falls from 4 to about 1.43 food per solar unit; the innovation merely moves production along the same frontier.
Original marginal cost is constant at 0.475 food per solar unit; the innovation eliminates increasing opportunity cost because both blocks improve.
Original marginal cost rises from 0.25 to 0.70 food per solar unit; the innovation expands solar capacity, with the two costs falling to 0.125 and 0.35.
Original marginal cost rises from 5 to 14 food per solar unit; unchanged maximum food means productive capacity cannot expand.

stem: Which statement is positive rather than normative?
choices: A binding rent ceiling reduces the quantity of rental housing supplied
The city should cap rents to protect tenants
Housing is too important to leave to markets
Fair rents matter more than landlord profits

stem: An adviser predicts a wage rule raises employed teenagers’ annual income by $8 million but reduces teenage employment by 3%. She recommends it because the income gain is worth the employment loss. A pilot instead finds a 1% job loss. Which conclusion separates evidence from values?
choices: The pilot makes the original employment prediction normative because a positive statement cannot be contradicted by data.
The pilot challenges the size of the positive employment prediction; it does not by itself establish the adviser’s tradeoff criterion.
The smaller loss proves the recommendation objectively correct, regardless of how the affected teenagers value work and income.
The recommendation makes both numerical predictions normative, so neither can be evaluated using pilot evidence.

stem: A report states: (1) a tax reduces cigarette purchases; (2) the tax burden falls heavily on low-income smokers; (3) therefore the tax is unjust. Which classification is correct?
choices: All three are positive, because technical wording removes every value judgment
Only statement 1 is positive
Statements 1 and 2 are positive; statement 3 is normative
Statements 2 and 3 are normative

stem: Streaming subscriptions are normal goods. Incomes rise, a rival streaming service lowers its price, and broadband needed for both services becomes more expensive. A manager credits income alone for rising subscriptions. Which inference is defensible?
choices: Income and the rival-price cut push demand right; broadband cost changes supply, so observed growth isolates the two demand effects.
Income pushes demand right; rival-price and broadband-cost changes push left, so observed growth need not measure the income effect alone.
Income pushes demand left; the rival-price cut and broadband cost push right, so observed growth rules out normal-good status.
All three changes push demand right; an unchanged subscription price would show that subscriptions rose along the old demand curve.

stem: Tea and coffee are substitutes. Coffee prices rise while consumer income falls, and tea is a normal good. What can be concluded about tea demand without knowing effect sizes?
choices: Tea demand rises because the substitute-price effect is larger than the income effect
Tea demand falls because the income effect is larger than the substitute-price effect
The direction of the tea-demand shift is ambiguous
Tea demand is unchanged because tea's own price did not change

stem: A market survey shows that at every possible price consumers now plan to buy more electric bikes than before. Which event cannot explain the change?
choices: A subsidy to buyers
A rise in gasoline prices
A fall in the price of electric bikes itself
Stronger preferences for low-emission travel

stem: Bakers pay $4 less in flour cost per loaf, but a new energy levy adds $6 per loaf. At the same time, a health report reduces buyers’ willingness to purchase bread. With unknown shift magnitudes, which conclusion is supported?
choices: Net unit cost falls $2, shifting supply right; demand shifts left, so price rises while quantity is ambiguous.
Net unit cost rises $2, shifting supply left; demand also shifts left, so quantity falls while price is ambiguous.
Both changes shift supply left, so price rises and quantity falls with no demand change.
Lower flour cost shifts supply right regardless of the levy, so quantity rises and price is ambiguous.

stem: Evaluate the competing effects of a cost-saving production technology and a new compliance cost. What can be inferred about the net supply shift without relative magnitudes?
choices: Supply must increase because technology reduces production cost.
Supply must decrease because compliance raises production cost.
The net supply direction is ambiguous without relative cost changes.
Supply must stay fixed because the two changes cancel by definition.

stem: Several firms leave a market, reducing the quantity offered at each fixed price. Demand is unchanged. At the new equilibrium, surviving firms sell more than each sold before, but total market sales are lower. Which explanation reconciles the observations?
choices: Market supply shifted left, raising price; survivors move up their own unchanged supply curves even though fewer firms reduce total output.
Market supply shifted right because each survivor sells more; the lower total shows demand must have shifted left too.
Market supply is unchanged because survivor technology is unchanged; exit is only a movement along aggregate supply.
Each survivor’s supply shifted left, lowering price; fewer sellers then raise each remaining firm’s quantity supplied.

stem: A widely reported health study increases consumers’ willingness to buy fresh berries. At the same time, frost destroys part of the berry crop. With ordinary downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping supply, and unknown effect sizes, which equilibrium conclusion is certain?
choices: Quantity rises; price may rise or fall because the two changes push price in opposite directions.
Price falls; quantity may rise or fall because lower crop output reduces sellers’ willingness to sell.
Price rises; quantity may rise or fall because the two changes push quantity in opposite directions.
Quantity falls; price may rise or fall because stronger willingness to buy offsets the crop loss.

stem: A market has Qd = 180 - 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P. At every price, demand then falls by 24 units and supply falls by 8 units. Which final change and explanation are correct?
choices: Price rises $4 and quantity falls 16 units; demand’s larger reduction raises price.
Price falls $4 and quantity falls 16 units; demand’s larger horizontal reduction dominates the price effect.
Price falls $4 and quantity rises 16 units; both curve reductions expand sales.
Price is unchanged and quantity falls 32 units; the horizontal reductions simply add.

stem: Unchanged linear schedules give Qd=900 and Qs=1,150 at $10, and Qd=1,100 and Qs=950 at $8. Sellers currently charge $10. An analyst calls the resulting surplus evidence of a supply shift and predicts it will persist even without a price control. Which correction is complete?
choices: The surplus is 250 at $10; price must rise to $11.25 and quantity 1,025, while a $10 ceiling would preserve the gap.
The surplus is 250 at $10; price can fall to $8.75 and quantity 1,025 along unchanged curves, while a $10 floor would preserve the gap.
The shortage is 250 at $10; price can fall to $8.75 and quantity 1,025 only if supply shifts left.
The surplus is 150 at $10; price can fall to $8 and quantity 950, while unchanged curves prevent further adjustment.

stem: Equilibrium rent is $1,400. A ceiling is set at $1,550. What is the immediate market effect?
choices: Shortage: the ceiling is binding
Surplus: the ceiling is binding
No effect: the ceiling is nonbinding
Tax wedge: the difference is $150

stem: At a binding rent ceiling, Qd=8,000 and Qs=5,600. Of the supplied units, 400 are assigned by waiting list; they are not additional apartments. Later, 300 landlords withdraw units while Qd at the ceiling is unchanged. An official subtracts the 400 waiting-list allocations from the later shortage. What is the correct diagnosis?
choices: Shortage rises from 2,000 to 2,300; waiting-list allocation reduces excess demand independently of the supplied apartments.
Shortage rises from 2,400 to 2,700; waiting lists allocate existing supply and do not add units or reduce the underlying gap.
Shortage falls from 2,400 to 2,100; withdrawals remove potential renters as well as the landlords’ supplied units.
Shortage stays 2,400; nonprice allocation prevents a change in the shortage when legal rent is unchanged.

stem: A rental market has Qd=10,000-2P and Qs=1,000+P. A $2,000 ceiling is introduced. Over time, 500 units are converted out of the regulated market at every rent, while demand is unchanged. Which sequence follows, and what can be inferred about tenants?
choices: Equilibrium was $3,000; surplus is initially 3,000 and later 3,500 units, so all tenants necessarily gain from easier apartment access.
Equilibrium was $3,000; shortage is initially 3,000 and later 3,500 units, while search and quality costs can offset some tenants’ posted-rent savings.
Equilibrium was $2,000; the ceiling is nonbinding initially, and conversion creates a 500-unit shortage only because demand shifts right.
Equilibrium was $3,000; shortage falls from 3,000 to 2,500 units, and lower legal rent guarantees every prospective tenant is better off.

stem: A wage floor of $16 is initially below an $18 equilibrium wage. Demand then falls; without the floor the new wage would be $14. At $16, firms now demand 90 workers and 130 want jobs. With all demanded jobs filled, what is the correct diagnosis?
choices: The floor remains nonbinding, with 130 employed and no surplus
The floor changes from nonbinding to binding, with 130 employed and a 40-worker shortage
The floor changes from nonbinding to binding, with 90 employed and a 40-worker surplus
The floor was binding in both periods, with employment fixed at 90

stem: At a binding price floor, sellers offer 1,900 units and buyers demand 1,250. The government purchases 300 units. How much unsold surplus remains?
A binding agricultural price floor is removed. Holding other conditions constant, which adjustment is expected?
choices: Price rises, quantity demanded falls, and quantity supplied rises
Price falls, quantity demanded rises, and quantity supplied falls
Price and quantity supplied both rise
A shortage necessarily replaces the surplus

stem: Untaxed price is $30. A $7 tax makes buyers pay $34 and sellers receive $27. Lawmakers propose collecting the same tax from buyers instead of sellers in the same competitive market, with unchanged demand, supply and enforcement. Which prediction correctly combines the observed burdens with the proposed change?
choices: Buyers bear $4 and sellers $3 per unit; collecting from buyers shifts the full $7 burden to buyers.
Buyers bear $4 and sellers $3 per unit; changing the statutory payer alone does not change those economic burdens.
Buyers bear $3 and sellers $4 per unit; changing the statutory payer alone does not change those burdens.
Buyers bear $7 and sellers $0 per unit; collecting from sellers would reverse those burdens.

stem: In a competitive market, a per-unit tax initially raises buyer price, lowers seller receipts and reduces trades. Several years later suppliers can adjust output much more easily, while demand responsiveness is unchanged. Which statement correctly distinguishes the initial effect from the later burden comparison?
choices: Initially buyers bear the full wedge; as supply becomes more elastic, sellers necessarily bear the full wedge.
Initially both sides bear part of the wedge; more elastic supply tends to move a larger share onto sellers.
Initially both sides bear part of the wedge; as supply becomes more elastic, a larger share tends to fall on buyers.
Initially seller receipts rise; later statutory collection determines which side bears the wedge.

stem: A $10 tax reduces equilibrium quantity only slightly in Market A but sharply in Market B. What is the strongest inference?
choices: Market A likely has less elastic demand and/or supply around equilibrium
Market A must have more elastic demand and supply
Tax revenue must be zero in Market A
The statutory side paying the tax differs across markets

stem: Demand is Qd=100-2Pb and supply is Qs=2Ps, where Pb is the buyer’s total price and Ps is the seller’s net receipt. A $5 unit tax is first remitted by sellers, then by buyers, with unchanged schedules and compliance. Which outcome and interpretation are correct?
choices: Seller remittance yields Pb=$25 and Ps=$20, while buyer remittance yields Pb=$30 and Ps=$25; legal assignment fixes who loses.
Both systems yield Pb=$27.50, Ps=$22.50 and Q=45; the legal payer changes but the same wedge determines economic incidence.
Both systems yield Pb=$25, Ps=$25 and Q=50; changing the remitter cancels the wedge from equilibrium.
Both systems yield Pb=$22.50, Ps=$27.50 and Q=45; sellers receive more than buyers pay because the tax is a transfer.

stem: Under a seller-remitted tax, buyers pay $52 and sellers keep $46 per unit. The same tax is reassigned to buyers, with curves unchanged. An invoice then asks buyers to pay sellers $52 plus a separate tax payment. Which correction preserves the original economic outcome?
choices: Pay sellers $52 and government $6, for $58 in total
Pay sellers $49 and government $3, for $52 in total
Pay sellers $46 and government $6, for $52 in total
Pay sellers $46 and government nothing, for $46 in total

stem: Labor demand is Ld=120-2Wf and supply is Ls=2Ww. Wf is the employer’s total cost and Ww is take-home pay. An $8 per-worker payroll tax is legally moved from firms to workers without other changes. Which prediction refutes the claim that firms’ economic burden disappears?
choices: Wf falls to $30 and Ww to $22, with employment 60; legal reassignment removes all employer burden.
Wf remains $34 and Ww rises to $34, with employment 52; workers now remit the tax from a higher net wage.
Wf remains $34 and Ww $26, with employment 52; each side still bears $4 relative to the untaxed $30 wage.
Wf rises to $38 and Ww stays $30, with employment 44; firms bear all tax whenever labor demand slopes down.

stem: In a competitive market, demand elasticity is Ed=-0.25 and supply elasticity Es=1.20 near equilibrium. A small unit tax is introduced. Later, buyers gain substitutes and Ed becomes -1.50 while Es stays 1.20. Which comparison is best, holding the initial price, quantity and tax size comparable?
choices: Buyers initially bear more; afterward sellers bear more, and the stronger demand response makes the tax-induced quantity reduction larger.
Sellers initially bear more; afterward buyers bear more, and stronger demand response makes the quantity reduction smaller.
Buyers bear more in both cases because the negative sign makes demand less elastic than every positive supply elasticity.
Burden shares reverse only if the law changes the tax remitter; elasticity changes affect quantity but not economic incidence.

stem: Demand elasticity is -1.80 and supply elasticity is 0.20 in a market. A small tax is imposed on sellers. Over time, sellers gain alternative uses for their resources and supply elasticity rises to 2.40, with demand elasticity unchanged. Compare equal small taxes from the same initial price and quantity. Which evaluation is correct?
choices: Buyers initially bear more, but sellers bear more later; the legal seller tax becomes binding only in the long run.
Sellers initially bear more, but buyers bear more later; greater supply responsiveness also increases the quantity response to the tax.
Sellers bear more in both periods because the statute requires them to remit the tax, regardless of alternatives.
Burden becomes exactly equal later because both elasticity magnitudes exceed one, making relative sizes irrelevant.

stem: Before a tax, market price is $40. After a $12 unit tax, buyers pay $43 and sellers receive $31. A reform puts legal remittance on buyers without changing behavior or the tax size. Which combined inference is supported?
choices: Buyers bear 75% and sellers 25%; demand is relatively less elastic, and remittance alone reverses the $43/$31 price pair.
Buyers bear 25% and sellers 75%; supply is relatively less elastic, and remittance alone leaves the $43/$31 price pair unchanged.
Buyers bear 25% and sellers 75%; demand is relatively less elastic, so buyer remittance makes buyers bear the entire $12.
Buyers bear 50% and sellers 50%; the $12 wedge must be split evenly once both sides participate in the market.

stem: A business owner already spent $2,000 on a project. Finishing the project costs another $500 and will bring in $800. What should matter for the decision?
choices: The extra $500 cost and extra $800 benefit
The full $2,500 spent across the whole project
Only the sunk $2,000
Only whether the project feels successful

stem: A neighborhood app awards a visible badge for weekly recycling. Participation rises among users who value recognition but barely changes for others. What is the best interpretation?
choices: A nonmonetary incentive can produce different responses across people
The badge guarantees recycling because everyone can see it
Recognition is not an incentive because no cash changes hands
Different responses prove the badge did not change any payoff

stem: A new toll reduces traffic on a busy road. What does this show?
choices: People respond to the higher cost of using the road
Scarcity has been eliminated
The road is now a public good
Demand for driving must have increased

stem: A delivery truck creates noise for residents who are not customers. Why is this an externality?
choices: The cost falls on third parties outside the delivery exchange
The firm pays for fuel and driver time
Customers receive packages they ordered
The service operates in a city market

stem: A market has one dominant seller that can influence price. Why might the market outcome be inefficient?
choices: Scarcity disappears when one seller dominates
Market power can distort price and quantity
Opportunity cost no longer applies
The dominant seller must produce the efficient quantity.

stem: An economist uses a PPF to show how producing more military goods requires producing fewer consumer goods. What is the model showing?
choices: Tradeoffs and opportunity cost
Tax incidence
A binding price ceiling
A market surplus

stem: An economy moves from a point inside its PPF to a point on the PPF. What happened?
choices: It reached an unattainable point
It used idle resources more efficiently
It created a tax wedge
It shifted demand left

stem: An economy gets better technology for producing both goods. What happens to its PPF?
choices: It shifts inward
It becomes a price ceiling
It shifts outward
It creates a shortage

stem: A point is outside the PPF today but becomes attainable after an increase in capital and technology. What changed?
choices: The market price was fixed
Demand decreased
The economy moved inside the PPF
The economy's productive capacity increased

stem: An economist says, 'A higher minimum wage will reduce employment among low-skill workers.' What kind of statement is this?
choices: Positive
Normative
A price floor
A circular-flow claim

stem: A commissioner says the city ought to favor safer streets even if travel takes longer. What makes this normative?
choices: The ability to measure travel time
The ranking of safety against travel time
The prediction that streets can change
The reference to a city decision

stem: The price of streaming subscriptions rises, and consumers buy fewer subscriptions. What happened?
choices: Quantity demanded decreased
Demand decreased
Supply increased
Demand shifted right

stem: Consumers expect laptop prices to rise next month, so more laptops are purchased today. What happens to current demand for laptops?
choices: Demand increases
Quantity demanded decreases
Supply decreases
Demand stays fixed because only current price matters

stem: A popular celebrity endorsement makes more buyers want a product at every price. What happens?
choices: Demand shifts right
Quantity demanded falls
Supply shifts left
The product's own price changed

stem: The price of tablets rises. What happens in the market for tablet cases, a complement?
choices: Demand for tablet cases decreases
Demand for tablet cases increases
Supply of tablet cases increases
Quantity supplied of tablets decreases

stem: The price of tea rises. If coffee is a substitute for tea, what happens to demand for coffee?
choices: Demand for coffee increases
Demand for coffee decreases
Quantity demanded of coffee decreases because coffee price changed
Supply of coffee decreases

stem: The price of a good falls, and sellers produce less of it. What happened?
choices: Quantity supplied decreased
Supply decreased
Demand increased
Supply shifted right

stem: A new machine lowers the cost of producing shoes. What happens to the supply of shoes?
choices: Supply increases
Supply decreases
Demand decreases
Quantity demanded decreases

stem: Several sellers leave the market. What happens to market supply?
choices: Supply decreases
Supply increases
Demand decreases
Quantity supplied rises

stem: An input used to make pizza becomes more expensive. What is the likely effect in the pizza market?
choices: Supply decreases and price rises
Supply increases and price falls
Demand increases and price rises
Quantity demanded increases because cost rose

stem: A product goes viral while firms' production conditions remain unchanged. How do the resulting demand shift and movement along supply change equilibrium?
choices: Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises

stem: Supply for a product decreases while demand stays the same. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
choices: Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises
Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls

stem: A market price is too low. Quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied. What pressure should occur in an unregulated market?
choices: Price should rise
Price should fall
Supply should vanish
Demand must be zero

stem: A market price is too high. Quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded. What pressure should occur in an unregulated market?
choices: Price should fall
Price should rise
Demand shifts right in response to unsold inventory
Supply shifts left before price can adjust

stem: A hurricane destroys part of the orange crop. What is the likely result in the orange market?
choices: Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
Quantity demanded rises because supply fell

stem: A new health report says blueberries are especially beneficial. What likely happens in the blueberry market?
choices: Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
Demand decreases, price falls, and quantity falls
Quantity supplied falls because demand rose

stem: The posted price is held below equilibrium, but buyers wait in long lines. What policy most likely caused this?
choices: A binding price ceiling
A binding price floor
A tax on sellers
An outward PPF shift

stem: A rent ceiling is set above the equilibrium rent. What is the likely result?
choices: The ceiling is not binding and has no effect
The ceiling creates a shortage
The ceiling creates a surplus
The ceiling shifts supply right

stem: A rent ceiling is set below equilibrium. Quantity demanded is 900 apartments and quantity supplied is 600. What occurs?
choices: A shortage of 300 apartments
A surplus of 300 apartments
A shortage of 1,500 apartments
No effect because ceilings are minimum prices

stem: A binding price ceiling tends to reduce the quality of rental housing because:
choices: Landlords have less incentive to maintain units when price cannot rise
Tenants always demand less housing at lower prices
Quantity supplied rises above quantity demanded
The ceiling is above equilibrium

stem: A minimum wage is set below the equilibrium wage. What is the likely result?
choices: The minimum wage is not binding
It creates unemployment
It creates a labor shortage
It shifts labor demand right

stem: A minimum wage is set above equilibrium. Labor supplied is 120,000 and labor demanded is 80,000. What is the labor surplus?
choices: 40,000 workers
80,000 workers
120,000 workers
200,000 workers

stem: A binding price floor in an agricultural market may lead to:
choices: Unsold surplus output
A shortage of the crop
A lower legal price
A movement down the demand curve caused by lower price

stem: A tax on sellers shifts the supply curve upward because:
choices: The tax raises the cost of selling each unit
The tax increases buyers' income
The tax makes demand perfectly elastic
The tax eliminates opportunity cost

stem: Before a tax, buyers pay $10 and sellers receive $10. After the tax, buyers pay $12 and sellers receive $8. What is the tax wedge?
A tax reduces the quantity sold from 100 units to 75 units. What is the best interpretation?
choices: The tax shrinks the size of the market
The tax eliminates scarcity
The tax increases both supply and demand
The tax causes quantity sold to rise

stem: A $6 tax causes buyers to pay $4 more than before and sellers to receive $2 less than before. Who bears more of the tax burden?
choices: Buyers
Sellers
Both sides bear zero burden
Only the government

stem: A tax is legally imposed on sellers, but buyers pay most of the burden. What explains this?
choices: Legal assignment does not determine economic burden
Sellers always avoid all taxes
Buyers became legally responsible for the tax after prices adjusted.
The market must have a price ceiling

stem: If demand is very inelastic and supply is elastic, who likely bears more of a tax?
choices: Buyers
Sellers
Both sides bear exactly zero
The side with more firms always bears it

stem: If supply is very inelastic and demand is elastic, who likely bears more of a tax?
choices: Sellers
Buyers
Only the government
No one because demand is elastic

stem: A binding price ceiling and a tax both reduce market efficiency, but they do so differently. Which statement is correct?
choices: A ceiling holds price below equilibrium, while a tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices
A ceiling always creates a surplus, while a tax always raises quantity
A tax eliminates scarcity, while a ceiling eliminates opportunity cost
Both policies are the same as a demand increase

stem: A price floor above equilibrium and a price ceiling below equilibrium both cause problems because:
choices: They prevent the market price from adjusting to equilibrium
They eliminate all gains from trade immediately
They make demand and supply irrelevant
They always increase the quantity traded

stem: A government policy keeps apartment rents below equilibrium. Which outcome is most likely over time?
choices: Shortages and nonprice rationing
Surpluses and unsold apartments
A rightward supply shift caused by lower rent
An increase in quantity supplied

stem: Why does the more elastic side of a market tend to bear less of a tax?
choices: It can adjust its behavior more easily in response to the tax.
A binding price floor absorbs part of the tax.
Elasticity affects only the legal assignment of the tax.
The more elastic side cannot change quantity when price changes.

stem: Which list contains all and only the efficient production points labeled in the PPF graph?
choices: A, B, C, D, E
A, B, C, D, F
A, B, C, E, G
A, B, D, E, F

stem: Refer to the PPF graph. Which point is attainable but inefficient?
choices: G
F
C
E

stem: Refer to the PPF graph. Which point is currently unattainable?
choices: F
A
G
D

stem: Refer to the PPF graph. Moving from B to C increases production of Good X by how many units?
Refer to the PPF graph. Moving from B to C requires giving up how many units of Good Y?
Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost of moving from C to D?
choices: 6 units of Good X
15 units of Good Y
20 units of Good Y
21 units of Good X

stem: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when moving from C to D?
choices: 6 units of Good Y
15 units of Good Y
2.5 units of Good Y
0.4 units of Good Y

stem: Use the graph. Compare the opportunity cost of Good X over A to B and D to E. Which numerical evidence and conclusion fit the PPF?
choices: The costs are 0.5 and 4 Y per X; opportunity cost rises as more X is produced.
The costs are 0.625 and 5 Y per X; opportunity cost stays constant as more X is produced.
The costs are 0.5 and 4 Y per X; opportunity cost stays constant as more X is produced.
The costs are 0.625 and 5 Y per X; opportunity cost rises as more X is produced.

stem: Refer to the PPF graph. If the economy moves from F to C, what has happened?
choices: The economy has moved from inefficient production to efficient production
The economy has moved from unattainable production to attainable production
The economy has reduced both goods
The economy has moved outside the PPF

stem: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which equilibrium is formed by D1 and S2?
choices: Price P1 and Quantity Q2
Price P2 and Quantity Q1
