Stay open to recover fixed building costs
Close at the normal time because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
Close only if average cost rises.

stem: A factory’s average cost is $14, while producing unit 101 raises total cost from $1,400 to $1,418. Which cost is relevant to the unit-101 decision?
choices: The $18 marginal cost of unit 101
The $14 average cost of existing output
The $1,418 total cost after production
The $1,400 cost already incurred

stem: A student studies an additional hour. The expected grade benefit is valued at 9 points and fatigue cost at 6 points. The net marginal benefit is:
choices: 3 points.
15 points.
6 points.
9 points.

stem: Marginal benefit is:
choices: The added benefit from one more unit.
A past benefit that cannot change.
Average benefit per unit.
Total benefit from all units.

stem: A cost is sunk when it:
choices: Will occur only if one more unit is chosen.
Has already occurred and cannot be recovered.
Changes with the current decision.
Equals the next-best alternative.

stem: The marginal rule says to continue while:
choices: Marginal benefit is at least as large as marginal cost.
Average cost is falling
Total benefit is positive
Past spending is large.

stem: A business earns $160,000 after explicit expenses. The owner gives up a $90,000 salary and $35,000 in rent. Economic profit is:
A restaurant owner uses a building she owns. Comparable rent is $40,000, and she gives up a $60,000 salaried job. The business earns $120,000 after explicit expenses. Economic profit is:
A self-employed designer earns $95,000 after explicit expenses but gives up a $72,000 salary and could rent the home studio for $18,000. Economic profit is:
An entrepreneur leaves a job paying $55,000 to run a business that earns $70,000 after paying all explicit expenses. Ignoring nonmoney benefits, the economic profit is:
Which seller is most clearly a price taker?
choices: A patented-drug producer.
A small grain farmer selling a standardized crop at a market quotation.
A sole local utility.
A platform with locked-in users.

stem: What makes sustained economic profit difficult in a competitive market?
choices: A single seller restricts output.
Buyers face high switching costs.
Entry by new firms expands supply.
Products become more unique.

stem: A market has many buyers and sellers and standardized products. What does this imply about an individual seller’s ability to set price?
choices: Each seller controls market demand.
Each seller can raise price without losing sales.
Buyers cannot compare offers.
An individual seller faces strong pressure to accept the market price.

stem: An online marketplace makes prices easy to compare and lets buyers switch with one click. This tends to:
choices: Create a monopoly automatically.
Make demand for every seller inelastic.
Reduce each seller’s ability to charge above rivals.
Eliminate all production costs.

stem: A price-taking seller is one that:
choices: Sets any price without losing customers.
Controls the total market supply.
Cannot noticeably affect the market price by changing its own output.
Faces no competitors.

stem: Which feature most supports a competitive market?
choices: One dominant seller.
Legal barriers blocking entry.
A unique product with no substitutes.
Many buyers and sellers with no single participant controlling price.

stem: Which observation most strongly contradicts the strict competitive-market model?
choices: A firm can raise price persistently without losing many customers.
A firm earns accounting profit in one month.
Market demand changes over time.
Some firms have different bookkeeping methods.

stem: A market has free entry but strong network effects favor the largest platform. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Legal freedom to enter makes the incumbent face perfectly elastic demand despite its user network.
Formal entry may be easy while effective competition remains weak.
Network effects remove the incumbent’s advantage because every entrant can start with an equally valuable user network.
The incumbent’s user advantage implies formal entry is restricted, so the premise of free entry cannot hold.

stem: A restaurant market has many sellers, but each offers a differentiated experience. Which statement is best?
choices: The market may be competitive in a broad sense without meeting the strict price-taking benchmark.
The large number of restaurants makes each a price taker despite customers’ preferences for particular experiences.
Differentiation gives each restaurant the pricing freedom of a sole supplier because other dining experiences are distinct.
Competition should be assessed only through price differences, since differences in service quality do not affect buyer choice.

stem: A firm in a competitive market raises price above the market price while rivals do not. The likely result is:
choices: Higher sales because price signals quality.
A sharp loss of customers to close substitutes.
No change because buyers cannot switch.
Automatic market-wide inflation.

stem: A licensing rule sharply limits new sellers. What is the most direct competitive effect?
choices: The rule guarantees lower prices.
The rule creates perfect information.
Reduced entry can increase the market power of existing sellers.
The rule makes every firm a price taker.

stem: A market has many sellers, but buyers face high search costs and cannot compare prices. Why might price-taking be weakened?
choices: Many sellers always eliminate market power.
High search costs strengthen competition by making buyers compare prices more carefully.
Price comparison is unrelated to competition.
Information frictions can give individual sellers some pricing discretion.

stem: Two exchanges each list hundreds of sellers of standardized grain. On X, buyers can immediately compare prices and switch suppliers. On Y, contracts impose large switching charges. Which claim best separates seller count from effective competition?
choices: An individual seller likely has less pricing discretion on Y because switching charges protect buyer choice.
The same seller count ensures equal pricing discretion even when switching costs differ.
An individual seller likely has less pricing discretion on X because buyers can readily use competing offers.
Standardization gives each seller a unique product, preventing price taking on either exchange.

stem: A market appears fragmented by seller count, but four firms own most capacity through subsidiaries. What should an analyst examine?
choices: Only the number of storefronts.
Whether prices are written in dollars.
Whether consumers enjoy variety.
Control of effective output rather than the number of brand names.

stem: A new technology lowers switching costs to nearly zero. Holding other factors constant, what competitive effect is most likely?
choices: Sellers face more elastic demand and less pricing discretion.
Sellers gain more market power.
Entry becomes legally impossible.
Market demand becomes perfectly inelastic.

stem: A wheat farmer sells at the posted market price because charging more would cause buyers to switch. This illustrates:
choices: Price-taking behavior.
Monopoly pricing.
A binding price floor.
Perfect price discrimination.

stem: If one small seller exits a highly competitive market, the market price usually changes little because:
choices: Demand becomes perfectly vertical.
The seller represents a tiny share of total market supply.
The seller owns a patent.
All remaining sellers coordinate prices.

stem: Which change would make a market less competitive?
choices: More firms entering.
Lower switching costs for buyers.
A merger that leaves one firm with substantial control over output.
Better price information.

stem: Why does easy entry matter in a competitive market?
choices: Economic profits attract new sellers, reducing market supply as existing firms divide sales among more rivals.
Economic profits attract new sellers, lowering each entrant’s costs until all firms share the same cost curve.
Economic profits attract new sellers, raising market demand as buyers redistribute purchases among rivals.
Economic profits attract new sellers, increasing competition and making those profits harder to sustain.

stem: A price taker is a seller that:
choices: Accepts the market price because its own output is too small to move it.
Sets the market price for all firms.
Has no production costs.
Faces no buyers.

stem: A market becomes more competitive when:
choices: One seller acquires rivals.
Entry and switching become easier.
Products lose all substitutes.
Buyers receive less price information.

stem: A faculty committee asks whether a new attendance rule will improve learning. An economist would first:
choices: Identify the behavioral mechanism and evidence needed to test it.
Declare the rule fair or unfair without analysis.
Assume attendance and learning are identical.
Ignore incentives created by the rule.

stem: When an economist estimates how a tax will affect employment, the economist is primarily:
choices: Making a moral judgment about fairness.
Providing positive analysis about likely consequences.
Guaranteeing the policy will pass.
Setting the tax rate by law.

stem: When policymakers ask an economist to compare costs and benefits, the economist should:
choices: Hide uncertainty to sound decisive.
Replace evidence with personal preference.
State assumptions and identify relevant tradeoffs.
Ignore who bears the costs.

stem: Which activity is most clearly part of an economist’s policy role?
choices: Voting on behalf of the legislature.
Enforcing the final regulation.
Declaring one value judgment scientifically correct.
Evaluating evidence about likely behavioral responses.

stem: Two studies estimate opposite effects of a policy. One uses a credible natural experiment; the other compares groups whose members chose whether to participate. What should matter most when evaluating the conflicting results?
choices: How convincingly each study establishes cause and effect.
Which result has the larger number.
Which author supports the preferred policy.
Whether both studies use percentages.

stem: An economist recommends a policy because it maximizes total surplus, while citizens prioritize equal treatment. The disagreement is primarily about:
choices: The arithmetic definition of surplus.
The normative criterion used to rank outcomes.
Whether incentives exist.
The distinction between micro and macro topics.

stem: A policy model predicts large benefits, but the data come from a different population and period. What is the central concern?
choices: Whether the evidence generalizes to the current setting.
Whether the policy has a money price.
Whether economists may use models.
Whether positive analysis is always normative.

stem: An economist is employed by an agency that benefits from a favorable estimate. What practice best protects credibility?
choices: Publish the preferred specification with full calculations, omitting the agency relationship to keep the report technical.
Disclose the agency interest, assumptions, alternatives and uncertainty so others can assess the estimate.
Have an agency colleague check the arithmetic, then report one point estimate to avoid confusing readers.
Report an interval from the chosen model, leaving model selection and alternative specifications to the agency.

stem: A policy has a positive expected net benefit but a small chance of catastrophic loss. Which addition is necessary?
choices: A claim that averages eliminate risk.
Removal of all low-probability outcomes.
Risk analysis beyond the expected-value calculation.
A conclusion based only on sunk costs.

stem: A report favors plan A because paid-work savings exceed its cash cost. A requires relatives to provide unpaid care; plan B purchases the same care. What comparison would correct the scope of the advice?
choices: Value caregiving time under both plans alongside cash and paid-work effects
Add unpaid care only to B because B records an invoice
Treat unpaid care as free because relatives are not paid
Remove paid-work savings so both plans contain only budget costs

stem: A model favors a recycling program if most households sort correctly. A pilot reports high collection but does not measure contamination; sorting is harder in the rollout area. What should precede the recommendation?
choices: Declare the program undesirable solely because compliance is uncertain
Measure correct sorting and test whether the ranking survives realistic rollout compliance
Treat collected tonnage as proof of the required compliance
Use the pilot average unchanged because the same program name is used

stem: A consolidation plan has aggregate gains but losses for remote users. A report says compensation makes everyone better off, although no compensation is funded. Which conclusion is warranted?
choices: An unfunded transfer can be counted as income already received
Any remote loss proves aggregate gains are mathematically impossible
Potential compensation does not establish actual gains for remote users; report the implemented distribution
Positive total gains mean the remote users must gain indirectly

stem: Two economists use different estimates of demand elasticity and reach different tax projections. What best explains the disagreement?
choices: They may share the same framework but use different empirical assumptions.
One of them must reject opportunity cost.
Economic analysis cannot use evidence.
Normative values are the only possible source of disagreement.

stem: An economist reports that a policy raises total surplus but imposes concentrated losses on one group. What should the report do next?
choices: Conclude that everyone benefits.
Separate the efficiency finding from the distributional consequence.
Ignore the losing group because total surplus rose.
Call the distributional judgment a positive fact.

stem: A forecast is highly sensitive to one uncertain parameter. The best policy advice is to:
choices: Use only the most favorable value.
Present one estimate as certain.
Report the sensitivity and show results under plausible values.
Remove the parameter from the model.

stem: A mayor asks whether rent control is “good.” What is the economist’s most useful first response?
choices: Answer solely from personal ideology.
Promise there will be no unintended consequences.
Treat the word good as a measurable price.
Clarify the objectives and analyze likely effects and tradeoffs.

stem: Positive policy analysis asks:
choices: What consequences are likely to occur.
Which outcome is morally best.
Which party should win.
Which value judgment is scientifically true.

stem: When a policy conclusion depends on an assumption, the economist should:
choices: Hide it from decision makers.
State the assumption and test how much it matters.
Treat it as a proven fact.
Replace it with a slogan.

stem: A bonus tied only to sales volume causes excessive discounting. What happened?
choices: Workers ignored the bonus and changed discounting for unrelated market reasons
Workers optimized the rewarded metric rather than total profit
The bonus eliminated every tradeoff involved in making sales
Sales volume became a public good shared equally by all firms

stem: A fee changes behavior for some people but not others. What is the best explanation?
choices: The fee is not an incentive.
All people have identical marginal benefits.
People face different constraints, preferences, and alternatives.
Only laws create incentives.

stem: A policy subsidizes an action many people already planned to take. What limits additional impact?
choices: Every payment creates an equal new action.
Subsidies cannot affect behavior.
The action has no opportunity cost.
Much of the spending is inframarginal rather than behavior-changing.

stem: A professor adds one point for each discussion post. How does the extra point affect the marginal decision to make one more post?
choices: The extra point raises the marginal benefit of one more post
The total course grade becomes the cost of every post
Scarcity disappears once points are available
The added point guarantees that every post improves learning

stem: A workplace gives public recognition to teams that finish safety training. What does the recognition directly change?
choices: The nonmonetary benefit of completing the training
The cash wage paid for every hour of training
The certainty that every employee completes training
The final safety outcome rather than the choice payoff

stem: A late fee is intended to:
choices: Eliminate opportunity cost.
Reward late payment.
Raise the cost of delaying payment.
Make demand perfectly inelastic.

stem: A policy rewards hospitals for reducing readmissions. Hospitals improve follow-up care but also become reluctant to admit high-risk patients. What is the strongest evaluation?
choices: Lower readmissions establish better care for the original patient population; admission changes are a separate efficiency gain.
High-risk avoidance explains the improvement completely; follow-up changes cannot independently contribute to the measured result.
Better follow-up establishes improved access; compare hospitals using raw readmission rates to retain the selection effect.
Improved follow-up and avoidance of risky patients can both lower readmissions; compare access and risk-adjusted outcomes.

stem: Why can a small probability of a severe penalty sometimes have little deterrent effect?
choices: People may discount unlikely enforcement or misperceive the risk.
Only rewards influence behavior.
The expected cost is always equal to the maximum penalty.
Penalties have no opportunity cost.

stem: A tax credit for home improvements is claimed by many households that would have renovated anyway. Why might the credit generate relatively little additional renovation?
choices: The credit has no budget cost.
A large share of payments does not change marginal behavior.
Households never respond to prices.
The policy creates a price floor.

stem: The same dollar penalty sharply changes behavior for low-income households but barely affects high-income households. What does this show?
choices: All people respond identically to a given dollar amount.
The penalty is not an incentive.
Responses depend on constraints and the size of the incentive relative to resources.
Income has no role in marginal choices.

stem: A school rewards perfect attendance, and some sick students attend class. This is:
choices: Proof that incentives never work.
A positive externality by definition.
An elimination of scarcity.
An unintended response to the incentive.

stem: A performance bonus is based only on the number of calls handled, and service quality falls. What design problem occurred?
choices: The metric rewarded quantity while omitting quality.
Workers ignored all incentives.
The bonus created a public good.
Higher output necessarily means higher quality.

stem: Which statement best captures an economic incentive?
choices: A change in expected benefits or costs that can alter behavior
Only a direct cash payment that rewards the intended behavior
A rule that guarantees every person makes the same choice
The final outcome observed after a policy is introduced

stem: Which statement describes an unintended response to an incentive?
choices: A planned result that occurs exactly as policy designers expected
People respond to a rule in a way that produces an unplanned result
Evidence that the original rule created no behavioral pressure at all
A response that every person makes in exactly the same way

stem: Which case is a negative externality?
choices: Noise from a venue reducing nearby residents’ well-being.
A buyer paying the posted price.
A student receiving private tutoring that affects only the student and tutor.
A firm lowering its own cost.

stem: Why might a public good be underprovided privately?
choices: Use by one person prevents all others from using it.
People can benefit without paying, weakening voluntary funding.
Exclusion is effortless.
Every consumer reveals exact willingness to pay.

stem: What is the standard efficiency concern with market power?
choices: Every firm earns zero accounting profit.
All prices fall below marginal cost.
Output may be restricted below the level where buyer value exceeds production cost.
Products become nonrival when one firm sets the market price.

stem: A shared office kitchen is repeatedly left dirty because each worker expects others to clean it. This resembles:
choices: A common-resource or collective-action problem.
A perfectly enforced private property right.
A positive price signal.
A competitive firm’s shutdown decision.

stem: At the next unit of a competitive product, a buyer values it at $18, the producer uses $14 of resources, and pollution harms neighbors by $6. Which outcome does a $6 per-unit tax encourage?
choices: Forgo the unit: private gains are $4 but net social benefit is -$2.
Produce the unit: the $4 private gain measures its full social benefit.
Produce the unit: $6 of tax revenue makes its net social benefit $4.
Forgo the unit: every taxed unit has zero social benefit.

stem: Why can a common resource be overused?
choices: It is nonrival and nonexcludable.
Users receive the private benefit while sharing depletion costs with others.
Its price is always above marginal cost.
No one can access it.

stem: A dominant seller withholds an additional unit that a buyer values at $25 even though producing it uses $18 of resources. There are no externalities. Which mechanism explains the lost efficiency?
choices: The withheld trade creates a $7 external pollution cost paid by a third party.
The seller’s lost sales revenue equals the social gain, regardless of production cost.
Restricting output can preserve the seller’s price while forgoing a trade with $7 of social gains.
Any price above resource cost proves that expanding output would reduce total surplus.

stem: A seller knows a used car’s quality, but buyers cannot distinguish good cars from bad ones. What problem can result?
choices: A public-good free-rider problem.
A positive production externality.
A binding price floor by definition.
Adverse selection from asymmetric information.

stem: Vaccination creates an external benefit, but a fixed number of appointments is already fully used. A subsidy is introduced without expanding capacity or changing how appointments are allocated. Which assessment best separates the externality diagnosis from this policy’s current effect?
choices: Private demand rises, but vaccinations cannot rise yet; additional spillover benefits require more capacity or a better allocation.
The subsidy necessarily raises vaccinations to the efficient quantity despite the fixed appointment limit.
Fixed capacity means the external benefit disappears and the original externality diagnosis is false.
Subsidy spending itself equals new transmission benefits even when the vaccinated group is unchanged.

stem: A fishery is open to many boats, and each boat ignores how its catch reduces future stocks for others. Which policy logic fits?
choices: Subsidize every additional catch.
Limit or price access so users face more of the depletion cost.
Remove all information about stocks.
Set a price ceiling on fish without limiting harvest.

stem: A broadband network has high fixed cost and low marginal cost. Marginal-cost pricing would expand valuable access but leave a financing deficit. Average-cost pricing can cover costs but excludes some users whose value exceeds marginal cost. Public support has a real collection cost. What information is needed to choose between the two rules?
choices: Only whether marginal-cost pricing creates an accounting loss, because loss proves social inefficiency.
Only whether average-cost pricing breaks even, because break-even proves maximum social surplus.
The extra access benefits net of resource cost, compared with the real cost of financing the deficit.
Only the subsidy payment, because every transferred dollar is a destroyed social resource.

stem: A factory’s pollution harms nearby residents without compensating them. This is:
choices: A public good.
A positive consumption externality.
A negative production externality.
A competitive price signal with no omitted cost.

stem: Which feature makes national defense a public good?
choices: It is sold by one private firm.
Its marginal cost is always zero.
Consumers can be excluded easily.
It is broadly nonrival and difficult to exclude nonpayers.

stem: An externality is:
choices: A cost or benefit affecting a third party outside the transaction.
Any change in the market price.
A government expenditure.
A cost paid fully by the buyer.

stem: A public good is defined by:
choices: Government ownership alone.
Nonrival consumption and difficulty excluding nonpayers.
A high market price.
Private benefits only.

stem: Price and quantity both rise. A report concludes that demand increased and that supply could not have changed. Which interpretation is strongest?
choices: Only a supply increase fits because more output always means greater supply.
A demand increase alone fits the observations, but simultaneous supply changes are possible; the two observations do not identify every shift.
Only a supply decrease fits because a higher price always means reduced supply.
Demand and supply must both be unchanged because equilibrium quantities cannot rise together with price.

stem: Resources currently used in a product would generate next year’s revenue of $120 and total opportunity cost of $140. An alternative use would generate revenue of $90 and opportunity cost of $70. Past spending is unrecoverable. Which allocation follows from the expected net-value signals?
choices: Stay because $120 revenue exceeds the alternative’s $90, even though opportunity cost is higher.
Stay until past spending is recovered because sunk costs determine the best future use.
Move to the alternative: expected net value improves from −$20 to +$20, regardless of unrecoverable past spending.
Move only if the alternative’s revenue exceeds $140, ignoring its lower opportunity cost.

stem: A trip gives a driver benefit $6, uses $3 of private resources and imposes $4 of delay on others. A congestion toll equals the external delay cost and its collection uses no resources. Which prediction explains the corrected price signal?
choices: The driver takes the trip because the $4 toll is a transfer and therefore cannot affect private incentives.
The driver declines because the toll creates $4 of additional social resource cost beyond the original delay.
The driver takes the trip because only the $3 private resource use can enter the efficiency comparison.
The driver faces $7 in private cost plus toll and declines the trip; this avoids a trip whose $7 social resource cost exceeds its $6 benefit.

stem: A hospital posts the real-time wait at each clinic, and patients shift toward shorter waits. The wait-time information acts like:
choices: A price floor.
A guarantee of unlimited capacity.
A nonmonetary signal coordinating demand across locations.
A supply curve shift caused by income.

stem: A rising market price typically signals producers that:
choices: Demand must have fallen.
Resources should leave the market immediately.
No adjustment is needed.
The good has become relatively more valuable to buyers or scarcer to supply.

stem: A price rises while quantity sold also rises. Which inference is best supported?
choices: Demand likely increased, but additional evidence is needed if several forces changed.
Supply must have decreased and nothing else changed.
The higher price caused quantity demanded to rise.
Price signals cannot coordinate markets.

stem: A firm earns losses despite producing a product consumers value. What allocation signal do losses send?
choices: Consumers place no value on the product.
Resources may create more value in alternative uses.
The firm should expand regardless of cost.
Losses prove the market is competitive.

stem: A high price reflects both strong demand and a temporary supply disruption. Why can the price alone be insufficient for policy diagnosis?
choices: The same price movement can arise from different underlying shifts.
Prices contain no information.
Demand and supply never change together.
A high price always proves monopoly power.

stem: A subsidy lowers the buyer’s out-of-pocket price while paying sellers an additional amount. How can the subsidy distort the price signal buyers receive?
choices: The resource cost disappears.
The social resource cost can be hidden from buyers by the subsidized price.
Sellers receive no incentive to expand.
Quantity demanded must fall.

stem: A congested road has no toll. What price-signal problem is present?
choices: The road has no opportunity cost.
Demand for travel must be zero.
Drivers do not face the full marginal congestion cost they impose.
A market price is unnecessary because congestion is beneficial.

stem: A sudden price spike attracts rapid entry, but the shock disappears before new capacity arrives. What does this show?
choices: The original price contained no information.
Supply never responds to incentives.
Entry always stabilizes price immediately.
Price signals can be accurate yet responses may arrive with lags.

stem: An electricity supplier charges more during evening peaks and less overnight. Some households can delay appliance use, while others need electricity immediately. Which response shows how the price signal can coordinate scarce capacity?
choices: Flexible users shift use into the evening, reducing peak pressure because peak prices are higher.
Inflexible users must stop consuming before the price difference can affect peak demand.
Flexible users shift some use overnight, reducing peak pressure without requiring every household to shift.
All households must use less electricity over the full day for timing prices to reduce peak demand.

stem: A government caps a medicine price and separately rations access through waiting lists. What has occurred?
choices: Scarcity has been eliminated.
The ceiling increased the legal market-clearing price.
Waiting time has no opportunity cost.
Nonprice rationing has replaced part of the suppressed price signal.

stem: A carbon price raises energy prices. What information is the policy trying to add to the market signal?
choices: The external climate cost associated with emissions.
A guarantee that all energy use ends.
The producer’s accounting profit only.
A fixed quantity demanded at every price.

stem: A drought raises the price of water-intensive crops. How does the price signal help coordinate adjustment?
choices: Consumers conserve and producers seek ways to expand or redirect supply.
Consumers buy more solely because price rose.
Producers reduce output because revenue is higher.
The price prevents scarcity from existing.

stem: The price of a product falls after a new production technology spreads. What information does the lower price convey?
choices: Demand must have increased.
The product can be supplied at lower cost or has become less scarce.
Every producer should enter immediately.
The product has become a public good.

stem: A shortage persists because a legal ceiling prevents price from rising. Which coordinating signal is muted?
choices: The signal to increase quantity demanded and reduce quantity supplied.
The signal that opportunity costs are zero.
The signal to conserve consumption and expand supply.
The signal that all buyers value the good equally.

stem: High profits in a market can function as a signal that:
choices: Consumers should stop valuing the product.
Entry must be legally prohibited.
Production costs are irrelevant.
Resources may earn more by moving into that activity.

stem: When a price rises, buyers generally receive a signal to:
choices: Conserve or seek substitutes.
Demand more because the price is higher.
Ignore scarcity.
Expand market supply themselves.

stem: What response does a higher market price normally encourage from sellers?
choices: Reduce output because revenue rises.
Expand quantity supplied when feasible.
Increase quantity demanded.
Treat costs as zero.

stem: At one price, Firm A supplies 8 units and Firm B supplies 11 units. Market quantity supplied is:
choices: 19 units.
8 units.
9.5 units.
11 units.

stem: The price of oranges rises, and growers offer more oranges while all nonprice determinants stay fixed. This is:
choices: An increase in supply.
An increase in quantity supplied.
A decrease in supply.
A decrease in quantity supplied.

stem: The price of an important input falls. What happens to supply, other things equal?
choices: Supply shifts left.
Quantity supplied falls along the curve.
Supply shifts right.
Demand shifts right.

stem: A subsidy lowers marginal cost by $3 per unit, while a regulation raises marginal cost by $3 per unit. What happens to supply if those are the only changes?
choices: Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers marginal cost by more than the regulation raises it
Supply shifts left because the regulation raises marginal cost by more than the subsidy lowers it
Quantity supplied rises along the original curve because the product's market price increases
The two per-unit effects offset, so supply is unchanged.

stem: Four firms each supply q=2P units at every price. Demand is Qd=120-4P. One firm exits permanently, with the surviving firms’ schedules unchanged. Which statement correctly compares market equilibrium before and after exit?
choices: Price rises from $10 to $12; quantity falls from 80 to 72 as remaining firms move along their unchanged individual schedules.
Price stays $10 and quantity becomes 60; unchanged individual schedules prevent equilibrium price adjustment.
Price falls from $10 to $8; exit shifts each surviving firm’s individual supply curve right.
Price rises from $10 to $12 and quantity rises from 80 to 96 because four firms remain in the aggregate schedule.

stem: Technology improves while the expected future selling price rises sharply and firms store current output. What is the strongest conclusion about current supply?
choices: Current supply increases because improved technology and storing output for future sale both add to current market supply.
The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the strength of each effect.
Current supply decreases because the expected future price rises sharply, which establishes that withholding outweighs the technology improvement.
Quantity supplied moves along one curve because both events change the product's current price.

stem: Market supply at a given price is the:
choices: Sum of the quantities all sellers are willing and able to offer.
Quantity supplied by the single largest seller at that price.
Average quantity each seller plans to produce at that price.
Total quantity buyers are willing and able to purchase at that price.

stem: A new machine lowers unit production cost, while a new per-unit environmental fee raises cost. Which conclusion about supply is justified without knowing the size of each change?
choices: Supply must shift right because improved technology outweighs any higher per-unit fee.
Supply must shift left because a new per-unit fee outweighs any technological saving.
Supply must remain unchanged because there is one cost decrease and one cost increase.
The net supply shift cannot be determined without comparing the two cost changes.

stem: Twenty new firms enter a market, but an essential input becomes more expensive for every firm. What is the most careful conclusion about market supply?
choices: Entry pushes supply right and higher input cost pushes it left, leaving the net effect uncertain.
Market supply must rise because entry outweighs the input-cost increase.
Market supply must fall because higher input costs outweigh entry.
Market supply stays fixed because both events only change quantity supplied along the curve.

stem: Demand rises and the market price increases. Firms respond by producing more with the same technology, input prices, and number of sellers. Which statement is correct?
choices: Supply shifts right because firms produce more.
Quantity supplied rises along an unchanged supply curve.
Supply shifts left because the product is now more expensive.
Both supply and quantity supplied must increase.

stem: Workers accept lower wages, but producers also expect the product’s future price to rise and hold inventory for later sale. What can be concluded about current supply?
choices: Supply must rise because lower wages dominate the decision to withhold inventory.
Supply must fall because withholding inventory dominates the wage reduction.
The net supply shift is uncertain because lower wages and inventory withholding work in opposite directions.
Supply stays fixed because wages and expected future prices only move firms along supply.

stem: At $30, three sellers offer 12, 18, and 25 units; at $35 they offer 16, 24, and 30 units. Calculate both market quantities and infer what the comparison represents.
choices: Market quantity rises from 55 to 70 units, representing movement along market supply
Market supply shifts right from 55 to 70 units because the number of sellers increases
Market quantity falls from 70 to 55 units, representing movement down market supply
Market supply shifts left by 15 units because individual quantities are aggregated vertically

stem: At a fixed price, 60 identical firms initially supply 8 units each. An input-cost decline raises each surviving firm’s supply to 10 units, but some firms exit. Total supply at that price is unchanged. How many firms exited, and what does the unchanged total imply?
choices: 10 firms; the cost and exit effects offset at this price.
12 firms; neither input costs nor firm exit shifted supply.
15 firms; a higher product price offset the firm exits.
12 firms; the cost and exit effects offset at this price.

stem: A per-unit input cost falls by $4, but a new per-unit tax raises cost by $6. Holding other determinants fixed, what is the likely supply effect?
choices: Supply shifts left because net marginal cost rises by $2 per unit.
Supply shifts right because any input-cost decline dominates a tax.
Supply is unchanged because the two policies offset exactly.
Only quantity supplied falls along the same curve.

stem: Producers expect a temporary price spike next month and can store the product cheaply. What pattern is most plausible?
choices: Current and future supply both rise because firms expand production immediately and store none of it.
Current supply falls as firms hold inventory, while future supply rises when the inventory is released.
Current supply rises as firms sell inventory before the expected spike, while future supply falls.
Current quantity supplied falls along one curve because the current product price decreases.

stem: A surge in demand raises the equilibrium price. Firms expand output, and new firms later enter the industry. Which sequence is correct?
choices: First supply shifts right; later quantity supplied falls along the curve.
Both responses are movements along the original supply curve.
First quantity supplied rises along the curve; later entry shifts market supply right.
Both responses are supply shifts caused by the good’s own price.

stem: A drought reduces crop yields, while the market price of the crop rises because demand is unchanged. What is the best description?
choices: Supply shifts right because the higher equilibrium price encourages more production after the drought.
Quantity supplied falls along the original supply curve while the curve itself remains unchanged.
Demand shifts left because the drought changes buyer preferences rather than production conditions.
Supply shifts left, and the higher price causes movement upward along the new supply curve.

stem: The government begins paying producers a subsidy for every unit sold. What happens to market supply, other things equal?
choices: Supply shifts left because the subsidy increases firms’ effective production cost.
Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers the effective marginal cost of selling output.
Quantity supplied rises along the original curve because only the market price changed.
Demand shifts right because the payment is received directly by buyers.

stem: The good’s own price declines while every non-price determinant stays fixed. Which demand-side change occurs?
choices: Demand increases through a rightward shift of the curve.
Demand decreases through a leftward shift of the curve.
Quantity demanded stays fixed because the curve did not shift.
Quantity demanded increases through a movement along the existing curve.

stem: Which event shifts demand for bus rides to the right?
choices: The price of subway rides, a substitute, increases.
The price of bus rides decreases while all non-price determinants remain fixed.
Bus companies add routes and lower their operating costs.
The cost of diesel fuel decreases for bus operators.

stem: Income falls and purchases of instant noodles rise. What does this evidence suggest?
choices: Instant noodles are a normal good for these consumers
Instant noodles are an inferior good for these consumers
A lower noodle price caused movement along the demand curve
A supply decrease raised purchases despite the income change

stem: Electric scooters are normal goods. Household incomes rise, but a close substitute becomes cheaper. At an unchanged scooter price, can we predict the direction of scooter purchases without knowing the strength of each effect?
choices: Yes, purchases rise; higher income and the cheaper substitute both push demand right.
Yes, purchases fall; higher income and the cheaper substitute both push demand left.
No; higher income pushes demand right while the cheaper substitute pushes it left.
No change occurs; an unchanged scooter price prevents any change in quantity purchased.

stem: Movie tickets are a normal good. Income rises, but the price of streaming subscriptions, a substitute, falls. What is the strongest conclusion about movie-ticket demand?
choices: Demand rises because higher income and a cheaper substitute both increase demand for movie tickets.
Demand falls because the cheaper substitute lowers ticket demand while income does not shift demand for a normal good.
Quantity demanded changes along one curve because both events change the ticket price
The net shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other

stem: Concert attendance falls after ticket prices rise. A fan claims demand decreased. Surveys show fans’ planned purchases at each fixed price are unchanged, but later a popular performer joins the tour. Which sequence is supported?
choices: The first decline is movement along demand; the later performer change can shift demand right.
The first decline is a leftward demand shift; the later performer change is movement down that curve.
Both events are movements along demand because each changes the number of tickets sold.
Both events shift demand left because ticket price and performer popularity are market conditions.

stem: Income rises for a normal good while the price of a close substitute falls. What can be concluded about demand for the normal good?
choices: The net demand shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other.
Demand must rise because income rises for a normal good.
Demand must fall because the substitute becomes cheaper.
Demand stays fixed; both changes are movements along the original curve.

stem: A survey shows buyers want more electric scooters at every listed price than they did last month. Which statement is most precise?
choices: Quantity demanded increased because the scooter price fell.
Demand increased, so the entire demand schedule shifted right.
Demand increased only at the market price.
The law of demand stopped applying to electric scooters.

stem: Coffee is a normal good. Consumer income rises, buyers expect coffee prices to fall next month, and the current price of tea, a substitute, rises. What can be concluded about current coffee demand?
choices: Demand must rise: two favorable determinants outweigh one unfavorable determinant regardless of their sizes.
Demand must fall: an expected future price decline outweighs current income and substitute-price effects.
Demand is indeterminate: income and the substitute price raise it, while waiting for a lower future price reduces it.
Demand is unchanged: income, expectations, and related-good prices affect only movement along the curve.

stem: A market price below equilibrium creates a:
choices: Surplus.
Balanced market.
Leftward demand shift.
Shortage.

stem: What pressure does a surplus create in an unregulated market?
choices: Sellers lower prices to clear unwanted inventories.
Buyers bid prices higher because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
Demand shifts right until buyers absorb every unit offered for sale.
Supply shifts left because firms are holding unwanted inventories.

stem: If demand increases while supply is unchanged, equilibrium price and quantity usually:
choices: Both decrease.
Both increase.
Price rises and quantity falls.
Price falls and quantity rises.

stem: Demand increases while supply decreases. Which equilibrium outcome is certain?
choices: The equilibrium quantity rises.
The equilibrium quantity falls.
The equilibrium price rises.
The equilibrium price falls.

stem: Both demand and supply shift left in the same market. Which equilibrium result can be stated without knowing the shift sizes?
choices: The equilibrium price rises.
The equilibrium price falls.
The equilibrium quantity rises.
The equilibrium quantity falls.

stem: At the current price, quantity demanded is 400 and quantity supplied is 520. Which explanation diagnoses the imbalance and traces the adjustment along the existing curves without a price control?
choices: A surplus pushes price down, raising quantity demanded and lowering quantity supplied until they converge
A shortage pushes price up, lowering quantity demanded and raising quantity supplied until they converge
A surplus shifts demand right while price remains fixed until inventories clear
A shortage shifts supply left while buyers reduce quantity demanded

stem: At the equilibrium price, quantity demanded is:
choices: Greater than quantity supplied.
Equal to quantity supplied.
Less than quantity supplied.
Unrelated to quantity supplied.

stem: Demand and supply both increase. The equilibrium quantity rises, but the equilibrium price is unchanged. What does this reveal?
choices: Neither curve shifted because an unchanged price proves the market did not move.
Demand increased more than supply, so price should have risen instead of staying fixed.
The price effects offset, while both shifts raise equilibrium quantity.
Supply decreased while demand increased, creating offsetting quantity effects.

stem: At the current price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. What market condition exists?
choices: A surplus exists because sellers offer more than buyers want.
A shortage exists because buyers want more than sellers offer.
The market is in equilibrium because both quantities are positive.
Demand must shift left before any price adjustment can occur.

stem: A policy proposal claims it will “improve fairness” and also predicts that employment will rise. What should an analyst do first?
choices: Separate the fairness judgment from the testable employment prediction.
Treat both statements as positive because they concern policy.
Reject both statements because models cannot study policy.
Combine both statements into one numerical forecast.

stem: A worker receives a 4 percent nominal wage increase while consumer prices rise 6 percent. What calculation is needed before judging the change in living standards?
choices: Add wage and price growth to obtain a 10 percent real gain.
Adjust the wage for inflation; the real wage fell about 2 percent.
Use the unemployment rate as the wage deflator.
Compare the nominal wage only with nominal GDP.

stem: A drought shifts the supply of staple food left, while a binding price ceiling remains fixed below the new equilibrium price. Which combined result is most likely?
choices: The shortage disappears because the ceiling protects buyers.
Quantity supplied rises because the legal price is unchanged.
The market reaches the new equilibrium without any rationing.
The shortage grows and nonprice rationing becomes more important.

stem: A country puts unemployed workers and idle factories back to work without gaining new technology. How does this appear on its PPF?
choices: Production moves to the existing frontier, showing greater efficiency but no growth.
The frontier shifts outward, showing growth in productive capacity.
Production moves outside the frontier, becoming unattainable.
The frontier shifts inward because idle resources were used.

stem: A technological improvement affects only the production of medical equipment, not food. How does the PPF change?
choices: The entire frontier shifts inward by the same amount.
The medical-equipment intercept moves outward; food stays fixed.
The frontier pivots outward toward the food axis only.
The economy moves along an unchanged frontier toward more food.

stem: Why is a typical PPF bowed outward from the origin?
choices: All resources are equally productive in every use.
Opportunity cost falls as specialization increases.
Specialized resources cause rising opportunity cost.
The economy is producing inside the frontier.

stem: Moving from bundle A to B gains 5 machines and sacrifices 10 tons of food. Moving from B to C gains another 5 machines and sacrifices 20 tons of food. What does the pattern show?
choices: The opportunity cost of machines rises from 2 to 4 tons of food per machine.
The opportunity cost of machines falls from 4 to 2 tons per machine.
The opportunity cost remains constant at 3 tons per machine.
Bundle C must lie inside the PPF because its food output is lower.

stem: Country A chooses more capital goods and fewer consumer goods today than Country B, with otherwise similar resources. What is the likely long-run implication?
choices: Country A must have a lower future PPF because current consumption is smaller.
Country A may gain more future capacity because it produces more capital goods now.
Country B necessarily grows faster because consumption creates capital automatically.
Neither choice can affect future production possibilities.

stem: A disaster destroys equipment used only to produce electric power, while agricultural capacity is unchanged. What happens to the PPF?
choices: It shifts outward equally for both goods.
It pivots inward toward the agricultural axis only.
Only the electric-power intercept moves inward.
It remains fixed because the economy can move along the frontier.

stem: A production point lies inside the PPF. How should it be classified?
choices: It is unattainable with current resources and technology.
It is efficient because it uses fewer resources.
It is attainable but inefficient because resources are underused.
It proves the economy has experienced long-run growth.

stem: For one poster, Team A gives up 2 flyers and Team B gives up 5. Another pair of teams each gives up 3 flyers per poster. Which pair has a basis for gains from specialization in this two-good model?
choices: Only the first pair, because its opportunity costs differ.
Only the second pair, because its opportunity costs match.
Both pairs, because having two teams is sufficient.
Neither pair, because both activities use scarce time.

stem: Maya voluntarily exchanges her spare notebook for Lee’s spare pen, and Lee voluntarily agrees. Both understand what they will receive. What does their choice suggest?
choices: They assign exactly the same value to the notebook and pen.
Maya expects a gain, while Lee expects a loss.
Each prefers what they receive to what they give up.
Lee expects a gain, while Maya expects a loss.

stem: Ana prepares 6 lessons per hour and Ben prepares 4. A coordinator concludes that Ana also has comparative advantage in lessons. What additional information would test that conclusion?
choices: How much tutoring each gives up per lesson.
How many lessons Ana and Ben produce together.
Whether Ana can prepare any lessons at all.
Whether the lesson count is measured per hour or per day.

stem: Lena gives up 1 report to make a presentation; Omar gives up 3. A manager assigns the next presentation to Omar because his opportunity cost is higher. If either can prepare it, what correction follows?
choices: Keep Omar; his assignment preserves 2 more reports.
Choose Lena; her assignment preserves 2 more reports.
Keep Omar; his assignment preserves 4 more reports.
Choose Lena; her assignment preserves 4 more reports.

stem: Lena gives up 1 report per presentation; Omar gives up 3. Lena offers one presentation to Omar for 2 reports. Ignoring exchange costs, who gains relative to doing the task themselves?
choices: Only Lena: she gains 1 report while Omar loses 1.
Only Omar: he gains 1 report while Lena loses 1.
Neither: each loses 1 report at this rate.
Both: Lena receives 1 more report than her cost, and Omar saves 1 report.

stem: Nia can produce more of either good per hour than Sol. Yet each loaf costs Nia 2 shirts and Sol 1 shirt in forgone output. With constant tradeoffs and no trade costs, which proposed loaf-for-shirt exchange can benefit both?
choices: Nia supplies loaves at 1.5 shirts per loaf.
Sol supplies loaves at 2.5 shirts per loaf.
Sol supplies loaves at 1.5 shirts per loaf.
Nia supplies loaves at 0.5 shirts per loaf.

stem: Specialization frees resources worth 60 units of output, but the proposed shipping plan uses 70 units. A different carrier would use 35 units and require 10 units of extra monitoring. Which plan increases net resources?
choices: Both carriers: the original gains 60 units and the alternative gains 95.
Only the alternative carrier: the original loses 10 units and the alternative gains 15.
Only the original carrier: monitoring makes the alternative lose 45 units.
Neither carrier: any positive exchange cost eliminates specialization gains.

stem: Opening trade yields consumer gains of $90 million and producer losses of $50 million. Moving displaced workers uses $12 million of real resources. A proposed $20 million domestic transfer to producers costs another $5 million to administer. Which evaluation includes efficiency and distribution?
choices: Net national gain is $3 million; producers remain $30 million below their initial position after the transfer.
Net national gain is $43 million; producers recover fully because the transfer exceeds adjustment costs.
Net national gain is $23 million; producers remain $30 million below their initial position after the transfer.
Net national gain is $28 million; producers recover fully because aggregate consumer gains exceed their losses.

stem: A gives up 6 grain per machine and B gives up 4. Technology lowers A’s cost to 3 while B’s cost stays 4. They had traded at 5 grain per machine. Which conclusion follows under constant costs?
choices: Machine comparative advantage stays with B; a rate between 3 and 4 benefits both because only absolute productivity changed.
Machine comparative advantage switches to A; the old rate of 5 still benefits both because it exceeds A’s new cost.
Neither has machine comparative advantage now; technological progress eliminates the need to compare forgone grain.
Machine comparative advantage switches to A; the old rate no longer benefits the importer, and a rate between 3 and 4 can benefit both.

stem: A project lead is faster at every task but delegates data entry. Which concept explains the choice?
choices: A price ceiling that limits payment for outsourced data entry
Absolute advantage because the lead is faster at data entry
Comparative advantage based on the opportunity cost of the lead's time
Elimination of scarce time after the work is delegated

stem: A city can buy snowplow service from a neighboring county for less than the resources required to provide it internally. What does opportunity-cost reasoning suggest?
choices: The city should remain self-sufficient even at a higher resource cost
The neighboring county cannot benefit from any voluntary contract
Money prices make the city's forgone alternatives irrelevant
Contracting can free city resources for other services

stem: Mira gives up 1 report to prepare a presentation; Sol gives up 3 reports. Which fact determines comparative advantage in presentations?
choices: Mira gives up fewer reports per presentation
Sol may complete more total tasks in a day
Mira charges a lower money price after exchange
Sol has a higher wage in an unrelated job

stem: With the same resources, East Farm can harvest 12 crates while West Farm can harvest 8. What does this establish?
choices: East Farm has an absolute advantage in harvesting crates
East Farm must have comparative advantage in every crop.
West Farm has the lower opportunity cost of harvesting
Both farms gain equally from every possible exchange

stem: Why can two people gain from trade even when one is better at producing both goods?
choices: The less productive person must accept a loss.
Absolute advantage guarantees equal output.
Their opportunity costs can still differ.
Trade removes the need to specialize.

stem: Specialization based on comparative advantage tends to:
choices: Make both producers self-sufficient.
Require identical opportunity costs.
Prevent either side from consuming outside its PPF.
Increase the combined output available for exchange.

stem: Voluntary trade occurs most directly because:
choices: Each side expects the exchange to improve its situation.
One side must be forced to surrender a good.
Both sides must value the goods equally.
Prices must be fixed by a government.

stem: At constant tradeoffs, Iona makes 32 badges or 8 signs daily; Paz makes 18 badges or 9 signs. Paz offers one sign for 3 badges. Express the offered trading price in signs per badge. Which statement correctly identifies the exporter of badges and compares that price with both producers’ opportunity costs?
choices: Paz exports badges; 3 signs per badge lies between the relevant costs
Iona exports badges; 1/3 sign per badge lies between costs of 1/4 and 1/2
Iona exports signs because its badge output is greater
Both have sign advantage because 3 exceeds both sign-output ratios

stem: Two producers have identical opportunity costs for both goods. What does the basic two-good model predict?
choices: Both gain automatically from complete specialization.
The producer with absolute advantage must import both goods.
No gains from specialization based solely on comparative advantage.
Any terms of trade will double total output.

stem: A trade rate equals the exporter’s opportunity cost exactly but remains below the importer’s opportunity cost. Which evaluation is precise?
choices: The exporter is indifferent while the importer captures the modeled gain
The exporter captures every gain because it supplies the good.
Both parties receive strict and exactly equal gains
Neither party can gain because the rate is on one boundary

stem: At constant tradeoffs, Slate can make 36 tiles or 12 sinks; Moss can make 24 tiles or 12 sinks. Slate doubles sink capacity without changing tile capacity. Which contract could now give both strict gains?
choices: Slate exports sinks for 1.75 tiles each
Moss exports sinks for 2.5 tiles each
Slate exports tiles for 0.4 sink each
Moss exports sinks for exactly 2 tiles each

stem: With constant tradeoffs per day, Fern can make 28 trays or 7 stools; Cove can make 18 trays or 9 stools. Which specialization and exchange can give both strict gains?
choices: Fern makes stools, Cove makes trays; 3 trays per stool
Fern makes trays, Cove makes stools; 5 trays per stool
Fern makes trays, Cove makes stools; 1 tray per stool
Fern makes trays, Cove makes stools; 3 trays per stool

stem: Two studios have constant daily tradeoffs. Alder can make 21 prints or 7 models; Brook can make 20 prints or 10 models. Which proposal benefits both at the margin?
choices: Brook exports models to Alder for 2.5 prints each
Alder exports models to Brook for 2.5 prints each
Brook exports models to Alder for 3.5 prints each
Brook exports models to Alder for 1.5 prints each

stem: Maya is faster than Leo at both coding and testing. Why might Maya still assign testing to Leo?
choices: Absolute advantage requires Maya to do both tasks.
Leo may have the lower opportunity cost of testing.
Testing cannot be traded within a team.
Maya’s wage automatically determines comparative advantage.

stem: Two regions specialize according to comparative advantage, but transport costs exceed the production gains. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Comparative advantage is mathematically impossible.
Absolute advantage has replaced opportunity cost.
The gross gains from specialization may be smaller than the costs of exchange.
Trade must still make both regions better off.

stem: A region can obtain one turbine by giving up 3 tons of grain through exchange or 5 tons by producing it internally. Which reasoning supports exchange?
choices: Importing the turbine has the lower opportunity cost in grain
Producing internally must be better because it avoids trade.
The money price eliminates the need to compare resources
Exchange guarantees equal gains for every resident

stem: Two firms specialize and create 40 extra units of combined output. A proposed exchange gives all 40 extra units to one firm. What is the strongest conclusion?
choices: Specialization created aggregate gains, but the proposed distribution may not benefit both firms
Comparative advantage is disproved whenever gains are unequal.
Any increase in combined output makes every exchange mutually beneficial
Equal gains are required before specialization can raise output

stem: With constant tradeoffs, Forge can make 36 panels or 12 motors; Harbor can make 20 panels or 10 motors. Forge imports a motor and pays an additional shipping cost of 0.5 panel per motor. Which quoted panel price gives both strict gains?
choices: 3 panels per motor
2.25 panels per motor
2 panels per motor
2.75 panels per motor

stem: A high-productivity surgeon is also the fastest typist in a clinic. The surgeon hires an assistant to type notes. What completes the economic explanation?
choices: The assistant must have an absolute advantage in typing.
The surgeon cannot have comparative advantage in surgery.
The surgeon’s opportunity cost of typing is high because typing displaces valuable surgical time.
Specialization matters only in international trade.

stem: Country A has comparative advantage in software. After trade opens, software employment rises but some hardware workers lose jobs. Which evaluation is strongest?
choices: The job losses prove comparative advantage was calculated incorrectly.
All workers must gain for trade to be efficient.
Comparative advantage predicts no sectoral adjustment.
Aggregate gains can coexist with transition costs and distributional losses.

stem: Suppose learning-by-doing lowers a nation’s future opportunity cost in a good it does not currently produce. What does this imply?
choices: Current comparative advantage may not fully describe future comparative advantage.
Opportunity costs can never change over time.
The nation must already have absolute advantage in that good.
Trade eliminates any reason to consider future productivity.

stem: Two firms specialize and increase combined output by 20 units, but contracting and monitoring cost 25 units. What follows?
choices: Comparative advantage does not exist.
The specialization creates gross gains but a net loss after transaction costs.
The firms must trade because output rose.
Transaction costs are transfers and cannot affect net gains.

stem: A country can import steel for 4 units of wheat per ton. Producing a ton domestically costs 6 units of wheat. Which statement is best?
choices: Domestic steel has lower opportunity cost.
The money price alone proves dumping.
Importing steel frees 2 units of wheat-equivalent resources per ton for other uses.
Importing steel reduces available resources by 2 units per ton.

stem: At constant tradeoffs, A makes 30 filters or 10 pumps; B makes 24 filters or 12 pumps. B exports pumps and pays shipping of 0.4 filter per pump. Which price gives both strict gains and gives B the larger per-pump gain measured in filters?
choices: 2.8 filters per pump
2.5 filters per pump
2.4 filters per pump
3 filters per pump

stem: Per hour a manager can make 6 sales or complete 12 accounts; an assistant can make 2 sales or complete 8 accounts. Each sale nets $100. Completing 24 accounts through the assistant also requires one hour of the manager’s supervision. Should the manager delegate the accounts, holding total paid hours fixed?
choices: Yes: delegation strictly gains 6 sales because the assistant’s forgone sales are the only cost to compare.
Indifferent: delegation sacrifices 12 sales including supervision, the same as completing the accounts personally.
No: delegation sacrifices 18 sales while direct typing sacrifices 8, so direct typing gains 10 sales.
No: the manager’s higher speed at both tasks proves delegation always lowers total sales.

stem: A trade agreement yields gross national gains of $100 million before $30 million of real adjustment costs. Before adjustment costs, consumers gain $160 million and displaced workers lose $60 million. A $60 million domestic compensation transfer would fully offset that loss but costs $15 million to administer. Which evaluation is correct?
choices: Net gain after administration is -$5 million; the compensation payment must be deducted again as a resource loss.
Net gain after administration is $70 million; the transfer automatically occurs when aggregate surplus rises.
Net gain after administration is $55 million; full compensation is feasible under the stated estimates but requires the transfer to be made.
Net gain after administration is $115 million; compensation increases national surplus by the amount workers receive.

stem: Rina can make 8 posters or 4 videos in a day. Malik can make 6 posters or 6 videos. Who has the comparative advantage in posters?
choices: Malik, because one poster costs him 0.5 video while it costs Rina 1 video.
Rina, because one poster costs her 0.5 video while it costs Malik 1 video.
Malik, because one poster costs him 1 video while it costs Rina 2 videos.
Neither, because one poster costs each of them 1 video at their stated output rates.

stem: Nora can edit 12 pages or design 3 graphics per hour. Eli can edit 8 pages or design 4 graphics. Who has the comparative advantage in graphics?
choices: Nora, because she edits more pages.
Nora, because one graphic costs her fewer graphics.
Eli, because one graphic costs him 2 edited pages rather than Nora’s 4.
Neither, because Eli has no absolute advantage in editing.

stem: Farm A can produce 20 crates of apples or 10 crates of pears. Farm B can produce 12 crates of apples or 12 crates of pears. Which specialization pattern follows comparative advantage?
choices: Farm A specializes in pears and Farm B in apples.
Both farms specialize in apples because apples output is larger.
Neither farm specializes because both can produce both goods.
Farm A specializes relatively more in apples and Farm B in pears.

stem: Ava gives up 2 cups of coffee to bake one loaf. Ben gives up 5 cups to bake one loaf. A trade price of one loaf for 3 cups of coffee is:
choices: Potentially beneficial to both Ava and Ben.
Beneficial only to Ava.
Beneficial only to Ben.
Outside the mutually beneficial range.

stem: Country X gives up 3 tons of wheat for one machine. Country Y gives up 7 tons. Which statement is correct?
choices: Country Y has the comparative advantage in machines.
Country X has the comparative advantage in machines.
Country X must also have the comparative advantage in wheat.
Comparative advantage cannot be identified from opportunity costs.

stem: After specialization, total production rises but one proposed trade leaves a producer worse off. What failed?
choices: Comparative advantage ceased to exist.
Specialization always lowers total output.
The proposed terms of trade were not mutually beneficial.
Absolute advantage made exchange impossible.

stem: Comparative advantage belongs to the producer who:
choices: Produces the largest amount of every good.
Charges the lowest money price after trade.
Has the highest income.
Gives up less of the alternative good.

stem: A mutually beneficial terms-of-trade price must generally lie:
choices: Between the two producers’ opportunity costs.
Above both opportunity costs.
Below both opportunity costs.
At the higher producer’s total output.

stem: Trade can benefit both sides because:
choices: One side is forced to accept a loss.
Specialization can increase combined output and exchange can share the gain.
Scarcity disappears after exchange.
Both sides must have identical skills.

stem: A student says elasticity is just the direction of a change. What correction is needed?
choices: Elasticity measures the size of a percentage response relative to a percentage change
Elasticity records only whether demand slopes down
Elasticity is the market price divided by income
Elasticity is another name for total revenue

stem: Which coefficient represents the strongest demand response to price?
Which observation is consistent with inelastic demand?
choices: Price rises 5 percent and quantity demanded falls 15 percent
Price falls 8 percent and quantity demanded rises 16 percent
Price rises 10 percent and quantity demanded falls 4 percent
Any change where quantity moves opposite price

stem: Which change most likely makes brand-level demand more elastic?
choices: Consumers become locked into annual contracts
The purchase becomes more necessary
Buyers have less time to adjust
Several close competing brands enter

stem: Which product characteristic most likely reduces demand elasticity?
choices: The item is a necessity with few substitutes
The item is a luxury with many substitutes
The market is narrowly defined
The purchase takes a large budget share

stem: Why is demand for one brand of salt more elastic than demand for salt as a category?
choices: Salt is measured in pounds
The brand has many close substitutes within the category
Category demand has a flatter slope in every graph
Brand demand ignores consumer preferences

stem: A vertical demand curve has elasticity:
choices: One
Infinity
Zero
A value that rises with price

stem: A horizontal demand curve has elasticity:
choices: Zero
One
Negative one
Effectively infinite

stem: A seller raises price and total revenue falls. What does the total-revenue test imply?
choices: Demand is elastic
Demand is inelastic
Demand is perfectly inelastic
Supply is elastic

stem: A seller raises price and total revenue rises. What does the total-revenue test imply?
choices: Demand is elastic
Demand is inelastic
Demand is unit elastic
Income elasticity is positive

stem: Which statement about unit-elastic demand is correct?
choices: Quantity does not respond to price
A price increase always raises revenue
The percentage changes offset, leaving total revenue about unchanged
Demand is horizontal

stem: Which situation most likely has highly inelastic short-run supply?
choices: Mass-produced notebooks next year
Cloud storage with unused servers
A storable manufactured input
Tickets for a stadium event already underway

stem: Supply becomes more elastic over time mainly because producers can:
choices: Change capacity, enter, exit, and substitute inputs
Make demand shift automatically
Eliminate scarcity
Set any price without losing buyers

stem: A positive income elasticity identifies:
choices: An inferior good
A normal good
Complements
Perfectly inelastic demand

stem: A negative income elasticity identifies:
choices: A normal good
Substitutes
An inferior good
Elastic supply

stem: A positive cross-price elasticity identifies:
choices: Complements
Inferior goods
Perfectly elastic goods
Substitutes

stem: A negative cross-price elasticity identifies:
choices: Complements
Substitutes
Normal goods
Unrelated goods by definition

stem: Which side of a market bears more of a tax, other things equal?
choices: The side named in the law
The side with lower elasticity
The side with the flatter curve regardless of axes
The side with more participants

stem: Refer to the graph. Which total revenue at B and interpretation of a small movement in either direction along demand are correct?
choices: $480; revenue is maximized there because demand is unit elastic.
$360; revenue is maximized there because demand is unit elastic.
$480; revenue is maximized there because demand is perfectly inelastic.
$360; revenue is maximized there because demand is perfectly inelastic.

stem: Which displayed demand curve has zero price elasticity?
choices: D2
D1
Both D1 and D2
Neither D1 nor D2

stem: Using the midpoint method, what is the price elasticity of demand for music subscriptions when price rises from $10 to $12 and quantity demanded falls from 1,000 to 800?
