Quantity demanded falls about 2 percent
Revenue is unchanged because demand is inelastic

stem: A planning model assumes a 7 percent income increase with income elasticity 1.3. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
choices: Demand rises about 5.4 percent
Demand rises about 9.1 percent
Demand falls about 9.1 percent
Demand rises exactly 1.3 percent

stem: A planning model assumes a 12 percent increase in a substitute’s price with cross-price elasticity 0.75. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
choices: Demand falls about 9 percent
Demand rises about 16 percent
Demand rises about 9 percent
Demand is unchanged because 0.75 is below one

stem: A planning model assumes a 10 percent increase in a complement’s price with cross-price elasticity −0.6. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
choices: Demand rises about 6 percent
Demand falls about 16.7 percent
Demand is unchanged because the coefficient is negative
Demand falls about 6 percent

stem: A planning model assumes a 9 percent output-price increase with supply elasticity 1.5. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
choices: Quantity supplied rises about 13.5 percent
Quantity supplied rises about 6 percent
Quantity supplied falls about 13.5 percent
Quantity supplied rises exactly 1.5 percent

stem: A planning model assumes a 20 percent wage increase with labor-demand elasticity 0.8. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
choices: Employment rises about 16 percent
Employment falls about 16 percent
Employment falls about 25 percent
Employment is unchanged because labor is a factor market

stem: A pharmaceutical patent expires and many close substitutes enter. Holding other determinants constant, what happens to the original brand’s demand elasticity and pricing power?
choices: Demand becomes less elastic and markup rises
Demand becomes perfectly inelastic because medicine is necessary
Demand becomes more elastic and sustainable markup falls
Elasticity is unchanged because only price affects demand

stem: A city evaluates a fuel tax using a one-month elasticity estimate. Why might this underestimate the tax’s eventual effect on fuel consumption?
choices: Short-run demand always has more substitutes
Long-run elasticity must equal zero
Tax incidence eliminates time-horizon effects
Long-run demand allows vehicle, residence, and commuting adjustments

stem: A university raises parking prices and observes little first-semester change, but large declines after students revise housing and transit choices. This illustrates:
choices: Demand becoming more elastic over time
Supply becoming perfectly inelastic
Income elasticity turning negative
A movement from elastic to inelastic demand

stem: A national market for all beverages is compared with demand for one flavor of one soda brand. Which statement is strongest?
choices: The national beverage market is more elastic because it contains more products
The brand-flavor demand is more elastic because the market is defined narrowly
Both have identical elasticity because they use the same currency
The brand flavor is less elastic because it has fewer buyers

stem: A firm’s demand curve becomes flatter after a rival enters, but the axes are rescaled at the same time. What is required before concluding that demand became more elastic?
choices: Only a visual comparison of slopes
Proof that the rival charges a lower nominal price
A unit-free elasticity calculation at comparable price-quantity points
A calculation of income elasticity

stem: Two products have identical slopes on graphs measured in different quantity units. Which conclusion is valid?
choices: They have identical elasticity everywhere
The product with larger units is more elastic
Both must be unit elastic
No elasticity ranking follows without price and quantity information

stem: Moving down a linear demand curve past the midpoint, what happens to elasticity, marginal revenue, and total revenue?
choices: Elasticity falls below one, marginal revenue becomes negative, and total revenue declines as quantity expands
Elasticity rises above one, marginal revenue stays positive, and revenue rises
Elasticity remains one and marginal revenue remains zero
Demand becomes perfectly elastic and revenue becomes infinite

stem: At the exact unit-elastic point on a smooth demand curve, a very small price change has what first-order effect on total revenue?
choices: A guaranteed large increase
Approximately no effect
A guaranteed large decrease
It makes total revenue equal total cost

stem: Why does maximum total revenue not necessarily identify the profit-maximizing output?
choices: Revenue and profit are always identical
Elasticity cannot be used by firms
Profit also depends on production costs and marginal cost
The revenue maximum occurs only under perfect competition

stem: A museum has near-zero marginal cost for another visitor before capacity. Why might it still avoid the unit-elastic revenue maximum?
choices: Unit elasticity always minimizes revenue
Marginal cost is the only determinant of demand
Elasticity is irrelevant when marginal cost is low
Capacity effects, congestion, mission goals, and segment pricing can change the objective

stem: A firm charges students less than business travelers for the same flexible software service. The pricing pattern is most sustainable when:
choices: The groups can be separated and business demand is less elastic
Students have less elastic demand and resale is costless
Both groups have identical elasticity
Marginal cost is higher for every student user

stem: An airline’s leisure customers become easier to identify, but ticket resale also becomes easy. What happens to elasticity-based price discrimination?
choices: Price discrimination becomes stronger automatically
Arbitrage undermines the ability to maintain different prices
Elasticity differences disappear by definition
The airline can ignore resale because seats are services

stem: A tax is imposed where demand is less elastic than supply. The statute is rewritten so buyers, rather than sellers, remit it. What happens to economic incidence?
choices: The burden shifts entirely to sellers
The burden becomes equal
The burden remains mostly on buyers
The tax disappears from market prices

stem: A labor tax is imposed where workers’ labor supply is much less elastic than firms’ labor demand. Who bears most of the burden?
choices: Firms through higher labor cost only
The government
Whichever party receives the tax form
Workers through lower after-tax compensation

stem: A subsidy is offered to buyers in a market with perfectly inelastic supply. Who captures the subsidy?
choices: Sellers through a higher market price
Buyers through a permanently lower net price
The benefit splits equally
No one because quantity cannot rise

stem: A commodity tax raises substantial revenue but creates little deadweight loss. Which combination best explains this?
choices: Demand and supply are highly elastic
Demand and supply are relatively inelastic
The tax is collected from producers
The commodity has a positive income elasticity

stem: A government wants the same revenue from two possible tax bases. Why might it prefer the less elastic base on efficiency grounds?
choices: The less elastic base guarantees equal burden sharing
Elasticity determines legal incidence only
The required wedge causes a smaller reduction in traded quantity
The more elastic base has no substitutes

stem: A congestion charge initially raises revenue but barely reduces traffic. Which change would make it more effective at reducing trips without changing the nominal charge?
choices: Making commuting more necessary
Shortening the adjustment period
Reducing information about alternatives
Expansion of reliable transit substitutes

stem: A tax raises a drink’s price by 10% and reduces its quantity demanded by 18%, measured over the same period with other demand determinants held constant. Buyers switch to untaxed close substitutes. Which conclusion best connects the measured response to tax design?
choices: Demand is elastic over the observed change (|Ed|=1.8); covering the close substitutes could reduce this substitution channel, but would not by itself determine the new tax revenue.
Demand is inelastic over the observed change (|Ed|=0.56); covering the close substitutes would necessarily lower tax revenue.
Demand is elastic over the observed change (|Ed|=1.8); changing the statutory payer would remove the substitution channel.
Demand is elastic over the observed change (|Ed|=1.8); covering the close substitutes would guarantee that quantity and tax revenue stay unchanged.

stem: A minimum wage has a larger employment effect in one industry than another. Which explanation is most directly elasticity-based?
choices: Workers are legally required to pay the wage
Labor demand is more elastic in the industry with the larger employment response
The industry has higher nominal revenue
Labor supply slopes upward in both industries

stem: Why is labor demand often more elastic when machinery can easily substitute for labor?
choices: Machinery makes labor supply more elastic
Wages become a smaller unit of measurement
Firms can change input mix more strongly after a wage increase
The output demand curve becomes vertical

stem: Demand for a firm’s output becomes more elastic. What is the likely effect on the firm’s derived demand for an input used in production?
choices: Input demand becomes perfectly inelastic
Input demand becomes unrelated to output price
Input supply becomes less elastic automatically
Input demand becomes more elastic

stem: A country’s export demand is highly elastic. Its currency appreciates, raising foreign-currency export prices. What is the likely quantity effect?
choices: A relatively large decline in exports
A small decline because export demand is elastic
No change because exchange rates affect only supply
An increase in exports

stem: Import supply to a small country is nearly perfectly elastic at the world price. A tariff is introduced. Which side is likely to bear most of the tariff?
choices: Foreign suppliers
Domestic import buyers
The burden must be equal
Domestic exporters

stem: A tariff reduces imports much more than forecast. Which prior assumption was probably too low?
choices: The income elasticity of domestic supply
The slope of the world price line in dollars
The price elasticity of import demand
The statutory tariff rate

stem: A coffee shortage raises coffee prices, and demand for tea rises sharply. What does this indicate about the relationship between coffee and tea and the sign of their cross-price elasticity?
choices: Coffee and tea are complements
Tea is an inferior good
Coffee supply must be perfectly elastic
Tea substitutes for coffee, so cross-price elasticity is positive

stem: The price of smartphones falls, and demand for mobile data plans rises. Which coefficient captures this relationship?
choices: A negative cross-price elasticity between phones and data plans
A positive income elasticity for phones
Price elasticity of phone supply
A positive cross-price elasticity because both demands rose

stem: An inferior good has income elasticity −0.2. How should the magnitude be interpreted?
choices: The good is a strong luxury because the magnitude is below one
Demand responds weakly to income changes, but in the opposite direction
Demand is perfectly income inelastic
The good must be a complement

stem: A normal good has income elasticity 0.9. A boom raises income. What is most likely?
choices: Demand falls because the coefficient is below one
Demand rises more than proportionally
Demand rises, but less than proportionally
Demand is unaffected

stem: A firm estimates a cross-price elasticity of nearly zero between two products. What is the best supported conclusion?
choices: They are definitively unrelated in every market and period
They are complements because zero is not positive
They are both necessities
Their demands show little observed relationship in the sampled range

stem: A demand estimate is elastic at the current price but the firm plans a large price cut. Why is using one constant coefficient risky?
choices: Elasticity may change along the demand curve and outside the estimated range
Elasticity always becomes infinite after a price cut
Percentage changes cannot be calculated for price cuts
Only supply elasticity changes with price

stem: A regression estimates a price coefficient in levels. Why can that coefficient not automatically be reported as elasticity?
choices: Every regression coefficient is already unit-free
Convert it using the current price and quantity scale
Elasticity ignores the price coefficient
Only cross-price coefficients require conversion

stem: A point elasticity is measured on a differentiable demand curve. Which expression combines slope with the current point?
choices: The absolute value of (dP/dQ) × (P+Q)
Q divided by P only
The absolute value of (dQ/dP) × (P/Q)
The slope squared

stem: For demand Q = 100 − 2P, what is elasticity at P = 20, where Q = 60?
choices: About 1.50
About 2.00
About 40.00
About 0.67

stem: For demand Q = 100 − 2P, what is elasticity at P = 40, where Q = 20?
For supply Q = 10 + 3P, what is point elasticity at P = 10, where Q = 40?
For supply Q = −20 + 4P, what is point elasticity at P = 10, where Q = 20?
A supply curve passes through the origin and is linear. What is point elasticity along the positive portion?
choices: Zero at every point
It rises from zero to infinity
It depends only on the currency unit
One at every point

stem: A linear supply curve intersects the quantity axis at a positive quantity. Along its positive-price region, supply elasticity tends to be:
choices: Less than one
Greater than one
Exactly one at every point
Negative

stem: A linear supply curve has a negative quantity intercept and crosses the price axis above zero. Along its positive-quantity region, supply elasticity tends to be:
choices: Less than one
Greater than one
Exactly zero
Negative because the intercept is negative

stem: A farm product has inelastic demand. A bumper crop shifts supply right. What likely happens to farmers’ total revenue?
choices: It rises because output always raises revenue
It is unchanged because supply shifted
It falls because the price decline dominates the quantity increase
It becomes equal to consumer surplus

stem: A farm product has elastic demand. A weather shock shifts supply left. What likely happens to farmers’ total revenue?
choices: It rises because price rises
It is unchanged because demand did not shift
It equals tax revenue
It falls because the quantity loss dominates the price increase

stem: A platform adds many alternative sellers, reducing buyers’ switching costs. What happens to seller-level demand?
choices: It becomes more elastic
It becomes more inelastic
It becomes perfectly inelastic
It changes only income elasticity

stem: A product initially has few close substitutes. A 10% price increase reduces its quantity demanded by 4%. Later, several close substitutes become available; the same 10% price increase reduces quantity demanded by 16%. The comparison uses the same adjustment period, and income, tastes and the product’s necessity status are unchanged. A manager claims the larger response is merely a movement along demand and provides no evidence that responsiveness changed. Which evaluation is strongest?
choices: Accept the claim: the ratios 0.4 and 1.6 describe movements along demand. Because the product itself is unchanged, responsiveness should be treated as constant despite the difference between those ratios.

Reject the claim: elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6 as close substitutes expand. Each price experiment moves along its own demand curve, while the comparison shows changed responsiveness across periods.
Reject the claim: elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6 because consumers have more time to adjust later. Equal experiment lengths do not constrain the time-horizon explanation for the larger response.

Reject the claim: elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6 because the product becomes more like a luxury. A larger observed response establishes changed necessity status despite the stated comparison controls.

stem: A loyalty program causes customers to forfeit points if they switch sellers. What is the likely short-run effect on demand elasticity?
choices: It raises supply elasticity
It makes income elasticity negative
It lowers demand elasticity by raising switching costs
It creates perfect competition

stem: A policy analyst uses demand elasticity to predict a quota’s price effect. What additional elasticity is essential?
choices: Income elasticity only
Cross-price elasticity only
No other elasticity is relevant
Supply elasticity

stem: A binding production quota reduces market quantity. In which demand case is the price increase likely largest?
choices: More inelastic demand
More elastic demand
Perfectly elastic demand
Demand with many substitutes

stem: A supply disruption occurs. Which market has the smallest price increase, other things equal?
choices: One with inelastic demand and fixed supply
One with elastic demand and elastic supply response from inventories
One with perfectly inelastic demand
One with no substitutes and no stocks

stem: A firm faces constant-elasticity demand with elasticity 2. Under the inverse-elasticity markup rule, how should its markup compare with the markup when elasticity is 4?
choices: A smaller markup because demand is less elastic
The same markup because both are elastic
A larger markup because demand is less elastic
Zero markup because elasticity exceeds one

stem: Why must the absolute demand elasticity exceed one for a standard positive-markup monopolist with positive marginal cost?
choices: Because demand would be upward sloping
Because total revenue would be zero
Because supply would become perfectly elastic
Otherwise marginal revenue would be nonpositive at the chosen output

stem: Compare the C→B and B→A intervals on the graph. Why can their elasticity classifications differ?
choices: The demand curve has different slopes in the two intervals
The percentage-change bases differ across the two intervals
Elasticity uses only the absolute quantity change
Elasticity is determined only by the direction of price

stem: Refer to the graph. A seller at A can choose the posted price at A, B, or C and can serve all buyers. It wants higher revenue while retaining at least 50 unit sales. Which price is best, and what explains the result?
choices: The price at C; its highest posted price also gives the highest revenue and meets the minimum.
The price at A; its largest quantity necessarily gives the highest revenue.
The price at B; revenue rises by 120 while sales remain above the minimum.
The price at B; revenue stays unchanged but sales rise above their level at A.

stem: A seller initially charges the price at C. Capacity is 70 units, and sales equal the smaller of demand and capacity. Using the graph, which alternative price earns more revenue, and why does the capacity constraint matter?
choices: B earns $400 versus $210 at A; using all quantity demanded at A would overstate actual sales.
B earns $480 versus $280 at A; demand elasticity guarantees all units demanded can be sold despite capacity.
B earns $400 versus $210 at A; demand elasticity guarantees all units demanded can be sold despite capacity.
B earns $480 versus $280 at A; using all quantity demanded at A would overstate actual sales.

stem: Use the labeled intervals to calculate midpoint elasticity on D1 and D2. Which statement follows?
choices: Only D1 is above the unit-elastic threshold
Only D2 is above the unit-elastic threshold
Both are exactly unit elastic
Neither curve can be classified

stem: The graph shows otherwise comparable products D1 and D2 over the marked price decrease. Which revenue changes and explanation using substitute availability are consistent with midpoint elasticity?
choices: D1: $400→$520; D2: $300→$280. More close substitutes is a plausible explanation for D1’s greater responsiveness.
D1: $450→$570; D2: $350→$330. More close substitutes is a plausible explanation for D1’s greater responsiveness.
D1: $450→$570; D2: $350→$330. More close substitutes is a plausible explanation for D2’s lower responsiveness.
D1: $400→$520; D2: $300→$280. More close substitutes is a plausible explanation for D2’s lower responsiveness.

stem: How do the absolute elasticity magnitudes of D1 and D2 compare?
choices: Both equal one
D1 equals zero while D2 approaches infinity
Both equal zero
D1 approaches infinity while D2 equals zero

stem: Refer to the graph. A buyer needs 90 units when price has risen from the common starting point to $8. Using midpoint supply elasticities, which comparison and procurement conclusion are supported?
choices: Short run about 0.75, long run 0.23; 90 units can be supplied only in the short run.
Short run about 0.23, long run 0.75; 90 units can be supplied only after the longer adjustment.
Short run about 0.23, long run 0.75; neither horizon can supply 90 units at $8.
Short run about 0.23, long run 1.33; longer-run supply is elastic because it is flatter.

stem: A price-comparison service makes close substitutes easier to find. Before its launch a 5% price increase reduced sales by 2%; afterwards the same increase reduces sales by 8%, over equal adjustment periods. Which interpretation and revenue prediction fit the evidence?
choices: Absolute demand elasticity falls from 2.5 to 0.625; a small price increase now tends to raise revenue.
Demand becomes more elastic solely because the firm moves upward along an unchanged demand curve; comparison information plays no role.
Absolute demand elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6; a small price increase now tends to reduce revenue because buyers can switch more easily.
Demand remains inelastic because both tests use the same price increase; quantity responses cannot change the classification.

stem: A health insurer lowers patients’ out-of-pocket price. What happens to the observed price sensitivity of patients at the point of service?
choices: Response to the provider’s price becomes identical to provider supply elasticity
Response to the provider’s price becomes unlimited whenever insurance is offered
Response to the provider’s price becomes income elasticity rather than price elasticity
Response to the provider’s price may weaken when insurance absorbs increases

stem: A seller forecasts that a 5% price rise will raise revenue using today’s demand elasticity of 0.4. A close substitute launches before the planned price rise. Which revision and test would make the forecast more defensible?
choices: Reestimate demand after entry; if elasticity rises above one, the predicted revenue effect can reverse.
Keep 0.4 because elasticity is a permanent property of the product; test only whether accounting costs changed.
Raise the revenue forecast automatically because a new substitute always increases demand for this seller’s product.
Use supply elasticity in place of demand elasticity because another producer has entered.

stem: A policymaker claims a tax on an inelastic good is painless because quantity barely changes. What is missing?
choices: Inelastic demand prevents any price change
Burden can be large even when deadweight loss is modest
Tax revenue must be zero
Only elastic goods create burden

stem: A product has very elastic demand and very inelastic supply. A demand increase occurs. Which short-run outcome is most likely?
choices: A small price rise and large quantity rise, given elastic demand
A large price fall and small quantity rise, given inelastic supply
A large price rise and small quantity rise, given inelastic supply
An unchanged price and quantity, given opposing elasticities

stem: A supply increase occurs in a market with highly elastic demand. Compared with inelastic demand, what happens?
choices: Quantity rises less and price falls more
Price and quantity do not change
Total revenue must always rise
Quantity rises more and price falls less

stem: Two customer groups buy the same product at the same price. A 4% price increase reduces Group A’s purchases by 2% and Group B’s by 8%. Both groups have the same adjustment period. B spends a larger income share on the product and has more substitutes. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: A is less responsive than B, consistent with the stated budget-share and substitution differences; equal prices do not imply equal elasticities.
A is more responsive than B because a smaller quantity response gives the larger elasticity.
Both have the same elasticity because price and adjustment period are the same; the responses measure supply instead.
The comparison proves that time horizon explains the difference, despite the identical adjustment periods.

stem: A seller sees no quantity response after a tiny price test. Why is concluding perfectly inelastic demand premature?
choices: The zero response estimates elasticity precisely at zero; repeat the same tiny test only to check the seller’s revenue arithmetic.
The test may hide a response because of noise, contracts or its size; vary the test and allow adjustment before treating demand as perfectly inelastic.
The test establishes elastic demand because buyers delayed purchases; a larger increase must therefore raise revenue.
The test establishes unit elasticity because quantity was stable; the next test should hold total revenue constant.

stem: An elasticity estimate is based on a period when income and competitor prices also changed. What is the core identification problem?
choices: The midpoint formula requires quantity to remain unchanged
A time series cannot contain movements along a demand curve
Income and competitor prices may also explain the quantity change
Changing income establishes that demand is perfectly elastic

stem: A firm’s price and quantity move in the same direction after a demand shift. Why can the observed ratio not be treated as price elasticity of demand?
choices: The observations prove a positive own-price demand elasticity
The observations establish that the product is an inferior good
The observations are invalid unless supply is perfectly inelastic
The observations reflect a demand shift, not a fixed demand curve

stem: A supply shift causes price and quantity to move in opposite directions. Under what condition can the resulting arc approximate demand elasticity?
choices: Stable demand plus an exogenous supply shift
Demand also shifts at the same time
The legal tax payer is known
Income elasticity equals one

stem: A demand shift causes price and quantity supplied to move in the same direction. Under what condition can the resulting arc approximate supply elasticity?
choices: Supply also shifts simultaneously
Stable supply plus an exogenous demand shift
Demand is perfectly inelastic
The product is a normal good

stem: A national housing-supply estimate is 1.2 over ten years. City A has little buildable land and a one-year planning horizon; City B has available land and a ten-year horizon. Which use of the estimate is defensible?
choices: Apply 1.2 to both cities because a national elasticity incorporates each local constraint equally.
Apply a larger elasticity to A because scarce land makes each price increase more valuable to owners.
Treat it as a starting point, not a common local forecast; A likely faces tighter short-run constraints, while B has more adjustment possibilities.
Apply zero elasticity to B because a longer horizon fixes the housing stock more tightly.

stem: An emergency suddenly makes a product necessary, while production capacity is fixed. What happens to short-run demand and supply responsiveness?
choices: Both become perfectly elastic
Demand becomes elastic while supply becomes infinite
Elasticity is unchanged because curves do not shift
Both may become more inelastic, amplifying the price response to a shock

stem: A market has perfectly elastic demand at the world price and upward-sloping domestic supply. A domestic production tax is imposed. What is the likely seller response?
choices: Domestic output falls; the consumer price stays at the world price
Domestic output stays fixed; the consumer price rises by the tax
Domestic output rises; the consumer price stays at the world price
Domestic output falls; the consumer price falls below the world price

stem: A market has perfectly elastic supply at a given price and downward-sloping demand. A consumption subsidy is offered. What is the likely outcome?
choices: Buyer net price is unchanged; seller price rises; quantity is fixed
Buyer net price falls; seller price is unchanged; quantity rises
Buyer net price rises; seller price is unchanged; quantity falls
Buyer net price falls; seller price rises equally; quantity is fixed

stem: A seller wants to maximize revenue with one uniform price. What information about elasticity is needed beyond knowing its value at the current price?
choices: Only whether the product is normal
Only supply elasticity
Elasticity at the current point and along the curve
The statutory tax rate

stem: A firm estimates the price elasticity of demand at 1.05, with a wide confidence interval spanning values below and above one. What is the prudent pricing conclusion?
choices: The price increase should lower revenue because the point estimate exceeds one; the interval affects the size but cannot affect the sign.
The price increase should raise revenue because the interval includes inelastic values; the point estimate affects the size but cannot affect the sign.
Revenue should be unchanged because the interval includes one; averaging elastic and inelastic estimates guarantees unit elasticity.
The revenue effect of a small price change is uncertain because plausible elasticity values fall on both sides of one; use cautious testing.

stem: A product is a necessity but has many close generic substitutes. Which determinant should dominate brand-level demand?
choices: Brand demand can be elastic even if category demand is inelastic, because consumers can switch brands without giving up the necessity.
Brand demand should be less elastic than category demand, because a brand includes fewer possible purchases than the category.
Brand and category demand should have equal elasticity, because both purchases satisfy the same basic need.
Brand demand can be elastic only if the entire category is a luxury, because generic substitutes cannot change necessity status.

stem: A product has no close substitutes today but represents a large budget share. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Few substitutes establish inelastic demand; budget share changes spending levels but cannot affect responsiveness.
Few substitutes restrain responsiveness while a large budget share encourages adjustment; estimate their combined effect in this market.
The large budget share establishes elastic demand; the absence of substitutes changes price but cannot affect responsiveness.
The two determinants imply unit elasticity; their opposing directions necessarily cancel quantitatively.

stem: A policymaker compares a steep supply curve and a flat demand curve drawn with different axis scales. What is the proper incidence method?
choices: Assign burden to the visually steeper curve
Assign burden to sellers by statute
Compare elasticity estimates, not visual steepness alone
Assume equal burden

stem: A market’s supply is inelastic today but highly elastic over five years. A permanent tax is imposed. How should incidence analysis change over time?
choices: If demand responsiveness is unchanged, the more elastic long-run supply tends to shift more of the burden to sellers.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, supply adjustment raises the quantity traded but leaves the burden shares at their short-run values.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, producers’ ability to adjust makes the statutory taxpayer bear a larger share over time.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, the more elastic long-run supply tends to shift more of the burden to buyers.

stem: A temporary tax expires before firms can adjust capacity. Compared with a permanent tax, who may bear more of the temporary tax?
choices: Producers, because short-run supply is less elastic
Consumers, because temporary taxes make demand vertical
The government
No one because the tax is temporary

stem: A crop quota reduces sales from 1,000 to 900 units and raises price from $10 to $12. Farmers’ variable production cost falls by $300, while administering the quota uses $1,200 of their resources. Which comparison avoids confusing revenue with profit?
choices: Revenue rises by $800 and profit must rise by $800 because the demand response is inelastic.
Revenue rises by $800, but net producer profit falls by $100 after cost savings and administration.
Revenue falls by $1,000 and profit falls by $1,900 because fewer units are sold.
Revenue rises by $1,200 and profit rises by $300 because use the old quantity at the new price.

stem: A seller estimates elastic demand but still raises price after a cost increase. Why is this not necessarily irrational?
choices: Elastic demand predicts a revenue loss from a price rise, so profit must fall by the same amount even if the firm avoids variable costs.
Elastic demand predicts a revenue gain from a price rise, and that gain is sufficient to establish a profit gain after the cost increase.
Elastic demand predicts a revenue loss from a price rise, but reduced unit sales and higher contribution margins may improve profit after the cost increase.
Elastic demand predicts unchanged revenue from a price rise, so the cost increase can be passed on without checking the quantity response.

stem: A seller expects a small discount to increase revenue from customers with elastic demand. Those customers can freely resell purchases to customers currently paying the regular price. Which issue must the forecast address before treating the two groups’ sales as separate?
choices: Resale guarantees the discount raises profit because every discounted sale is an additional market sale.
Resale makes both groups’ demand perfectly inelastic because the seller names two prices.
Resale affects fixed cost only, so it can be ignored when estimating demand responses.
Resale can shift regular-price purchases into the discounted channel; evaluate that switching as well as each group’s quantity response.

stem: An importer initially cuts foreign-goods purchases by 2% when their domestic-currency price rises 5%. After close domestic substitutes appear, the same price increase cuts imports 9%. If foreign prices and currency needed per imported unit are unchanged, which implication follows?
choices: Import demand becomes more elastic, so the derived quantity demand for foreign currency becomes more responsive to the same domestic-currency price change.
Import demand becomes less elastic because 9% is larger than 2%, so foreign-currency purchases become less responsive.
The foreign-currency quantity must rise when imports fall, because each imported unit now requires more foreign currency.
Derived demand is unchanged because domestic substitutes cannot affect purchases of foreign goods.

stem: A rival cuts its price 10%. Your product’s cross-price elasticity with that rival is +1.5, while your own-price elasticity is −0.5. Holding your price and other determinants fixed, which forecast and interpretation fit?
choices: Your sales rise about 15%; positive cross-price elasticity means the goods are complements.
Your sales fall about 15%; the positive cross-price elasticity indicates substitutes.
Your sales rise about 5%; use own-price elasticity with the rival’s price cut.
Your sales fall about 0.15%; multiply by the elasticity as though it were already a percentage.

stem: Income is forecast to rise 5%. Transit demand has income elasticity −0.6; leisure-rail demand has income elasticity +1.4. Prices and other determinants are fixed. Which forecast separates the sign from responsiveness?
choices: Transit demand rises about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; discard the minus sign before forecasting.
Transit demand falls about 0.6%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 1.4%; coefficients are percentage changes themselves.
Transit demand falls about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; the estimates classify transit as inferior over this range.
Both demands rise 5% because the income shock is common to the two markets.

stem: A producer’s price rises 8%. Its short-run supply elasticity is 0.25 and its long-run elasticity is 1.5, each applicable near the initial price. Which forecast and explanation fit, with other determinants held constant?
choices: Quantity supplied rises 12% in the short run and 2% in the long run because time reduces adjustment options.
Quantity supplied rises 8% in both periods because elasticity measures the direction but not the size of the response.
Quantity supplied falls 2% then 12% because the higher output price raises the firm’s input costs by definition.
Quantity supplied rises about 2% in the short run and 12% in the long run as capacity and inputs can adjust.

Add it because total hospital benefit is large
Do not add it because any displaced activity is sunk

stem: A research grant has spent $2 million. Another experiment costs $180,000 and has a 40% chance of producing evidence worth $600,000. Ignoring other outcomes, should it run?
choices: Run because expected marginal benefit is $240,000
Stop because the $600,000 benefit is uncertain
Run only to justify the $2 million already spent
Stop because total spending would rise

stem: A retailer’s first three added inventory batches have net marginal benefits of $6,000, $2,000, and -$1,500. A fourth would have +$500 only if the third is purchased. How many additional batches should the retailer buy?
choices: Buy two batches
Buy four batches
Buy three batches
Buy one batch

stem: A hospital evaluates all benefits and costs using the same points scale. One treatment provides 88 benefit points and has a 42-point supply cost. The staff could instead remain available for emergencies, an alternative valued at 35 points. A different treatment method reduces the supply cost by 8 points but also reduces the benefit by 12 points. Which treatment method provides the greater net benefit compared with keeping the staff available for emergencies?
choices: The original treatment, with an 11-point net gain
The cheaper method, with a 15-point net gain
Neither, because readiness must be added to benefit
Both versions give the same gain because both save supplies

stem: Adding one more flight would bring in $80,000 in revenue, incur $54,000 in operating costs, and impose $18,000 in expected delay costs on other flights. What is its net marginal benefit?
A software team’s next round of development work has a 50% chance of creating $180,000 in value and costs $70,000. It also delays maintenance worth $25,000. What should it do?
choices: Do not run it because expected benefit $90,000 is below relevant cost $95,000
Run it because possible benefit is $180,000
Run it because development cost alone is below expected benefit
Do not run it because uncertainty makes expected benefit zero

stem: The next two maintenance zones add benefits of 18 and 13 points and operating costs of 10 and 11 points. Opening either requires a one-time setup cost of 9 points. Zones must be opened in order. Which option has the greatest net benefit?
choices: Open both zones, gaining 1 point
Open neither, because the first zone alone loses 1 point
Open only the first, gaining 8 points
Open both, gaining 10 points

stem: A pollution rule’s next reduction step yields $4.8 million in health benefits, costs firms $3.6 million, and reduces recreational value by $1.5 million. Based on social marginal analysis, should the additional reduction be required?
choices: Do not require it because social marginal cost is $5.1 million
Require it because compliance cost alone is below benefit
Require it because total prior health benefits are large
Do not require it because all environmental policy is costly

stem: Total benefit at five inspection stations is $900,000 and total cost is $610,000. At six they are $970,000 and $688,000. Station six also displaces a separate activity worth $9,000. How much added benefit would make station six break even?
A police department considers one more patrol. Crime reduction is valued at $120,000, added payroll is $75,000, and the officers would forgo training worth $38,000. What is net marginal benefit?
Sequential grants have expected net benefits of $2.0m, $0.7m, -$0.4m and $0.6m. Each later grant requires all earlier grants. How many maximize total expected net benefit?
choices: Four grants, yielding $2.9m
Two grants, yielding $2.7m
Three grants, yielding $2.3m
One grant, yielding $2.0m

stem: A program's average benefit is 16 points per participant. The next participant adds 9 benefit points and 7 cost points; accommodating that participant also lowers benefits to existing participants by 3 points. What is the correct marginal decision?
choices: Reject; the overall incremental net benefit is -1 point
Accept; 9 exceeds the direct cost of 7
Reject solely because 9 is below the average of 16
Accept; a positive average establishes a positive marginal gain

stem: A plant's prepaid lease is unchanged. An extra order earns $760 and needs $490 in materials and $140 in overtime. It also occupies capacity that could earn $160 net on another order. What minimum price increase makes accepting it break even?
A utility considers one more conservation rebate. Expected energy savings are $130, rebate administration costs $90, and customer hassle is valued at $45. What is the social decision?
choices: Do not offer it because marginal social cost is $135
Offer it because administrative cost is below savings
Offer it because total energy savings remain positive
Do not offer it because rebates are transfers

stem: A campaign has already spent $400,000. A final placement costs $60,000 and yields additional revenue of $100,000 if it succeeds, otherwise zero. With no other effects, which success probability makes the placement break even?
choices: A probability above 100% because past spending must be recovered

stem: An emergency agency can pre-position one more team. Expected response benefit is $500,000, deployment costs $320,000, and the team’s best alternative assignment is worth $210,000. What should it do?
choices: Do not deploy because relevant marginal cost is $530,000
Deploy because direct cost is below expected benefit
Deploy because emergency benefits are not monetary
Do not deploy because prior readiness spending is sunk

stem: At 12 trips a route has total benefits of 840 points and costs of 610. At 13 trips these become 892 and 655. At 14 they become 930 and 699. With no later trips available, which expansion from 12 is best?
choices: Add one trip; the two increments net +7 and -6 points
Add two trips because total benefit still exceeds total cost
Add neither because both trips raise total cost
Add two trips because 14 trips has the highest total benefit

stem: A farm’s next fertilizer application raises crop value by $1,100, costs $760, and increases expected water cleanup by $390. Which statement is correct?
choices: Do not apply because marginal social cost exceeds benefit by $50
Apply because private marginal profit is $340
Apply because total crop revenue is positive
Do not apply because fertilizer cost is sunk

stem: A university pilot has spent $6 million. Extending it costs $900,000 and yields $1.1 million in expected benefit, while ending now requires $250,000 in transition cost. What is best?
choices: Extend because its future net gain exceeds the cost of ending
End because total spending is already too high
Extend only to avoid wasting the $6 million
End because transition cost is less than extension cost

stem: A city adds park lighting in blocks. Marginal benefits are 100, 82, 61, and 40; private costs are 55 each, but marginal light-pollution costs are 10, 18, 25, and 32. How many blocks should be lit?
choices: Two blocks
One block
Three blocks
Four blocks

stem: A nonprofit is considering one more meal-delivery route. The route would generate $900 in attributable donations, cost $620 for food and fuel, and use volunteer time that would otherwise provide tutoring worth $310. Should the nonprofit add the route?
choices: Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $930
Add it because direct cost is below donations
Add it because volunteer time is unpaid
Do not add it because total program costs are high

stem: An inspection costs $70,000 and prevents $500,000 in repairs if it finds a defect in time, otherwise saving nothing. It displaces work worth $20,000. What detection probability makes the inspection break even?
A data center’s next cooling upgrade saves $140,000 in expected outages, costs $100,000, and uses technicians who could complete security work worth $50,000. What should it do?
choices: Do not upgrade because relevant marginal cost is $150,000
Upgrade because outage savings exceed direct cost
Upgrade because technicians are already salaried
Do not upgrade because total cooling spending is high

stem: A school intervention’s next class has gross benefit 44 points, delivery cost 30, and teacher fatigue cost 9. A later class would yield gross benefit 50 but requires this class first. What should the school do now?
choices: Deliver the next class because its net marginal benefit is 5
Skip to the later class because its gross benefit is higher
Stop because combined cost is positive
Deliver only if average class benefit rises

stem: A city can buy sensors sequentially. Direct MBs are 90, 72, 50 and 31; MCs are 40, 60, 55 and 48. A linked alert system worth 25 becomes feasible only with at least three sensors and costs no more. Which number maximizes total net benefit?
choices: Three: totals are 50, 62, 82 and 65 for one through four sensors.
Two: the third direct MB is below MC, so any linked benefit must be excluded.
Four: four sensors have the largest total direct benefit regardless of incremental cost.
One: its individual net benefit is largest, so later positive gains should be ignored.

stem: A project has spent $5 million irreversibly. Finishing costs $900,000 and yields $1 million. Canceling costs $180,000. Selling the project as-is brings $350,000 but requires $120,000 of transfer work and avoids cancellation fees. Which choice is best?
choices: Sell: its $230,000 future net value exceeds finishing’s $100,000 and canceling’s -$180,000.
Finish: the $1 million receipt is the largest, and the sunk investment should be recovered before considering a sale.
Cancel: its $180,000 outlay is below finishing cost, so the sale receipt should not affect the comparison.
Finish: the relevant sale alternative is $350,000 minus the entire $5 million already spent.

stem: A hospital can add a mobile unit with expected benefits of $700,000 and direct costs of $520,000. Its team would abandon prevention work worth $210,000. Hiring temporary prevention staff costs $140,000 and preserves all that work; no other constraints change. Which plan maximizes incremental benefit?
choices: Add the unit and hire temporary staff: net gain is $40,000, versus a $30,000 loss if prevention is displaced.
Do not add the unit: the $210,000 prevention value must be lost under every plan.
Add the unit without replacement: its $180,000 cash surplus establishes the largest social gain.
Add the unit and hire staff: net gain is $250,000 because preserved prevention is an extra benefit above the baseline.

stem: A manufacturer can hire a worker for one job that adds $1,400 in output. Wages are $980 and equipment costs $260 but can be resold for $100 after the job. The worker’s workstation could instead be rented out for $190 during the job. Which net contribution is relevant?
choices: $70: subtract wages, net equipment cost and forgone workstation rent.
$260: subtract wages and net equipment cost but ignore the owned workstation.
$160: subtract wages and the full equipment purchase but ignore resale and rent.
-$30: subtract wages, the full equipment purchase and rent, ignoring resale.

stem: A cleanup method yields $500 in health benefits, costs the operator $370 and damages habitat by $150. A gentler method gives the same health benefit, costs $430 and causes $20 of habitat damage. Which method is socially preferable, and what would an operator ignoring habitat costs choose?
choices: Society prefers the gentler method ($50 net); the operator prefers the original ($130 private net versus $70).
Society prefers the original ($130 net); the operator prefers the gentler method because its habitat damage is lower.
Both prefer the original because its cash cost is lower and habitat losses are transfers between users.
Both reject cleanup because the original method’s $520 social cost proves every available method has negative net benefit.

stem: A preventable failure has a 25% probability and would cost $800,000. Prevention costs $170,000 and eliminates the loss. A perfect test costs $20,000 and permits prevention only when failure would otherwise occur. For a risk-neutral decision maker, which strategy has the lowest expected cost?
choices: Test then prevent if needed: $62,500, versus $170,000 for unconditional prevention and $200,000 for no action.
Prevent unconditionally: $170,000, versus $220,000 for testing because testing cannot change the failure probability.
Take no action: $0, because a 25% possible loss is not a current cash outlay.
Test then prevent if needed: $190,000, because prevention must be paid even after a negative test.

stem: Total benefit rises from $140 to $158 when a fifth unit is added, while total cost rises from $92 to $107. What is the fifth unit’s net marginal benefit?
A warehouse’s average handling cost is $9 per box, but the next box costs $13 to handle and creates $15 in margin. What should it do?
choices: Handle it because $15 exceeds the $13 marginal cost
Reject it because marginal cost exceeds average cost
Handle it only if average cost falls below $9
Reject it because total handling cost rises

stem: A firm can run up to four ads. Their marginal benefits are $90, $70, $45, and $20; each ad costs $50. How many ads should run?
choices: Two ads
One ad
Three ads
Four ads

stem: A project has an unrecoverable $8,000 design cost. Finishing costs $3,000 and yields $4,200; cancellation costs $400. Which comparison is relevant?
choices: Finish for a $1,200 future gain versus paying $400 to cancel
Compare the full $11,000 spending with $4,200 revenue
Finish only to recover the $8,000 design cost
Cancel because any remaining cost is harmful

stem: A sixth quality inspection lowers expected defect losses by $260 and costs $210 in labor. What is the correct next-step decision?
choices: Perform it because avoided loss is a marginal benefit above cost
Skip it because inspection creates a positive labor cost
Perform it only if total defect losses become zero
Skip it unless average inspection cost falls

stem: One more worker adds $620 in output but requires $480 in wages and $90 in added equipment use. What is the worker’s net marginal contribution?
Total benefit is 50 and average benefit is 10. One more unit raises total benefit to 57. What is marginal benefit?
Marginal cost is $12 and marginal benefit is $17. What should happen?
choices: Take the next unit because benefit exceeds cost
Stop because the unit has a positive cost
Add $12 and $17 before deciding
Use average cost instead of marginal cost

stem: Which value is average rather than marginal?
choices: Total cost divided by all units produced
The change in cost from one more unit
The benefit added by the next unit
A future cost avoided by stopping now

stem: A $100 fee is refundable if a project stops today. Is it sunk for today’s decision?
choices: No, because stopping can still recover it
Yes, because it was paid in the past
Yes, because every prior payment is sunk
No, because future costs can never matter

stem: One more sale brings $30 in revenue and requires $22 in added cost. What is net marginal benefit?
Scarcity forces a student to choose between work and study. How can a higher wage create an incentive?
choices: It raises the opportunity cost of study relative to work
It eliminates the need to choose between uses of time
It guarantees the student stops studying
It changes scarcity into abundance

stem: A fee makes one more downtown trip costlier. How does marginal analysis describe the incentive?
choices: It raises the marginal cost of the next trip
It raises the total benefit of every past trip
It guarantees no one travels downtown
It removes the opportunity cost of alternatives

stem: When a product’s price rises, buyers purchase less while sellers offer more. What common connection explains both responses?
choices: The price change creates different incentives for buyers and sellers
Buyers and sellers face identical benefits from the higher price
The higher price guarantees every buyer exits the market
Supply and demand responses require moral approval of the price

stem: A policy aims to reduce congestion but rewards agencies only for bus tickets sold. What problem can this funding rule create?
choices: The rewarded measure may redirect behavior away from the stated policy objective
Announcing a goal automatically determines how agencies respond to the reward
Ticket sales are identical to reduced congestion
An incentive exists only after congestion falls

stem: A library begins charging a late fee. What response becomes more likely?
choices: More borrowers return books on time
Every borrower returns every book early
Borrowers view late returns as more rewarding
The fee guarantees that no book is ever late

stem: A school offers preferred event seating to students with strong attendance. What kind of payoff changed?
choices: A nonmonetary benefit of attending school
The cash wage paid for attending school
The legal penalty for missing school
The final attendance outcome itself

stem: A city adds a refundable deposit to beverage bottles. Which choice identifies the incentive?
choices: Recovering the deposit by returning the bottle
The number of bottles ultimately recycled
Public support for cleaner streets
A guarantee that every bottle is returned

stem: A sales representative earns a commission on each completed sale. What does the commission directly do?
choices: Raises the benefit of completing another sale
Guarantees that every customer will buy
Makes product quality irrelevant to buyers
Removes the representative’s opportunity costs

stem: An insurer raises the copay for an optional clinic visit. Holding other factors fixed, patients are most likely to:
choices: Become less likely to schedule the visit
Schedule every optional visit immediately
Ignore the copay because costs are not incentives
Treat the copay as a reward for using care

stem: A shop offers free shipping only on orders above $50. Which behavior does the threshold encourage?
choices: Adding items to bring some orders above $50
Reducing every order below $50
Buying exactly the same basket in every case
Avoiding online shopping regardless of preferences

stem: A store offers a one-day discount on umbrellas before a storm. What response is most directly predicted?
choices: Some customers become more likely to buy that day
Every shopper buys an umbrella
The discount guarantees the store earns more profit
Customers must morally approve of discounts

stem: A nonprofit grant rewards providers for placing clients in jobs that last at least 30 days. Providers avoid applicants needing intensive support and favor easy placements. Which redesign would reward successful placements without encouraging providers to avoid clients who need more support?
choices: Reward sustained outcomes while adjusting targets for client difficulty
Pay only for the raw number of 30-day placements
Remove all performance information from funding decisions
Assume selection disappears when providers share the mission

stem: An energy plan combines a peak-hour surcharge, a monthly conservation badge, and a rebate for smart thermostats. Which analysis is strongest?
choices: The surcharge targets peak timing, the badge targets status, and the rebate changes equipment cost; responses depend on constraints.
The surcharge and badge both reward lower total use, while the rebate leaves the cost of conservation equipment unchanged.
The rebate targets peak timing, the surcharge targets equipment purchase, and the badge reveals each household’s willingness to pay.
The three measures all lower the same marginal electricity price, so peak-use changes identify their separate contributions.

stem: A hospital bonus rewards low average treatment cost. Managers discharge patients earlier, but readmissions rise. Which redesign best aligns the incentive with patient outcomes?
choices: Include readmissions and health outcomes alongside treatment cost
Increase the reward for low initial cost alone
Judge success only by the number of discharges
Remove monitoring because outcomes vary across patients

stem: A fine rises from $100 to $500 while the actual probability of detection falls from 80% to 10%. Drivers are risk neutral and understand those probabilities. Reform C instead keeps the $500 fine and restores detection to 20%. Which comparison of expected penalties is correct?
choices: The initial change lowers expected penalty from $80 to $50; C raises it to $100, strengthening deterrence relative to both earlier rules.
The initial change raises expected penalty from $80 to $500; C lowers it to $100 because more detection reduces risk.
The initial change leaves expected penalty at $80; C leaves it unchanged because headline fines determine all deterrence.
The initial change lowers expected penalty from $100 to $50; C restores it only if every violator is detected.

stem: A university funds departments for graduates employed within 30 days. Programs steer students toward quick-placement jobs and away from longer searches for better matches. What is the central design problem?
choices: The measured deadline rewards placement speed rather than match quality
Employment funding cannot influence advising behavior
Quick placement guarantees the best long-run outcome
The stated career goal prevents any unintended response

stem: A conservation policy combines a usage fee, public recognition, and exemptions for medical needs. Which assessment is most defensible?
choices: Different households face different effective incentives, so response and burden will vary
The usage fee guarantees identical reductions for all households
Recognition is irrelevant because it is not money
Exemptions prove the policy has no behavioral effect

stem: A hospital is paid for each procedure but penalized for readmissions. Which response best reflects both incentives?
choices: It may increase profitable procedures while investing in follow-up that lowers readmissions
It must reduce every procedure because penalties dominate rewards
It will ignore follow-up entirely because only direct procedure payments can ever affect hospital behavior
The payment design guarantees the socially optimal treatment mix

stem: A school rewards high test pass rates. Administrators shift tutoring toward students just below the cutoff and away from students far behind. What is the strongest interpretation?
choices: A threshold metric changes where effort has the highest measured payoff
The reward guarantees equal gains for every student
Tutoring shifts prove the pass-rate reward was not an incentive
The stated goal determines behavior more than the measured target

stem: An environmental fee applies only when emissions exceed a monthly cap. A factory shifts production between months to remain below the cap without lowering annual emissions. What happened?
choices: The threshold changed timing rather than the underlying annual outcome
The fee created no incentive because annual emissions stayed constant
Any legal response must satisfy the policy’s broader objective
A fee cannot affect production timing

stem: An office awards contracts to the lowest bidder but later faces frequent requests for costly changes to the work. How could it change its selection rule to address this incentive problem?
choices: Evaluate expected total cost and performance, not the opening bid alone
Raise the reward for submitting any low opening bid regardless of later changes to the work
Ignore later requests for changes because the opening bid was lower
Require every bidder to choose the same production method

stem: A deductible rises from $100 to $1,000. Which prediction is best without knowing patient income, health risk, or alternatives?
choices: Use of covered services tends to fall, but response size can vary widely
Every patient reduces covered care by exactly the same percentage after the deductible change
No response is possible because insurance already exists
The higher deductible guarantees better health decisions

stem: A police department rewards citation counts. Citations rise, public trust falls, and serious-case work receives less time. Which conclusion is warranted?
choices: The metric changed behavior but did not capture the department’s full objective
Falling trust proves the citation reward cannot influence officer behavior or case priorities in any meaningful way
More citations establish that public safety necessarily improved
Economic analysis requires moral approval of the reward

stem: A teacher bonus depends on class-average scores. Teachers provide extra review but also discourage low-performing students from testing. What should an evaluator conclude?
choices: Higher scores may reflect both extra instruction and changed test participation; compare learning for the original student group.
Higher scores measure extra instruction if bonuses are uniform; excluding weak students then represents improved classroom efficiency.
Changed participation fully explains higher scores; extra review has no independent effect once selection incentives exist.
Average scores remain comparable across years if the test is unchanged; student participation changes affect only the sample size.

stem: A university receives funding for degrees completed on time. Advising improves, but difficult required courses are weakened. What is the strongest interpretation?
choices: Funding rewards completion speed, so advising effort and lower course standards can both improve the metric without equal learning gains.
Funding rewards educational quality, so faster completion and easier courses jointly establish more learning per enrolled student.
Easier courses explain completion gains entirely, so advising improvements cannot contribute to the measured funding outcome.
Faster completion reduces students’ time costs, so course standards have no additional role in evaluating the policy’s net benefit.

stem: A congestion charge is announced, but drivers believe cameras identify only 5% of violators. Which factor most limits deterrence?
choices: The low perceived probability of paying the charge
The charge is negative rather than positive
Driving has benefits as well as costs
A legal charge cannot change expected costs

stem: A health insurer waives copays for preventive visits but raises emergency-room copays. Which response is most defensible?
choices: Lower preventive prices and higher emergency prices encourage substitution, but access and urgent needs constrain which patients can switch.
The price changes chiefly reduce total visits; patients with limited preventive access can substitute as readily as other patients.
The preventive subsidy raises income rather than relative prices; changes in emergency use therefore identify only the copay increase.
Emergency use should fall most for unavoidable acute cases; elective preventive care is least responsive to the lower copay.

stem: A city pays restaurants for each kilogram of food donated. Donations rise, but some restaurants overproduce near closing time. What does this show?
choices: The payment rewards donated kilograms, so it can induce both recovery of surplus food and production that would not otherwise occur.
The payment rewards avoided waste, so additional production confirms that previously wasted food has been redirected efficiently.
Overproduction indicates stronger final-consumer demand; donated kilograms are therefore unrelated to the payment’s production incentive.
Donations transfer food between users, so extra production costs cancel from welfare whenever recipients value the donated meals.

stem: A housing program withdraws $1 of aid for each $1 of additional earnings over a threshold. Which behavioral pressure follows?
choices: Earning just above the threshold may provide little immediate net gain
Every recipient stops working completely
The rule rewards every additional dollar of earnings with an equal dollar of net income
Aid withdrawal is an outcome rather than an incentive

stem: A credit card offers triple points for travel. One customer travels more; another keeps the same trips and switches cards. What is the lesson?
choices: The same reward can change how much one customer travels and which card another uses
Only the customer who travels more responded to the incentive
A reward is ineffective unless total travel rises for everyone
Card switching cannot be an incentive response

stem: A factory posts team safety rankings without cash prizes. Reporting rises, but some teams relabel minor incidents as near misses. Which conclusion is best?
choices: Status rewards can change reporting and relabeling; independently measured injuries are needed to identify real safety improvement.
Higher reporting shows actual injuries increased; relabeling minor cases changes only terminology and not the measured ranking.
Relabeling improves risk classification; higher ranking positions therefore identify better safety even without independent injury data.
Noncash status rewards mainly reveal team preferences; higher reported safety establishes that effort rose equally across teams.

stem: A charity matches the first $100 of each donation. A donor planning to give $300 still gives $300. How should the match be evaluated for that donor?
choices: It transfers funds but does not change this donor’s marginal giving decision
It necessarily causes an additional $100 donation
The donor did not face an incentive because the entire planned gift amount was chosen before the match
The match reduces the benefit of donating

stem: A platform threatens suspension for false listings, but enforcement reviews only complaints from paying users. What response is most plausible?
choices: Expected sanctions differ by customer group, so sellers may redirect deception toward users whose complaints do not trigger review.
A uniform suspension penalty creates equal deterrence across users, so different complaint review rules mainly affect paperwork.
Paying users receive more review, so sellers face a stronger incentive to deceive them in order to cover expected sanctions.
The threat discourages entry by dishonest sellers, so surviving sellers’ choices between user groups are unaffected by enforcement.

stem: A government contract pays builders for finishing early and penalizes visible defects, but not hidden maintenance problems. What risk remains?
choices: Rewards cover speed and observable defects, so effort can shift from hidden durability toward the measured dimensions.
The defect penalty prices all quality losses, so earlier completion also establishes greater hidden durability.
The speed reward and defect penalty create opposing incentives, so their combined effect on effort must be zero.
Maintenance is paid later, so hidden durability is a sunk cost and should be excluded from evaluating the contract.

stem: A farm subsidy pays per acre planted with one crop. Farmers expand acreage onto less suitable land. Which part is the incentive and which is the response?
choices: Per-acre payment is the incentive; expansion onto marginal land is a response
Expanded acreage is the incentive; payment is the outcome
Crop suitability is the incentive; planting is moral approval
The subsidy is neither because planting was already possible

stem: An employer replaces a late-arrival reprimand with a small fee deducted from pay. Some workers become more punctual; others treat lateness as a purchasable option. What does this show?
choices: The fee changes both the monetary consequence and its perceived social meaning, allowing deterrence for some and purchased lateness for others.
The fee lowers the monetary cost for every worker, so mixed punctuality must reflect differences in measured arrival times.
The fee strengthens social disapproval for every worker, so treating lateness as purchased shows workers no longer respond to payoffs.
The fee converts lateness into a market transaction, so workers’ prior response to social reprimands is irrelevant to the change.

stem: A transit agency offers off-peak discounts. Flexible riders shift trips, while shift workers cannot. Which evaluation is strongest?
choices: The price incentive changes trip timing mainly for riders with feasible alternatives
The discount is not an incentive because some riders cannot respond
All riders receive identical benefits from changing travel time
The policy guarantees total ridership will rise

stem: A streaming service removes a cancellation fee but adds a loyalty reward after twelve months. Which decision does the rule most directly influence?
choices: Whether subscribers stay through the twelfth month
The quality of every program on the service
The certainty that all subscribers remain
Subscribers’ moral judgment of loyalty programs

stem: A warranty pays repair shops a flat amount per claim. Shops begin avoiding complex claims and completing simple ones quickly. What caused the pattern?
choices: A uniform payment changes the payoff differently for low-cost and high-cost claims
The flat payment guarantees equal service across claims
Avoiding difficult cases proves payments cannot affect selection
Claim complexity is irrelevant whenever prices are fixed

stem: A sports contract pays a large bonus for games played. An injured athlete returns early and performs poorly. Which conclusion is most defensible?
choices: The bonus increased pressure to play but did not guarantee a beneficial outcome
The poor performance proves the bonus was not an incentive
Bonuses influence effort but never participation decisions
Playing establishes that the athlete approved of the contract design

stem: A nonprofit grant rewards the number of people enrolled, not services completed. Enrollment rises and completion falls. Which measure is being optimized?
choices: The funded enrollment count rather than the broader service objective
Completion because it is the organization’s stated mission
Both measures equally because they concern the same clients
Neither measure because nonprofits do not respond to funding

stem: A delivery platform guarantees a minimum hourly payment only while drivers are actively carrying orders. Which response is plausible?
choices: Drivers may favor longer trips or avoid unpaid waiting when choosing orders
Every driver accepts the shortest available trip
The guarantee removes all opportunity costs of time
Payment rules cannot change which orders drivers select

stem: A city raises water prices after a monthly allowance and also publishes neighborhood conservation rankings. What response should be expected?
choices: Price and status pressures may reduce use by different amounts across households
The ranking is irrelevant because only prices are incentives
Every household cuts water use by the same quantity
Lower use is guaranteed wherever both incentives exist

stem: A criminal fine is tripled while the probability of detection falls by two-thirds. Without more information, what can be concluded?
choices: Expected monetary penalties are unchanged, while perceived detection and risk attitudes can still alter deterrence.
Expected monetary penalties triple, while lower detection only changes the timing of the payment.
Expected monetary penalties fall by two-thirds, while the larger fine affects only the maximum possible loss.
Expected monetary penalties are unchanged, so deterrence must remain unchanged for every risk attitude.

stem: A news site pays writers for clicks, excluding later subscriptions. A sensational headline yields 10,000 more clicks than a sober version and $200 more advertising revenue, but is expected to lose renewals worth $350. Writers expect higher pay from the sensational headline. Which diagnosis and redesign fit?
choices: The metric rewards a privately attractive choice that lowers expected site revenue by $150; include retention-adjusted value rather than clicks alone.
The extra clicks raise site revenue by $200 net of renewals; retain the click metric because readers revealed stronger demand.
The lost renewals show writers ignored the incentive; raise the click rate to align their choices with longer-run subscriptions.
The headline lowers site revenue by $550; replace performance pay with a renewal count that ignores advertising value.

stem: Two households each use 10 peak-hour energy units. A $5 surcharge per unit leads a flexible household to shift 6 units off peak, but a household using continuous medical equipment cannot shift any. A proposed $50 lump-sum credit is independent of peak use. Which evaluation is correct?
choices: The surcharge cuts combined peak use by 6 units; the credit relieves bills but preserves the $5 marginal incentive and does not remove the medical constraint.
The surcharge cuts combined peak use by 10 units; the credit removes the $5 marginal incentive for both households.
The surcharge cuts combined peak use by 6 units; a $50 credit necessarily restores the flexible household’s original peak usage.
The surcharge has no incentive effect on the medical household; its unchanged use proves it bears no additional economic cost.

stem: A firm can gain $900 from violating a rule. Detection is currently 10% and the fine is $4,000. Reform A doubles the fine; reform B raises detection to 30% with the original fine. For a risk-neutral firm maximizing expected monetary payoff, which reform deters the violation?
choices: Only B: A leaves a $100 expected gain, while B creates a $300 expected loss.
Only A: A creates a $3,100 expected loss, while B leaves a $600 expected gain.
Both: either a larger fine or more inspection necessarily makes expected violation payoff negative.
Neither: the $900 benefit exceeds the detection probability under both reforms.

stem: A salesperson earns $200 per completed sale but repays it if the product is returned. A risky sale has a 50% return probability and takes effort worth $80. A suitable sale has a 10% return probability and takes effort worth $120. Which choice maximizes expected net commission, and what if chargebacks are removed?
choices: With chargebacks choose suitable ($60 versus $20); without them choose risky ($120 versus $80).
With chargebacks choose risky ($120 versus $80); without them choose suitable ($60 versus $20).
Choose risky under both rules because the headline commission is the same and its effort cost is lower.
Choose suitable under both rules because a lower return probability always outweighs any difference in effort.

stem: Two jobs have identical duties and working hours. On-site work pays $900 weekly but requires $80 travel spending and 8 travel hours valued at $15 each. Remote work pays $760 with no commute. Which job has the higher net weekly value, and what if travel time falls to 2 hours?
choices: Remote leads by $60 initially; after the shorter commute on-site leads by $30.
On-site leads by $140 initially; after the shorter commute it still leads by $140.
Remote leads by $20 initially; after the shorter commute on-site leads by $90.
Remote leads by $60 initially; after the shorter commute it still leads by $60.

stem: A clinic receives $20 per reported vaccination. Reports rise from 1,000 to 1,300. An independent audit finds 200 duplicate entries and 1,100 distinct vaccinations; comparable unfunded clinics’ distinct vaccinations rose 5%. If the same trend would have applied, which estimate and incentive diagnosis are strongest?
choices: About 50 distinct vaccinations above the 1,050 counterfactual; paying for verified unique patients would reduce rewards for duplicate records.
About 300 distinct vaccinations above baseline; paying for verified unique patients would remove the incentive for useful outreach.
About 100 distinct vaccinations caused by funding; the comparison clinics are irrelevant once an audit verifies the total.
About 250 distinct vaccinations above the counterfactual; duplicate entries are a transfer and should be counted as health benefits.

stem: A warehouse pays a bonus for packages shipped per hour but charges workers for verified damage. What response is most plausible?
choices: Workers balance speed against the expected cost of damage
Workers maximize speed because only rewards affect behavior
Damage must fall to zero for the incentives to exist
Every worker chooses the same speed regardless of risk

stem: A parking fine doubles, but patrols become rare. Why might violations change little?
choices: The expected penalty may remain small because enforcement is unlikely
A larger statutory fine can never affect behavior when drivers know it exists
Drivers respond only to rewards, not penalties
Low enforcement guarantees more violations by every driver

stem: Two employees receive the same attendance bonus. One changes her schedule; the other has caregiving duties and cannot. What does this show?
choices: The same incentive can produce different responses under different constraints
The bonus was not an incentive for either employee because their outcomes differed
A valid incentive must change everyone’s behavior
Constraints matter only when incentives are nonmonetary

stem: A delivery app rewards drivers for accepting a high share of requests. Some drivers accept deliveries they are unlikely to complete and cancel later. What problem does this reveal?
choices: The reward encourages drivers to improve their acceptance rating by taking requests they later cancel
The reward cannot be an incentive because cancellations rose after accepted jobs
Acceptance rate measures service quality perfectly
The response proves drivers ignored the metric

stem: A company offers either a $40 bonus or public recognition for completing training. Some workers value one more than the other. What follows?
choices: Monetary and nonmonetary incentives can differ in strength across people
Only the cash option can change expected benefits
Recognition guarantees completion among all workers
Different preferences mean neither option is an incentive

stem: A gym charges a missed-appointment fee but waives it when members cancel a day ahead. Which decision does the rule most directly influence?
choices: Whether members cancel early instead of simply not appearing
Whether every member continues the gym membership
Whether exercise produces health benefits
Whether members morally approve of cancellation rules

stem: A call center rewards short calls and separately penalizes repeat complaints. How should agents respond?
choices: Balance speed against the risk that poor service triggers repeat complaints
Make every call as short as possible because rewards dominate penalties
