Ignore both rules unless all agents respond identically
Guarantee perfect service because two incentives are present

stem: A $500 attendance bonus is offered, but an employee misses work during a medical emergency. Was the bonus still an incentive?
choices: Yes; it changed the payoff but did not guarantee attendance
No; an incentive exists only when it changes the observed behavior in every single case
No; bonuses must overcome every constraint
Yes; it guaranteed attendance for all other workers

stem: An economist says a fine creates an incentive to avoid an action. Does that statement approve of the fine?
choices: No; identifying a changed cost is separate from moral approval
Yes; economic analysis always endorses any incentive whose likely response it successfully predicts
Yes; only approved penalties affect behavior
No; fines are outcomes rather than incentives

stem: Can two people respond differently to the same parking fee?
choices: Yes; constraints, preferences, and alternatives can differ
No; the same dollar fee produces the same response
Only if one person misunderstands the fee
No; different responses mean the fee is not an incentive

stem: A school gives public recognition rather than cash for attendance. Can recognition be an incentive?
choices: Yes; nonmonetary benefits can change behavior
No; only money changes benefits or costs
Only if recognition has a fixed cash value
No; recognition is the final policy outcome

stem: A large fine is almost never enforced. Why may it have little effect?
choices: The expected consequence is weak when detection is very unlikely
Penalties cannot be incentives
The fine guarantees compliance even when detection and enforcement are extremely unlikely
Only the stated policy goal influences behavior

stem: With the same amount of labor, North can produce 8 baskets or 4 blankets, while South can produce 6 baskets or 6 blankets. Assuming constant tradeoffs, which specialization follows comparative advantage?
choices: North: blankets; South: baskets.
North: baskets; South: blankets.
North: both goods; South: neither.
South: both goods; North: neither.

stem: How does a PPF help identify comparative advantage?
choices: Its tradeoff reveals opportunity cost
Its size alone identifies advantage
It removes the need to compare alternatives
It proves every trade beneficial

stem: For one additional solar panel, Arlo gives up 2 batteries and Bela gives up 4 batteries. Tradeoffs are constant. Arlo can make more units of either product per hour. Which specialization follows comparative advantage?
choices: Arlo: both products; Bela: neither.
Arlo: batteries; Bela: panels.
Arlo: panels; Bela: batteries.
Bela: both products; Arlo: neither.

stem: Why can terms of trade connect specialization to mutual gain?
choices: A rate between costs can let both sides save resources
Any trading rate guarantees equal gains to both sides.
The rate erases tradeoffs
Only a boundary rate makes both better off

stem: Ana gives up 2 baskets to make one table; Bo gives up 5 baskets. Who has comparative advantage in tables?
choices: Ana, because she gives up fewer baskets
Bo, because he gives up more baskets
Ana only if she makes more of both goods
Neither, because money prices are missing

stem: One worker can finish more of both tasks than a coworker. Why might the coworker still specialize in one task?
choices: The coworker may have the lower opportunity cost in that task
The faster worker should perform both tasks because they produce more of each.
Comparative advantage requires equal productivity
Specialization removes every tradeoff

stem: Priya gives up 1 design to write a report; Luis gives up 4 designs. If they specialize by comparative advantage, who writes reports?
choices: Priya, because her opportunity cost is lower
Luis, because his opportunity cost is higher
Both must split report writing equally
Whoever has the higher total output in both tasks

stem: Why can specialization according to comparative advantage expand what two producers can consume?
choices: It can increase combined production available for exchange
It guarantees each producer can make every good more efficiently.
It makes opportunity costs identical
It removes scarcity from both producers

stem: A baker makes more bread and cakes than a helper. What must be known before assigning both tasks?
choices: Their opportunity costs for bread and cakes
Only the baker’s total output in both goods.
The price of imported flour
Whether the helper likes cake

stem: Nia gives up 2 posters per video; Omar gives up 5. Who should specialize in videos?
choices: Nia, because her opportunity cost is lower
Omar, because he gives up more posters per video.
Both, because gains must be equal
Neither, because totals are missing

stem: A can make 12 X or 24 Y and B can make 10 X or 10 Y. After full specialization, B sends A 4 X for 6 Y. A previously consumed 4 X and 12 Y. What is A's gain?
choices: The same 4 X and 6 additional Y
Four additional X and the same Y
Six additional X and 4 additional Y
No gain because A exports output

stem: C can make 16 cloth or 8 wine; D can make 6 cloth or 12 wine. They fully specialize, and C trades 4 cloth for 4 wine. Before trade, C consumed 12 cloth and 2 wine while D consumed 2 cloth and 8 wine. What are the gains?
choices: C gains 2 wine; D gains 2 cloth
C gains 4 wine; D gains 4 cloth
C gains 2 cloth; D gains 2 wine
Each gains 2 units of both goods

stem: East can make 12 drones or 18 radios per day; West can make 6 drones or 24 radios. Costs are constant. West offers 1.5 radios per drone, then raises its offer to 2.5. Ignoring exchange costs, which evaluation is correct?
choices: East exports drones; the first offer leaves East indifferent, while the second gives East 1 radio and West 1.5 radios of gain per drone.
West exports drones; the first offer leaves West indifferent, while the second gives West 1 radio and East 1.5 radios of gain per drone.
East exports drones; both offers give strict gains, and the second divides 2.5 radios of gain equally between the two producers.
East exports drones; the first offer benefits both, while the second makes West lose because the rate exceeds East’s opportunity cost.

stem: A can make 12 machines or 24 tools; B can make 6 machines or 12 tools. After training, B can make 6 machines or 24 tools with the same resources. With constant costs, what changes in the case for specialization?
choices: Initially costs are equal; after training A has machine advantage, B has tool advantage, and a rate between 2 and 4 tools per machine can benefit both.
Initially A has both advantages; after training B has both advantages, and any positive tools-per-machine rate can benefit both.
Initially costs are equal; after training B has machine advantage, A has tool advantage, and a rate between 2 and 4 tools per machine can benefit both.
Initially costs are equal; after training costs remain equal because B’s machine capacity is unchanged, so no strict mutual-gain interval appears.

stem: River can produce 18 X or 6 Y; Hill can produce 12 X or 8 Y. What is each producer’s opportunity cost of one unit of Y, measured in units of X?
choices: River: 3 X; Hill: 1.5 X
River: one-third X; Hill: two-thirds X
River: 12 X; Hill: 18 X
River: 2 X; Hill: 3 X

stem: North can make 20 chips or 10 sensors; South can make 12 chips or 12 sensors. A technology change lets North make 40 sensors with unchanged chip capacity. What changes?
choices: North gains comparative advantage in sensors and South in chips
North keeps comparative advantage in chips because its chip output is unchanged
South gains comparative advantage in both goods
Equal opportunity costs eliminate specialization

stem: Ava’s cost of one crate is 2 sacks; Ben’s is 5 sacks. At exactly 2 sacks per crate, which statement is correct?
choices: Ava is indifferent and Ben can gain from buying the crate
Both receive strict gains from the trade.
Ben is indifferent and Ava captures every gain
The rate lies strictly between their opportunity costs

stem: One bolt costs East 0.5 panel and West 1.25 panels. What range of trading prices, measured in panels per bolt, makes both producers better off than producing the goods themselves? Exclude prices at which either producer only breaks even.
choices: More than 0.5 but less than 1.25 panels per bolt
More than 2 but less than 4 bolts per panel.
At least 0.5 and at most 1.25 panels per bolt
Less than 0.5 panels per bolt only

stem: A consultant completes more audits and presentations than an associate. A manager concludes the consultant should do both. What is missing?
choices: The opportunity cost of assigning the consultant to each task
Only the consultant’s total output in both tasks.
A guarantee that specialization divides gains equally
The money price of international exports

stem: Specialization raises combined output, but a proposed exchange rate lies above both producers’ costs for the exported good. What follows?
choices: Higher output creates potential gains, but this rate will not benefit both sides
Every feasible exchange must share the production gain.
The higher-cost producer now has comparative advantage
Both sides are strictly better off because specialization occurred

stem: A workshop's cost of a motor is 2 batteries; its trading partner's is 5. The workshop exports motors and pays 1 battery in shipping per motor. Measured in motors per battery, what range of trading prices makes both partners better off after shipping costs? Exclude break-even prices.
choices: Between 1/5 and 1/3 motor per battery
Between 1/5 and 1/2 motor per battery
Between 3 and 5 motors per battery
Between 1/3 and 1/2 motor per battery

stem: After specializing, a workshop has 30 panels. It can trade panels for motors at 3 panels per motor. Its former bundle was 16 panels and 3 motors. Which integer trade leaves it with strictly more of both goods?
choices: Trade 12 panels for 4 motors
Trade 9 panels for 3 motors
Trade 15 panels for 5 motors
Trade 6 panels for 2 motors

stem: North specializes at 24 fish and South at 12 nets. North trades 8 fish for 4 nets. Their autarky bundles were North 12 fish and 3 nets, South 6 fish and 6 nets. What are their gains?
choices: North gains 4 fish and 1 net; South gains 2 fish and 2 nets
North gains 8 fish and 4 nets; South gains 8 fish and 4 nets
North gains 4 fish and 4 nets; South gains 2 fish and 6 nets
North gains 12 fish and 1 net; South gains 2 fish and 2 nets

stem: One printer costs X 3 scanners and Y 7 scanners. X exports a printer at a quoted price of 6 scanners but Y must also use 2 scanners for shipping. What would make both strictly better off?
choices: A quoted price strictly between 3 and 5 scanners
Any quoted price strictly between 3 and 7 scanners
The existing price of 6 because it is below Y's domestic cost
A price of 7 because it exactly matches Y's production cost

stem: Specialization yields 14 extra units. Under one exchange, Metro gains 10 units while Harbor gains 4. Which conclusion is accurate?
choices: Both gain, but the terms divide the gain unequally
Unequal gains mean Harbor cannot benefit.
Each side must gain 7 units
Only Metro has comparative advantage

stem: At constant tradeoffs, Oak can make 24 racks or 8 desks; Pine can make 18 racks or 9 desks. Oak adopts a tool that raises its desk maximum to 16 without changing racks. Which conclusion follows?
choices: Oak switches to comparative advantage in desks; a 1.75-rack desk price can then benefit both
Pine retains desk advantage because its rack maximum is lower
Oak has comparative advantage in both goods because both maxima exceed Pine's
The old 2.5-rack desk price still gives Oak strict gains when it imports desks

stem: With constant tradeoffs, Ridge can make 24 maps or 12 models. Vale can make 18 maps or m models. Ridge exports models at 1.5 maps each and claims both gain strictly. Which value of m makes the claim consistent?
choices: No positive m; Ridge loses at the stated export price
m = 6; Vale's higher cost suffices for mutual gains
m = 9; matching costs makes this price mutually beneficial
m = 18; Vale's higher model productivity guarantees mutual gains

stem: Coast’s opportunity cost of one unit of cocoa is 3 units of tea; Ridge’s is 6 units of tea. What range of trading prices, measured in units of cocoa per unit of tea, makes both producers better off? Exclude break-even prices.
choices: More than one-sixth and less than one-third
More than one-third and less than one-sixth
More than 3 and less than 6
At least one-sixth and at most one-third

stem: Two labs each sacrifice 4 tests for one prototype at constant tradeoffs. One lab doubles its maximum output of both goods. What changes in the pure comparative-advantage model?
choices: Its capacity rises, but equal opportunity costs still leave no strict specialization gains at any common price
It gains comparative advantage in both goods because both maxima double
A price of 4 tests now gives both a strict gain on each prototype
Doubling capacity halves its opportunity cost of a prototype

stem: Specialization creates a gross gain of 24 units of a common consumption good. Shipping uses 5 units and verification uses 7. The proposed division gives one party 15 units of gross gain and assigns it both costs. Does that party gain, and what net gain remains for the other?
choices: Yes, it gains 3 units; the other gains 9
Yes, it gains 15 units; the other gains 9
No, it loses 12 units; the other gains 24
Yes, both gain 12 units

stem: An engineer needs 2 hours per design and 1 hour per inspection. A technician needs 6 hours per design and 2 hours per inspection. They move one inspection from the engineer to the technician, who gives up one-third of a design. What net design capacity is freed?
choices: One-sixth of a design
One-half of a design
One-third of a design
Five-sixths of a design

stem: Mesa specializes at 30 meals and Bay at 15 repairs, then exchanges 10 meals for 5 repairs. A report says Mesa gains 5 meals and 1 repair, while Bay gains 2 meals and 3 repairs. Which pair of autarky bundles makes all four claims consistent?
choices: Mesa: 25 meals, 6 repairs; Bay: 12 meals, 13 repairs.
Mesa: 15 meals, 4 repairs; Bay: 8 meals, 7 repairs.
Mesa: 20 meals, 5 repairs; Bay: 10 meals, 10 repairs.
Mesa: 5 meals, 4 repairs; Bay: 8 meals, 2 repairs.

stem: One machine costs Alpha 2 kits and Beta 6 kits. Compare rates of 3 and 5 kits per machine. Which statement is true?
choices: Both work, but 5 shifts more modeled gain to Alpha
Only the 3-kit rate lies between the two opportunity costs.
Only the 5-kit rate is between costs
Both divide the gain equally

stem: A problem gives specialization output and a trading rate but no pre-trade consumption bundle. Can a unique numerical consumption gain be found?
choices: No; the autarky comparison is underdetermined
Yes; the trading rate determines the pre-trade consumption bundle.
Yes; combined output equals each gain
No; trade gains can never be measured

stem: A technology has increasing rather than constant opportunity cost. Which conclusion is supported?
choices: Both producers can gain through specialization without either specializing completely
Both producers must always specialize completely.
Opportunity cost becomes irrelevant after exchange
Absolute advantage fixes every output

stem: Combined consumption rises by 9 units, but one party gains 11 while the other loses 2. What is the correct evaluation?
choices: Aggregate gain exists, but the trade is not mutually beneficial
Both parties gain because their combined consumption increases.
The losing party has advantage in both goods
Each gain must be reset to 4.5

stem: Delta can make 24 files or 8 reviews; Echo can make 15 files or 10 reviews at constant tradeoffs. Delta doubles review productivity without changing files. A contract exchanges one review for 2 files. What changes?
choices: The cost difference disappears, and the old contract no longer gives both strict gains
Delta gains review advantage because 16 exceeds Echo's 10
Echo retains review advantage because 15 is below Delta's 24 files
Both now gain strictly at every price between 1.5 and 3 files

stem: A lens costs Urban 0.25 sensor and Rural 0.5 sensor. Urban proposes exporting lenses at 3 lenses per sensor, and pays shipping of 0.05 sensor per lens. Which assessment is correct?
choices: Both gain: Urban nets more than 0.25 sensor per lens and Rural pays less than 0.5
Urban loses because three is larger than both stated opportunity costs
Rural loses because the reciprocal price is above 0.5 sensor per lens
Both are indifferent because shipping makes the costs equal

stem: Lumen specializes at 32 lamps and Shade at 16 rugs. Their autarky bundles were Lumen (16 lamps, 4 rugs) and Shade (8 lamps, 8 rugs). Lumen now sends 18 lamps for 3 rugs, with no exchange costs. A planner says higher combined output proves both receive more of both goods. Which evaluation follows?
choices: The claim holds: Lumen gains 2 lamps and 1 rug; Shade gains 10 lamps and 5 rugs.
The claim fails: Lumen gains 2 lamps and 1 rug; Shade loses 10 lamps and 5 rugs.
The claim holds: each receives half of the combined increase of 8 lamps and 4 rugs.
The claim fails: Lumen loses 2 lamps and 1 rug; Shade gains 10 lamps and 5 rugs.

stem: Before specialization, two workshops jointly consume 18 frames and 10 cushions. Specialization produces 23 frames and 13 cushions; transport uses 2 cushions. Which claim follows before the remaining goods are divided?
choices: The available bundle rises by 5 frames and 1 cushion, but individual gains depend on the division
Both parties necessarily gain 5 frames and 1 cushion each
Net cushion gain is 3 because transport is separate from production
One party's loss is impossible whenever both aggregate quantities rise

stem: A static two-good model finds gains from specialization. Which conclusion goes beyond that result alone?
choices: Every long-run trade policy benefits every worker and industry
Lower opportunity cost identifies comparative advantage.
Terms inside the bounds can create mutual gains
Specialization can raise output under the assumptions

stem: Arbor specializes at 28 timber and Basin at 14 tools. Their autarky bundles were Arbor (14 timber, 3 tools) and Basin (6 timber, 7 tools). Basin offers 4 tools for t units of timber. With no exchange costs, which range of t gives each party strictly more of BOTH goods than in autarky?

Quartz can make 10 chips or 20 screens; Sable can make 4 chips or 20 screens. Costs are constant. Quartz exports chips and uses resources worth 0.5 screen per chip to arrange delivery. At 5 screens per chip, who strictly gains? If the rate falls to 4, what changes?
choices: At 5 only Quartz strictly gains; at 4 both gain, with Quartz gaining 1.5 screens and Sable saving 1 screen per chip.
At 5 both strictly gain; at 4 only Sable gains, because delivery raises Quartz’s opportunity cost to 4.5 screens per chip.
At 5 only Sable strictly gains; at 4 both gain, with Sable gaining 1.5 screens and Quartz saving 1 screen per chip.
At 5 neither strictly gains; at 4 Quartz loses 0.5 screen, because delivery costs must be added to Sable’s production cost.

stem: Cedar can make 30 boards or 10 doors; Dune can make 16 boards or 8 doors. A tool doubles Dune’s board capacity without changing door capacity. Costs are constant. A proposed contract keeps Dune exporting doors at 2.5 boards per door. Which revision follows?
choices: Reverse the specialization: Dune now exports boards, Cedar exports doors, and a rate strictly between 3 and 4 boards per door can benefit both.
Keep Dune exporting doors at 2.5 boards per door, because its door capacity and therefore its door opportunity cost are unchanged.
Reverse the specialization but retain 2.5 boards per door, because any rate above Dune’s original cost benefits both after the tool.
Stop specialization because Dune’s higher board output gives it absolute and comparative advantage in both goods.

stem: Orchid specializes at 36 flowers and Reed at 18 baskets. Autarky bundles were Orchid (18 flowers, 4 baskets) and Reed (9 flowers, 9 baskets). They exchange 12 flowers for 6 baskets. Carrier A consumes 1 of Orchid’s received baskets in transport; carrier B consumes 3. No other goods are lost. Which carrier leaves BOTH parties with strictly more of each good than in autarky?
choices: Both carriers: Orchid keeps 5 baskets with A and 7 with B.
Only carrier B: Orchid keeps 3 baskets with A and 5 with B.
Only carrier A: Orchid keeps 5 baskets with A and 3 with B.
Neither carrier: Orchid keeps 3 baskets with A and 1 with B.

stem: Haven gives up 3 grain per turbine and Isle 7. Haven exports turbines; Isle also uses resources worth 1 grain per imported turbine to transport them. Compare offers of 4 and 6 grain per turbine. Which contract strictly benefits both after transport?
choices: Only 4 does: Haven gains 1 and Isle gains 2 grain; at 6 Isle is indifferent after transport.
Both do: Haven gains more at 6, while Isle still gains 1 grain because transport does not enter comparative cost.
Only 6 does: Haven gains 3 and Isle gains 1 grain; at 4 Haven is indifferent after transport.
Neither does: the transport cost makes every rate between production opportunity costs unprofitable for the importer.

stem: Peak specializes at 40 services and Glen at 20 devices. Autarky bundles were Peak (20 services, 6 devices) and Glen (10 services, 10 devices). Proposal A exchanges 16 services for 8 devices; B exchanges 22 services for 8 devices. Each party prefers more of either good when the other is unchanged; no other preferences or costs are given. Which assessment is justified?
choices: A gives both more of both goods; B gives Peak fewer services but more devices, leaving its welfare change undetermined.
B gives both more of both goods; A gives Glen fewer devices but more services, leaving its welfare change undetermined.
Both give both more of both goods; each party is better off without needing further preference information.
Neither gives either more of both goods; each party’s welfare change under both proposals remains undetermined.

stem: Team A can prepare 12 briefs or 6 charts daily. Team B can prepare 8 briefs or 8 charts. Who has comparative advantage in briefs?
choices: Team A; one brief costs 0.5 chart rather than 1 chart
Team B; it can make more charts.
Team A; it has comparative advantage in both outputs
Neither; their maximum outputs differ

stem: Kai needs 2 hours per cabinet and 1 hour per shelf. Ren needs 3 hours per cabinet and 3 hours per shelf. Who has comparative advantage in cabinets?
choices: Kai; a cabinet costs 2 shelves rather than Ren’s 1 shelf
Ren; a cabinet costs 1 shelf rather than Kai’s 2 shelves
Kai; fewer hours always means comparative advantage in both goods
Neither; hours per unit cannot reveal opportunity cost

stem: If one mug costs a studio 2 bowls, what is the opportunity cost of one bowl, measured in mugs?
choices: One-half mug
Two mugs.
Four mugs
One mug

stem: Farm C can grow 24 corn or 12 beans; Farm D can grow 10 corn or 10 beans. Which specialization follows comparative advantage?
choices: Farm C grows corn and Farm D grows beans
Farm C grows beans and Farm D grows corn
Both farms grow only corn
Neither farm can specialize without a money price

stem: One lamp costs Ari 2 rugs and costs Bea 6 rugs. Which rate for 1 lamp could provide strict gains to both?
choices: 4 rugs per lamp
2 rugs per lamp
6 rugs per lamp
8 rugs per lamp

stem: Two workshops each give up exactly 3 frames to produce one desk. What does the basic model imply?
choices: Neither has comparative advantage in desks based on these costs
The workshop with greater desk output must specialize in desks.
Both receive strict gains from any desk price
One workshop must have comparative advantage in both goods

stem: A can produce 16 apples or 8 pears; B can produce 9 apples or 9 pears. Who has comparative advantage in apples?
choices: A; one apple costs 0.5 pear
B; one apple costs 1 pear
A; it has advantage in both
Neither; only money costs count

stem: One file costs Town 3 reports and City 7 reports. Which rate can strictly benefit both?
choices: 5 reports per file
3 reports per file
7 reports per file
9 reports per file

stem: When two producers face different tradeoffs, which one holds comparative advantage in an activity?
choices: The producer with lower opportunity cost
The producer who gives up more
The producer with the highest wage
The producer who makes most of everything

stem: If one producer makes more of both goods, must that producer make both?
choices: No; specialization depends on relative opportunity costs
Yes; absolute advantage determines both assignments.
Yes; the slower producer should never produce
No; productivity data never matter

stem: If 1 X costs 2 Y, what is the cost of 1 Y?
choices: One-half X
Two X.
Four X
One X

stem: Does higher combined production make every proposed exchange beneficial?
choices: No; the trading terms still determine who gains
Yes; every exchange shares the additional output.
Yes; gains are always equal
No; specialization cannot raise output

stem: A trading rate equals one producer's opportunity cost. Is that producer strictly better off?
choices: No; that producer may be indifferent
Yes; every boundary rate gives strict gains
Yes; gains must be equal
No; both must be indifferent

stem: A policy forecast is testable, but the economist also recommends adoption. How should the forecast and recommendation be distinguished?
choices: Both are positive claims because the recommendation follows evidence
Positive analysis informs a separate normative choice
Both are normative because the topic is public policy
The forecast itself determines whether the policy should be adopted.

stem: A model’s conclusion depends on a particular assumption. What should an economist explain when using the model to advise policymakers?
choices: Report only the baseline result
Drop the assumption from the analysis
How the conclusion changes when the assumption changes
Delay all advice until the assumption can be proven true.

stem: A subsidy changes behavior beyond its intended target. Which economic idea helps explain these additional responses?
choices: Only the directly targeted behavior should be included in the analysis
Responses outside the target are irrelevant to the policy’s effects
Unintended responses occur only when enforcement fails.
Incentives can create unintended consequences

stem: An economist estimates how a bus fee changes ridership. What role is primary?
choices: Scientist analyzing a testable consequence
Adviser making a value judgment about whether the fee is fair
Policymaker deciding whether the fee should be adopted
Administrator responsible for enforcing the fee.

stem: An adviser compares costs borne by commuters and taxpayers. What should the adviser make explicit?
choices: The combined cost alone, without showing how it is divided between the two groups.
The costs each group bears and the tradeoffs between the policy alternatives.
The adviser’s preferred outcome alone, without showing the costs of other choices.
The taxpayers’ costs alone, without including the costs borne by commuters.

stem: Why can economics inform but not dictate a school policy?
choices: Economics cannot measure the effects of school policies
School policies have no economic tradeoffs
The final choice also depends on social values
Evidence cannot help identify the likely consequences of alternative policies.

stem: A forecast gives a range rather than one number. Why?
choices: The range identifies which policy society should prefer
A range means the evidence is too weak to be useful
Every value inside the range is equally likely.
Policy effects are uncertain, not guaranteed

stem: What can an economist contribute without choosing society’s values?
choices: Evidence about likely consequences
Choose society’s moral priorities
Decide which policy lawmakers must adopt
Guarantee that the chosen policy will succeed.

stem: A forecast gives a range of possible effects rather than a single estimate. What does the range acknowledge?
choices: The true effect is guaranteed to lie inside the range
Uncertainty in the predicted effect
The range identifies the policy society should prefer
Every value in the range is equally likely.

stem: A policy creates winners and losers. What should analysis show?
choices: Only the total effect on surplus
Only which groups lose
The distribution as well as the total effect
Ignore distribution whenever the aggregate effect is positive.

stem: Volunteers in a training pilot earn more later. A second study assigns training by lottery and finds little effect. Before recommending expansion, what should the adviser resolve?
choices: Whether volunteer enthusiasm proves the training caused their earnings
Whether the lottery result makes all participant preferences irrelevant
Whether selection explains the first result and whether the lottery setting fits expansion
Whether the larger positive estimate is easier to communicate

stem: Policy A creates $40 million of gains for high-income households and $10 million of losses for low-income households. Policy B creates $22 million of gains for low-income households and costs high-income households $5 million. With no other effects, which advice distinguishes efficiency from distribution?
choices: A has the larger unweighted net gain, while B favors low-income households; the ranking depends on the stated social criterion.
B has the larger unweighted net gain, while A favors low-income households; efficiency alone therefore selects B.
A has the larger unweighted net gain, so it necessarily satisfies a goal of improving low-income households’ welfare.
B favors low-income households, so A cannot have a positive unweighted net gain even if its benefits exceed losses.

stem: A subsidy model estimated that firms would add 100 jobs when credit was available at 5%. Credit is now rationed and borrowing costs 12%; the model still predicts 100 jobs because it treats financing as fixed. What is the best next analysis?
choices: Keep the 100-job forecast because the subsidy is unchanged; treat financing as an unrelated macroeconomic detail.
Reestimate firms’ financing responses and compare predictions under feasible credit conditions before transferring the old forecast.
Replace 100 jobs with the latest observed hiring total; that difference directly measures the subsidy’s causal effect.
Reject all subsidy models because one institutional change means simplified forecasts cannot provide policy evidence.

stem: Two advisers agree that a flood barrier yields $60 million in avoided damage, costs $35 million and relocates 200 households. One favors it; the other rejects involuntary relocation. Which further step would clarify rather than merely repeat their disagreement?
choices: Collect a more precise construction-cost estimate until both advisers must adopt the same view of relocation.
Add the number of relocated households directly to the dollar cost and select the policy with the smallest sum.
State the relocation criterion, examine feasible less-displacing alternatives and show how each changes net benefits and affected households.
Treat the shared positive net benefit as evidence that objections to relocation are errors in economic forecasting.

stem: A pilot worked elsewhere but institutions differ locally. What is the key warning?
choices: A successful pilot automatically generalizes to other settings
Institutional differences matter only for normative judgments
A large effect elsewhere guarantees a large local effect.
Evidence may not transfer to the new setting

stem: A model omits enforcement costs. What should the policy estimate do?
choices: Include feasible implementation and administration costs
Ignore enforcement costs if the policy objective is worthwhile
Count only the direct statutory cost of the program
Assume administration uses no scarce resources.

stem: An efficient proposal conflicts with a legal-rights goal. What follows?
choices: The efficient proposal must be adopted
Efficiency evidence does not uniquely decide social desirability
The legal-rights goal is irrelevant to policy evaluation
The conflict proves the proposal is economically inefficient.

stem: A recommendation changes under plausible assumptions. What should the economist do?
choices: Report only the baseline estimate
Use the assumption that produces the most favorable result
Report sensitivity rather than one certain answer
Delay all advice until uncertainty is eliminated.

stem: Two advisers accept the same estimate: consolidating offices saves staff time but lengthens rural travel. One favors consolidation and the other opposes it. Which information best explains their different recommendations?
choices: Which adviser used more decimal places in the shared estimate
Whether the two advisers agree that travel is measurable
Whether consolidation is being proposed by a public institution
How each weighs staff savings against rural access

stem: Two access plans have the same total measured benefit. One imposes concentrated losses on residents with few alternatives; the other spreads smaller losses. What additional step supports a defensible recommendation?
choices: Choose either plan because equal totals establish identical welfare for every resident
Increase numerical precision until one value criterion becomes unnecessary
Count only beneficiaries because costs are already reflected in the total
State how concentrated hardship is weighed, and show each plan's distribution

stem: A permit reform saves time for compliant firms but increases inspections. It has positive net benefit at high compliance and negative net benefit at low compliance. Local compliance is unmeasured. What advice is best supported?
choices: Present the conditional ranking and seek local compliance evidence before a firm recommendation
Recommend adoption because the favorable scenario is feasible
Reject because one plausible scenario has losses
Average the two outcomes without assessing how likely each is

stem: A school schedule saves paid staff hours but shifts supervision to families. The measured gain disappears when family time is valued at its next-best use. Which revision follows?
choices: Treat the original cash saving as false because the wider net gain disappeared
Report the wider resource comparison and explain why a budget saving need not be a social gain
Keep the original conclusion because only paid hours use scarce resources
Count the family time twice, once as cost and once as a separate loss of the same activity

stem: An adviser reports a narrow forecast interval based on one assumed take-up rate. Credible alternative take-up rates reverse the recommendation. What uncertainty is missing?
choices: A value judgment proving which take-up rate is true
Evidence that no economic forecast can ever inform a choice
Uncertainty about the behavioral assumption, beyond precision conditional on that assumption
Only rounding uncertainty in the reported forecast

stem: Two policy models fit the pilot. One attributes improved attendance to transport; the other to reminders sent at the same time. The rollout can fund only one. What evidence most directly helps the adviser choose?
choices: A larger pilot that always combines both services
The political popularity of the combined pilot as proof of causality
The pilot's total attendance without a breakdown of interventions
Comparable groups receiving transport alone and reminders alone

stem: An economist identifies the schedule with the highest total measured benefit. Citizens prefer another because it guarantees a minimum service level to every district. Which advice respects both roles?
choices: Explain the cost of the service guarantee and make the ranking criterion explicit
Treat the citizens' preference as a statistical error in the benefit estimate
Describe the maximizing schedule as morally required by the calculation
Alter the benefit numbers until both schedules receive the same ranking

stem: A small pilot pays shops to repair items and records strong gains. Nationwide adoption induces shops to relabel routine maintenance as repairs. What should a follow-up evaluation change?
choices: Infer zero genuine gains solely because some reporting changed
Measure additional genuine repairs and account for the changed reporting incentive
Use reimbursement counts unchanged because the pilot already validated the measure
Treat all repairs after adoption as caused by the payment

stem: A proposed tax is projected to create $80 million in national efficiency gains but $50 million in losses concentrated in one region. Those regional losses are already included in the national estimate. A domestic transfer could offset them at $8 million of administrative cost, but the regional loss estimate is uncertain. Which advice is sound?
choices: Net expected national gain after administration is $72 million; test regional-loss scenarios and compensation feasibility before making a distributional recommendation.
Net expected national gain after compensation is $22 million; subtract the regional losses again because concentration makes them additional costs.
Net expected national gain after compensation is $122 million; add the transfer because recipients experience it as a benefit.
Net expected national gain is $80 million under every scenario; positive national gains guarantee each region can implement compensation itself.

stem: Model A predicts a transit subsidy raises ridership mainly by attracting former drivers. Model B predicts the same total increase mainly by shifting riders from unsubsidized buses. Both fit current totals. The policy goal is fewer car trips. What evidence best discriminates between the models for this decision?
choices: Collect more precise total ridership counts after the subsidy; equal predictions imply either model establishes equal car-trip reductions.
Track prior travel modes and changes against a credible untreated comparison; total ridership fit alone cannot identify car-trip displacement.
Choose A because its mechanism matches the goal; a policy-relevant mechanism needs no separate test once totals fit.
Average the predicted ridership increases; averaging identical totals also identifies how many riders switched from cars.

stem: A school policy has estimated net benefits of $12 million and reduces access for rural pupils. An alternative yields $8 million and preserves access. The adopted charter requires preserving rural access unless no feasible alternative exists. What conclusion follows from the estimates and criterion together?
choices: The first policy must satisfy the charter because its larger net benefit proves no economically feasible alternative exists.
The alternative’s access benefit proves its unweighted net benefit exceeds $12 million even though the estimate is $8 million.
The first policy leads on unweighted net benefits, but the feasible alternative satisfies the stated access constraint; surplus alone does not justify overriding it.
Neither estimate is positive analysis because the access constraint makes factual policy comparisons inherently normative.

stem: A safety rule would prevent $10 million of harm with full compliance and require $4 million of compliance resources. Current enforcement induces only half the affected firms to comply; assume benefits and compliance costs scale proportionally. An extra $1 million enforcement program would raise compliance to 80%. Which assessment is correct?
choices: Net benefit rises from $3 million to $4.8 million; enforcement spending is a transfer and should not reduce the gain.
Net benefit falls from $6 million to $3.8 million; compare actual enforcement with the original full-compliance forecast.
Net benefit stays $6 million; the legal rule fixes compliance benefits regardless of enforcement behavior.
Net benefit rises from $3 million to $3.8 million; the extra enforcement gains $0.8 million despite falling short of full compliance.

stem: Two economists use different demand estimates. What can explain different forecasts?
choices: Different scientific judgments about evidence
One economist must have made an arithmetic mistake
Different forecasts can only come from different value judgments
Empirical disagreements cannot be informed by additional evidence.

stem: Two advisers agree on a policy’s predicted effects but place different weight on equity. What explains their disagreement?
choices: Their estimates of the policy’s effects
Their normative values
Their definitions of the economic variables
One adviser must have interpreted the data incorrectly.

stem: A policy raises total surplus but harms one region. What should analysis report?
choices: Only the increase in total surplus
Only the regional loss, because any loser makes the policy inefficient
Efficiency and distribution separately
A single efficiency conclusion without reporting who gains and loses.

stem: A rule changes incentives in an unexpected way. What should advisers examine?
choices: Only the response the rule was intended to create
Treat unexpected behavior as irrelevant to the policy analysis
Assume the original behavioral prediction remains correct.
Likely behavioral responses and unintended effects

stem: Economists disagree because one trusts a different study. What differs?
choices: Their scientific judgment about evidence
Their normative values must differ
One economist must be irrational
Evidence becomes irrelevant once economists disagree.

stem: Two economists agree on a policy’s effects but place different weight on fairness when judging the policy. What explains their different recommendations?
choices: Their scientific forecasts
Their normative evaluation
One economist must have misread the data
Economic analysis cannot distinguish factual claims from value judgments.

stem: Why examine enforcement before recommending a rule?
choices: Enforcement affects legality but not economic outcomes
Assume full compliance when evaluating a proposed rule
Implementation changes costs and behavior
Implementation costs are irrelevant before adoption.

stem: Can economists scientifically determine society’s values?
choices: Yes; economic expertise identifies the morally best outcome
Yes; estimating consequences also determines which values society should hold
No; they can clarify consequences and tradeoffs
Yes; economists receive decision-making authority from their technical expertise.

stem: Does efficiency prove a policy is socially best?
choices: Yes; efficiency incorporates every social objective
Yes; distribution does not matter when total surplus rises
Yes; economists can rank competing social values scientifically.
No; other values and distribution may matter

stem: Is a policy forecast a guarantee?
choices: No; it depends on evidence and assumptions
Yes, if the forecast comes from a strong model
Yes, if the confidence interval is narrow
Yes, if the economist has no conflict of interest.

stem: Must disagreement between economists reflect different political views?
choices: Yes; all disagreement among economists is ideological
No; evidence, models, or values can differ
Yes; economists working in the same field would otherwise reach the same conclusion
Yes; empirical evidence cannot produce different interpretations.

stem: Limited resources force a city to choose projects. Which ideas connect?
choices: The concepts are related only because they share vocabulary
No causal or tradeoff connection is required
Scarcity creates an opportunity cost equal to the best forgone project
Opportunity cost is unrelated to scarcity once the city has chosen a project.

stem: A bonus changes effort until added benefit no longer exceeds added cost. Which ideas connect?
choices: No causal or tradeoff connection is required
Incentives determine behavior without any need to compare marginal benefits and costs.
The concepts are related only because they share vocabulary
Incentives alter behavior evaluated at the margin

stem: A PPF shows a lower opportunity cost for one producer. What follows?
choices: Comparative advantage can guide specialization and trade
The lower-opportunity-cost producer should avoid specialization because both producers can trade.
The concepts are related only because they share vocabulary
No causal or tradeoff connection is required

stem: A pollution rule is predicted to cut emissions but raise bills and is recommended as fair. What must be combined?
choices: Once the rule reduces emissions, no further economic analysis is needed.
Market-failure logic, positive evidence, and normative policy judgment
The concepts are related only because they share vocabulary
No causal or tradeoff connection is required

stem: A scenario mentions scarcity and opportunity cost. What makes analysis integrated?
choices: It uses scarcity to identify the forgone next-best alternative
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis

stem: A policy changes incentives and marginal benefits. What reasoning is required?
choices: Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Compare the changed marginal benefit and cost created by incentives
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis

stem: A PPF move is described. What connection should be made?
choices: Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
The slope or tradeoff reveals opportunity cost
Simply repeat both vocabulary words

stem: A market failure is identified. What policy step remains?
choices: Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Compare feasible remedies and their tradeoffs

stem: A policy claim mixes prediction and advice. What should be separated?
choices: The positive effect claim and normative recommendation
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis

stem: Two producers specialize. What completes the reasoning?
choices: Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Compare opportunity costs and feasible terms of trade
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis

stem: Pollution changes a firm’s private marginal choice. What connection matters?
choices: The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
Marginal analysis can compare private and social cost
The outcome is a public good by definition
A large firm merely changes its own cost

stem: A public-good rule changes incentives to contribute. What connection matters?
choices: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
It is rival with fully enforceable private access
Free-riding incentives can reduce voluntary provision
It is a private good supplied by government

stem: A policy addresses hidden quality but is costly to administer. What should advisers do?
choices: Administrative incentives and information do not matter
Any intervention is automatically costless
Identifying failure proves one remedy is optimal
Compare information gains with implementation tradeoffs

stem: A neighbor bears smoke from a restaurant exhaust fan. What feature identifies an externality?
choices: The outcome is a public good by definition
A third party bears a cost outside the transaction
A large firm merely changes its own cost
The effect falls only on the buyer and seller

stem: A storm-warning signal can serve another listener without reducing its value and nonpayers are hard to exclude. What is it?
choices: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
It is a private good supplied by government
A public good
It is nonrival but easy to exclude

stem: A seller can profitably influence price by restricting output. What concern appears?
choices: A negative externality imposed on third parties
A public-good free-rider problem
A common-resource overuse problem.
Market power

stem: A subsidy addresses a spillover but attracts costly gaming. What follows?
choices: Any intervention that targets a spillover is automatically costless.
Identifying failure proves one remedy is optimal
Correcting one failure can create implementation costs and distortions
Administrative incentives and information do not matter

stem: A monopoly also pollutes. Why separate the mechanisms?
choices: Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
A high price by itself establishes market failure
The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
Output restriction and third-party harm imply different wedges

stem: A crop price rises after a drought reduces harvests. A separate processing plant also discharges unpriced waste into a river. Which diagnosis and targeted response distinguish scarcity from market failure?
choices: The crop price can signal genuine scarcity; a policy aimed at the waste should target its external cost rather than treating the high price alone as proof of failure.
Both are market failures solely because prices and waste increased, so a price ceiling necessarily corrects both.
Neither can be market failure because any outcome with a market price is efficient.
The drought is asymmetric information and the waste is merely a transfer between buyers and sellers.

stem: Buyers cannot observe product risk before purchase. Mandatory disclosure accurately reports it, but only in a format most buyers cannot interpret. A simplified tested label helps buyers compare risks at lower reading cost. Which comparison is defensible?
choices: Accurate disclosure necessarily eliminates the problem regardless of comprehension, so testing the label adds no information.
Both address an information problem, but the tested label can improve usable information more effectively; accuracy alone does not establish that the first format changes decisions.
The unreadable format solves an externality while the label creates monopoly power.
Neither addresses market failure because information costs cannot affect mutually beneficial trades.

stem: A corrective policy would prevent $120 of external harm while using $35 of compliance resources and $100 of administrative resources. A simpler policy prevents $80 of harm and uses $20 in total resources. Which recommendation follows from these estimates alone?
choices: The full policy is preferable because it prevents more harm, regardless of implementation cost.
Both policies are equally desirable because each reduces a market failure.
The full policy has net benefit −$15 and the simpler policy +$60; the simpler remedy is preferable to both the full policy and doing nothing.
Doing nothing is preferable because any administrative cost makes intervention inefficient.

stem: A product is expensive because its inputs are scarce. Is that alone market failure?
choices: No; high cost alone does not identify an efficiency wedge
The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
A high price by itself establishes market failure

stem: A city dislikes unequal restaurant access. What must be shown for textbook market failure?
choices: Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
A mechanism causing private incentives to diverge from social efficiency
A high price by itself establishes market failure
The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified

stem: A lake is rival in use but access is difficult to restrict. Which problem fits?
choices: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
It is a private good supplied by government
A common-resource overuse problem
It is nonrival but easy to exclude

stem: An insurer cannot observe customers’ risk types before pricing. What issue fits?
choices: Both sides possess the same relevant information
The problem is only that future outcomes are uncertain
A spillover harms an unrelated third party
Asymmetric information may distort participation

stem: A navigation app is nonrival after creation but can exclude unpaid users. What is the best conclusion?
choices: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
It is a private good supplied by government
It is nonrival but easy to exclude
It is not a pure public good because exclusion is feasible

stem: A fishery uses quotas, but regulators cannot observe illegal catch. What complicates the remedy?
choices: Enforcement and information constraints affect performance
Any intervention is automatically costless
Identifying failure proves one remedy is optimal
Administrative incentives and information do not matter

stem: A hospital knows treatment quality better than patients. What broad failure may arise?
choices: Both sides possess the same relevant information
Relevant information is asymmetric across the transaction
The problem is only that future outcomes are uncertain
A spillover harms an unrelated third party

stem: A festival can run late, end early, or run late with sound insulation. Relative to ending early, running late adds $1,000 of gains to attendees and organizers and $1,400 of resident harm. Insulation costs $600 and reduces that harm to $200. Ignore bargaining costs. Which arrangement maximizes net gains, and what remains to be negotiated?
choices: End early; all late operation has negative social value even with insulation.
Run late without insulation; the $1,000 private gain establishes efficiency.
Run late with insulation; divide its $200 net gain through compensation.
Run late with insulation; resident compensation itself adds another $200 of social benefit.

stem: An exclusive right lets an innovator charge above marginal cost. Removing it would expand current access but could reduce future investment in similar products. Which evidence is needed before claiming removal raises welfare?
choices: Only the current markup, because all markups equal net profit and total social loss.
Only the innovator’s revenue, because consumer gains are transfers that cannot affect welfare.
Only the number of new buyers, because future incentives are unrelated to exclusive rights.
Gains from additional current trades and the size of any resulting loss of valuable future innovation.

stem: A poor neighborhood lacks groceries because operating costs are high. Why is failure not automatic?
choices: Undesirability alone does not prove an efficiency wedge
The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
A high price by itself establishes market failure

stem: A health agency observes that a vaccine subsidy increases vaccinations but an unrelated change also reduces exposure to infection. Which additional evidence is needed to judge whether the subsidy improves efficiency?
choices: Only the subsidy budget, because larger transfers imply larger social gains.
The marginal spillover benefit at the new quantity, the real cost of extra doses, and policy implementation costs.
Only the number of new doses, because each added dose must be efficient.
Only recipients’ private willingness to pay, because the outside benefit is already in every purchase.

stem: An open-access aquifer is depleted. What private-social divergence occurs?
choices: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
It is rival with fully enforceable private access
Each user ignores depletion costs shared by others
It is a private good supplied by government

stem: A used-device seller knows battery quality that buyers cannot see. What can follow?
choices: A spillover harms an unrelated third party
Both sides possess the same relevant information
The problem is only that future outcomes are uncertain
Hidden quality can drive better devices from the market

stem: A platform has market power and users create privacy spillovers. What is the best diagnosis?
choices: Separate the output distortion from third-party privacy costs
A high price by itself establishes market failure
The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency

stem: A nonrival, nonexcludable water-quality alert system would generate $12,000 in total benefits and cost $8,000 to operate. Individual fee collection would cost $5,000; a binding cooperative funding agreement would cost $1,000. Both could fund the same service. Which evaluation is correct if there are no other effects?
choices: Individual collection creates $4,000 of net gains because collection uses no resources.
The cooperative creates $3,000 of net gains; individual collection costs exceed the $4,000 operating surplus.
Both methods create $12,000 of net gains because users benefit whether or not they pay.
Neither can work because a private agreement cannot finance a nonexcludable service.

stem: A disclosure rule is forecast to prevent $90 of harm at $20 resource cost. A pilot finds that confusion causes $35 of additional harm and that only $50 of the original harm is actually prevented. A simpler label prevents $40 at $10 cost with no added confusion. Which comparison uses the observed performance?
choices: The original rule has +$70 net benefit because forecasts should replace contradictory pilot evidence.
The original rule has +$30 net benefit because confusion is only a transfer, making it equivalent to the simpler label.
The original rule has net benefit −$5, while the simpler label has +$30; revise the policy despite its initially plausible mechanism.
Neither can be compared because any information rule guarantees an efficient outcome.

stem: A fishery’s paper quota is strict, but hidden catches make actual harvest high. A feasible alternative combines verified landing reports with transferable catch rights. What evidence would establish that this alternative improves net social benefit?
choices: The new quota is numerically smaller, regardless of hidden catches or enforcement costs.
Quota holders receive valuable rights, so their transfer income equals the total welfare gain.
Trading occurs frequently, so actual harvest must equal the legally allowed total.
Reduced depletion losses exceed added monitoring and adjustment costs, while transfers permit lower-cost compliance.

stem: A market maximizes measured total surplus but distributes it unequally; no externality, information gap, market power or public-good problem is identified. Policy A transfers $30 between participants without resource cost or changed behavior. Policy B makes the same transfer but destroys $8 of gains through changed allocation. Which assessment is correct?
choices: Inequality motivates a separate equity judgment; A preserves measured surplus while B trades $8 of it for the same intended redistribution.
Both policies correct a demonstrated efficiency failure because any unequal outcome is inefficient.
B must be more efficient because changing allocation proves it addresses a market failure.
A raises total surplus by $30 while B raises it by $22 because transfers are new resources.

stem: Why may a busy road be overused when access is free?
choices: Drivers share congestion costs imposed on one another
The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
The outcome is a public good by definition
A large firm merely changes its own cost

stem: Why may a privately funded flood barrier receive too little support?
choices: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
People can benefit without paying
It is rival with fully enforceable private access
It is a private good supplied by government

stem: Why can hidden borrower risk reduce lending to reliable applicants?
choices: A spillover harms an unrelated third party
Both sides possess the same relevant information
Lenders lack information borrowers possess
The problem is only that future outcomes are uncertain

stem: A dominant platform blocks entry and reduces trades. What is the core concern?
choices: Blocking entry makes the platform nonexcludable
Reducing trades creates a public-good free-rider problem
The platform’s size by itself proves a negative externality.
Market power can keep quantity below the efficient level

stem: Is every undesirable outcome a market failure?
choices: The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
No; a specific efficiency mechanism must be identified
A high price by itself establishes market failure

stem: Does inequality alone define market failure?
choices: The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
A high price by itself establishes market failure
No; distribution and efficiency are distinct questions

stem: What makes an effect an externality?
choices: It spills onto a third party outside the transaction
The outcome is a public good by definition
A large firm merely changes its own cost
The effect falls only on the buyer and seller

stem: How does market power differ from an externality?
choices: Market power requires a third-party spillover outside the transaction
It influences market terms rather than imposing a third-party spillover
Market power makes the good nonrival and nonexcludable
Market power occurs only when income is distributed unequally.

stem: Does finding market failure prove any intervention is better?
choices: Any intervention is automatically costless
Identifying failure proves one remedy is optimal
No; feasible remedies also have costs and limits
Administrative incentives and information do not matter

stem: With full resource use and constant tradeoffs, an economy can make 100 food units or 50 medical units. Medical-only technology doubles maximum medical output, leaving maximum food unchanged. At 60 food, compare feasible medical output before and after; then assess an observed rise from an interior point to the old frontier.
choices: Medical capacity rises from 20 to 50; every output increase from an interior point proves the whole frontier shifted equally.
Medical capacity stays 20 because food technology is unchanged; only a move to a new point on the old line is possible.
Medical capacity rises from 40 to 80; an interior-to-frontier move reduces efficiency because fewer resources remain idle.
Medical capacity at 60 food rises from 20 to 40; the separate interior-to-old-frontier move is improved utilization, not evidence of that technology shift.

stem: An economy initially produces 60 units of each good inside a frontier that permits 80 of each together. Reemploying idle labor reaches 80 of each. New machinery then permits 100 of each together. A planner attributes the entire increase to growth in productive capacity. Which counterfactual best exposes the error?
choices: Without new machinery, reemployment could still reach 80 of each; only the later extension beyond the old feasible set demonstrates added capacity.
Without reemployment, machinery could not affect the frontier, because a frontier is defined by actual rather than possible output.
Without new machinery, output must remain at 60 of each, because any increase in both goods requires an outward frontier shift.
Without reemployment, the old frontier would automatically move inward to the observed 60-unit bundle.

stem: Is a point inside the PPF unattainable?
choices: Yes; any point not on the frontier is unattainable
Yes; only points on the PPF are feasible
Yes; producing inside the frontier requires more resources than the economy has.
No; it is attainable but inefficient

stem: Does moving along a PPF represent economic growth?
choices: No; it reallocates production on the same frontier
Yes; any movement to a different production mix is economic growth
Yes; producing more of one good means productive capacity has increased
Yes; moving along the frontier shifts it outward.

stem: What shifts a PPF outward?
choices: Moving from one point to another on the existing frontier
More resources, better technology, or improved productive capacity
Reallocating idle resources without changing productive capacity
Producing more of one good by giving up some of the other.

stem: Why can opportunity cost rise along a bowed-out PPF?
choices: Because the money price of the expanding good rises
Because the economy becomes less efficient as it moves along the frontier
Resources differ in suitability across uses
Because scarcity disappears for the good produced in larger quantities.

stem: An economist predicts job losses and recommends against a rule. What additional judgment turns the prediction into policy advice?
choices: The existence of a measurable employment effect
The fact that the rule is a government policy
The recommendation adds a value judgment about the predicted cost
The use of an economic forecast.

stem: A model predicts a tax effect under stated assumptions. Why is it positive?
choices: Because the prediction supports the tax
Because the model is written in technical language
Because the prediction must be true if the assumptions are stated.
Evidence could test the conditional prediction

stem: A library reports that Sunday hours increased visits. What makes this positive?
choices: The increase in visits is a desirable outcome
Library officials support Sunday hours
The report is written confidently, so the claim must be true.
Visit records could test the claimed increase

stem: “The library should stay open Sundays because access matters.” Why is this normative?
choices: It recommends a choice using a value judgment
Sunday visits can be counted
The statement concerns a public institution
Evidence could show whether Sunday hours increase attendance.

stem: A forecast that later proves false can still be positive when:
choices: The forecast was made by an expert
Evidence could in principle have tested it
The forecast described an outcome people wanted
The forecast was stated with certainty.

stem: Which claim is normative in a school debate?
choices: Average class size fell by two students last year
Smaller classes increased per-student spending
The district ought to favor smaller classes despite higher costs
Enrollment is projected to rise next year.

stem: Which claim is positive in a transit debate?
choices: The city should make transit more affordable
Lower fares are fairer to low-income riders
Expanding transit access is more important than balancing the transit budget.
A lower fare increased weekday ridership

stem: A report defines success only as maximum total surplus. What choice is normative?
choices: Calculating total surplus from observed prices and quantities
Selecting total surplus as the sole ranking criterion
Measuring how total surplus changes after the policy
Estimating the policy’s effect on output.

stem: Two analysts agree that an archive plan preserves more records but delays public access. One recommends it; the other rejects it. What additional finding would show a factual disagreement as well as a value disagreement?
choices: They agree on the delay but differ on whether it is acceptable
They use the same probabilities but prefer different distributions of access
They assign different probabilities to permanent record loss under the alternative
They give different ethical priority to immediate public access

stem: A report predicts gains and calls them worth unequal losses. What is normative?
choices: The judgment that gains justify the losses
The prediction that the policy creates gains
The estimated size of the gains
The measured distribution of gains and losses.

stem: What best tests “a fee reduces congestion”?
choices: A survey asking whether residents support the fee
Traffic counts before and after comparable changes
A council vote to adopt the fee
A statement from officials that congestion will fall.

stem: Why is “Policy A is responsible” not automatically positive?
choices: The statement mentions a policy
The word responsible refers to a measurable outcome
Responsible may hide an unstated value standard
Any sentence about policy performance is positive.

stem: A subsidy is predicted to raise enrollment and is therefore recommended. Which split is correct?
choices: Both parts are positive because enrollment can be measured
Both parts are normative because a subsidy is a policy
The forecast is positive; the recommendation is normative
The forecast is normative; the recommendation is positive.

stem: “The policy benefits most residents, so it is just.” Where is the normative step?
choices: The claim that most residents benefit
The number of residents affected by the policy
The measured size of the benefits.
Calling the distribution just

stem: What could test the claim that a road fee reduces congestion?
choices: Traffic counts around comparable fee changes
A survey asking whether drivers think the fee is fair
A city council vote on the fee
A statement from officials that the fee will work.

stem: When can “the project has positive net benefits” be positive?
choices: Always, because net benefits are measured in dollars
When inputs and the net-benefit rule are empirically checkable
Never, because the word benefits is inherently normative
